Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following statements best describes what is meant by a 'project'?
o: A temporary endeavour undertaken to deliver a defined and unique output
An ongoing operation undertaken to sustain routine business functions
A continuous process undertaken to provide day-to-day customer support
A permanent department established to deliver repeatable services
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is a unique, transient endeavour with a defined beginning and end, undertaken to deliver specified objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a project?
o: An objective to deliver a unique output
A permanent team structure that continues indefinitely
A temporary nature, disbanding once objectives are met
A defined start point and a defined end point
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Projects are staffed by temporary teams assembled for the objective and disbanded on completion, so a permanent structure is not a project characteristic.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates work that would be classified as a project?
o: Answering routine user queries on a support helpdesk each day
Processing the organisation's payroll at the end of every month
Maintaining a client's existing software system throughout the year
Implementing a new customer relationship management system over six months
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A time-bounded initiative delivering a unique output, such as a new CRM system, is a project; the others are ongoing, repeatable business-as-usual tasks.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project is undertaken to deliver an output. How is that output most accurately described?
o: A permanent departmental responsibility
A sustained operational service function
A defined product, service or result
An adaptable ongoing support mechanism
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: APM describes a project's output as a defined product, service or result achieved within agreed constraints.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why is the temporary nature of a project important to the way it is managed?
o: It ensures defined objectives are delivered within a bounded time frame
It removes the need for any stakeholder involvement during delivery
It guarantees the team can immediately be reused on other work
It aligns all delivery activity strictly to the financial year
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Being time-bounded focuses the project on achieving its specific objectives within defined constraints rather than continuing indefinitely.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new appraisal system must be handed to HR within six weeks. What best distinguishes this project from HR's business-as-usual work?
o: The HR department holds greater control over the project budget
The project has a defined end date and delivers a unique output
The project exists to support HR's routine daily operations
The project is concerned only with engaging its stakeholders
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project delivers a one-off output within defined constraints and then closes, whereas HR's ongoing work is repeatable business-as-usual.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is most characteristic of business-as-usual rather than of project work?
o: Producing a unique output using temporarily assigned resources
Delivering a defined scope within a fixed time frame
Delivering repetitive tasks and services on a continuous basis
Following a phased life cycle to achieve set objectives
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Business-as-usual maintains ongoing, repeatable services and functions, unlike the unique, time-bounded outputs of a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement most accurately expresses the difference between a project and business-as-usual?
o: Business-as-usual has a defined end point, while projects continue indefinitely
Projects are delivered by a permanent team, while business-as-usual is not
Projects deliver defined change, while business-as-usual sustains current operations
Business-as-usual delivers unique outputs, while projects avoid any change
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Projects create change and specific deliverables, whereas business-as-usual keeps existing services running.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A finance team updates spreadsheets and processes invoices every day. How should this work most appropriately be classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves regular, repeatable tasks
Business-as-usual, because it has a sponsor and a budget
A project, because it is constrained by time and cost
A project, because it is carried out by a skilled team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Regular, repeatable work that maintains an ongoing service is business-as-usual, not a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A company produces a one-off prototype for a client using a new design method. How is this effort correctly classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves routine manufacturing
A project, because it is a unique activity with defined outcomes
A project, because it forms part of regular production
Business-as-usual, because the client places orders frequently
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Creating a unique prototype with defined outputs is a time-bounded, one-off endeavour, which makes it a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement best defines project management as understood within the APM Body of Knowledge?
o: The application of processes, methods and knowledge to achieve defined project objectives
The routine monitoring of daily operational activities within a permanent department
The forecasting of resource requirements across the whole organisation each year
The assignment of repetitive tasks to staff within ongoing business functions
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is the application of processes, methods, knowledge, skills and experience to achieve the project objectives within agreed constraints.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: You are delivering a new company intranet. Which of the following actions best reflects a project management activity?
o: Developing a risk register to manage delivery uncertainty
Running day-to-day maintenance on the existing intranet
Forwarding supplier invoices on to the procurement team
Producing the weekly staff timesheets for the HR team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Actively managing delivery risks is part of the structured, controlled approach that characterises project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: What is the primary purpose of project management within an organisation?
o: To take over the responsibilities of programme management
To standardise every routine operational procedure in use
To provide a controlled framework for delivering unique objectives
To remove the need for any risk and issue management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management exists to provide structure, control and clarity so that defined, unique objectives are delivered.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A complex product must be delivered by combined IT and engineering teams. Which action best demonstrates project management?
o: Applying methods and tools to plan, execute and control delivery
Hiring additional administrative staff for routine services
Documenting every staff role across the whole organisation
Processing staff annual leave requests through a central team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Applying structured methods, processes and tools to plan and control the delivery is the essence of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is not part of managing a project?
o: Identifying and managing project risks
Resolving issues that arise during delivery
Continuously delivering an ongoing business function
Communicating with project stakeholders
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management concerns temporary, defined outputs; the continuous delivery of a business function is business-as-usual, not project work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Suppliers across time zones face delays because responsibilities are unclear. Which core purpose of project management is being undermined?
o: Establishing a clear framework of control and governance
Removing the need for stakeholder input entirely
Delivering the final product without any change
Minimising all administrative overhead on the project
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A key purpose of project management is to provide clear control and governance, including defined roles and responsibilities for decision-making.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Keeping a logistics project aligned to the sponsor's strategic vision is best described as an example of what?
o: One of the fundamental purposes of project management
A post-project review conducted after handover
A portfolio management responsibility above the project
A quality assurance activity carried out independently
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Ensuring the project stays aligned to organisational strategy and the sponsor's objectives is a core purpose of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following best summarises the key purpose of project management?
o: To take the place of business-as-usual activities
To help organisations deliver change and achieve specific objectives
To increase permanent headcount in operational areas
To standardise routine reporting across all departments
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management enables organisations to deliver change and meet specific time, cost and quality objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A charity is running a time-limited fundraising campaign. Why is managing it using project management principles appropriate?
o: Because the campaign forms part of routine operations
Because fundraising is a continuous, repeatable task
Because project management suits one-off, goal-focused initiatives
Because the campaign has no defined end point
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is designed for temporary initiatives with clear objectives and a defined end, which fits the campaign.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A sponsor wants ongoing visibility of progress and risk on a six-month IT upgrade. Which function of project management supports this?
o: Providing structured monitoring and control of delivery
Shifting the project's focus towards routine operations
Reducing the frequency of staff performance reviews
Allocating additional resources to business operations
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Structured monitoring, reporting and control of progress and risk are central functions of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Several related projects are managed together to improve customer service and maximise value. What are they collectively part of?
o: A portfolio
A business case
A programme
A risk register
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to deliver benefits not available from managing them individually.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A manager selects and prioritises all of an organisation's projects to align with strategy and balance resources. What are they managing?
o: A single workstream
A portfolio
A programme
A delivery team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management selects and prioritises projects and programmes across the organisation to meet its strategic objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Your project is one of eight coordinated under a wider business change programme. What is the role of programme management here?
o: To coordinate and align related projects for greater benefit
To focus only on your project's budget and schedule
To monitor health and safety across the organisation
To take over the duties of the individual project sponsors
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates and aligns related projects so they contribute to wider, shared business benefits.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: What is the key distinction between a programme and a portfolio?
o: A programme coordinates related projects; a portfolio oversees all projects and programmes
A programme contains only unrelated projects, while a portfolio does not
A programme is aligned to strategy, whereas a portfolio is not
A portfolio is always smaller in scale than a programme
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme manages a set of related projects, while a portfolio spans the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: The board reviews every current project across IT, finance and HR to reallocate funding by business priority. What process is this?
o: Configuration management
Programme planning
Change control
Portfolio management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management provides strategic oversight, prioritisation and resource balancing across all of an organisation's initiatives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A retailer runs related projects for online ordering, a mobile app and supply-chain automation. What ensures they are aligned for maximum benefit?
o: Programme management
Quality assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates related projects so their combined benefit exceeds what each project could achieve alone.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a portfolio management responsibility?
o: Selecting the right mix of projects to align with strategy
Ensuring two related projects are delivered in sync
Monitoring an individual project's risk register
Defining the detailed scope for a single project
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management ensures the right projects and programmes are chosen and prioritised to meet strategic goals.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A PMO balances resource allocation and risk exposure across a suite of unrelated IT and marketing projects. What is being demonstrated?
o: Operational management
Programme governance
Portfolio management
Project assurance
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Balancing investment, resources and risk across unrelated projects to serve organisational strategy is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between project, programme and portfolio management?
o: Programme management replaces portfolio management in smaller organisations
Projects are managed independently of any portfolio or programme structure
Portfolio management provides strategic alignment, while programmes coordinate related change
There is no meaningful overlap between the three disciplines
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management aligns all projects and programmes to strategy, while programmes coordinate related change and projects deliver defined outputs.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new CEO cancels two projects, starts three, and groups related initiatives into one programme. Which type of management is being applied?
o: Programme assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
Operational leadership
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Prioritising, terminating and initiating initiatives across the organisation to reflect strategy is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: During an overseas product launch, the team flags that new tax legislation has been enacted. Which PESTLE category does this relate to?
o: Technological
Sociological
Environmental
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: New legislation, including tax law, falls under the legal category of PESTLE, which covers the laws and regulations affecting a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why might a project manager carry out a PESTLE analysis during the initiation of a project?
o: To identify external factors that could influence the project
To map out the internal work breakdown structure
To set the payment schedule agreed with contractors
To evaluate the team's internal communication styles
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE analysis is used to identify external, macro-environmental factors that may affect the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A general election is called midway through a public infrastructure project. Why would a PESTLE analysis be helpful in this situation?
o: It defines the contractual process for resolving disputes
It helps assess how the political change may affect the project
It calculates the project's critical path far more precisely
It improves the breakdown of the technical design work packages
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE helps the project manager identify and assess external factors, here political change, that may affect the project, feeding risk identification and planning.

n.0: Dispute resolution is set out in the contract, not in a PESTLE analysis.
n.2: Critical path analysis comes from the schedule network, not from PESTLE.
n.3: Breaking down design work is done through the WBS, not PESTLE.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A sponsor is concerned that high inflation and rising interest rates could affect a capital investment project. Which PESTLE category applies?
o: Legal
Technological
Economic
Environmental
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Inflation and interest rates are economic factors, which directly influence a project's cost and viability.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A city-centre event project faces growing scrutiny over its impact on local air quality and pollution. Which PESTLE category does this most relate to?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Pollution, air quality and sustainability concerns fall under the environmental category of PESTLE.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A team reviews trends in renewable-energy legislation to see how they could shape a new facility's design. Which tool are they most likely using?
o: SWOT analysis
PESTLE analysis
MoSCoW prioritisation
Cost-benefit analysis
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE analysis identifies and assesses external factors, such as legislation, that could influence project outcomes.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A risk on a healthcare project is patient resistance to digital appointment systems. Which PESTLE category does this best fit?
o: Sociological
Economic
Technological
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Public attitudes and cultural acceptance of change fall under the sociological category of PESTLE.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following best explains the value of carrying out a PESTLE analysis at the start of a large project?
o: It helps anticipate external influences on the project's success
It defines the individual responsibilities within the team
It identifies the project's key delivery milestones
It estimates the cost baseline used for procurement
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE surfaces external threats and enablers early, helping the project anticipate factors beyond its direct control.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new data protection regulation takes effect during your design phase. Which analysis would help you understand its implications for the project?
o: A lessons-learned report
PESTLE analysis
A RAID log
Monte Carlo simulation
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE assesses how external legal and political factors, such as new regulation, may affect the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: On a rural community project, an ageing population and strong local distrust of outside organisations threaten delivery. These are examples of which PESTLE factor?
o: Economic
Environmental
Political
Sociological
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Demographics, attitudes and cultural factors such as an ageing population and distrust of outsiders are sociological factors in the project's external environment.

n.0: Economic factors include things like unemployment, inflation and exchange rates.
n.1: Environmental factors concern the natural environment, such as weather, pollution and sustainability.
n.2: Political factors concern government policy, elections and political stability.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: During an induction session, how would you best explain to a trainee what the term 'project management' means?
o: The application of processes, methods, skills and knowledge to achieve specific project objectives
The ongoing balancing of an organisation's investments against its available resources
The grouping of related projects so that benefits are delivered beyond individual efforts
The continuous administration of repetitive tasks to sustain everyday business performance
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is defined as the application of processes, methods, skills, knowledge and experience to achieve the project's objectives; the other options describe operations, programme and portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new team member asks how the discipline of project management should best be defined in practice.
o: The steady supervision of recurring departmental duties within fixed annual budgets
The organising of resources purely to reduce day-to-day operational running costs
The prioritising of competing initiatives to reflect the organisation's changing strategy
The application of knowledge, tools and techniques to deliver objectives within agreed constraints
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management applies knowledge, tools and techniques to deliver objectives within the constraints of time, cost and quality; the distractors describe operations and portfolio activity.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A manager claims that project management is simply 'getting the work done'. Which correction is the most accurate?
o: It is the day-to-day running of a settled service once it has been established
It is the informal delegation of tasks to whoever happens to have spare capacity
It is the planned application of processes and skills to achieve defined objectives
It is the ongoing ranking of investments to match the organisation's overall strategy
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is a planned, structured application of processes and skills to defined objectives, not informal task allocation, operations or portfolio prioritisation.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following activities most accurately represents what project management involves when delivering a project's objectives?
o: Selecting which proposed initiatives should receive investment in each financial year
Planning, monitoring and controlling all aspects of a project to meet its objectives
Directing a coordinated set of projects to realise combined organisational benefits
Delivering identical outputs repeatedly to satisfy steady and predictable customer demand
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management plans, monitors and controls all aspects of a project to achieve its objectives; the others describe business as usual, programme and portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A colleague asks you to complete the sentence 'project management is the application of...' as accurately as possible.
o: ...governance rules to coordinate a portfolio of unrelated investments
...financial controls to maximise the return from routine operations
...processes, methods, knowledge and skills to achieve the project objectives
...standard operating procedures to sustain continuous business services
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: The recognised definition is the application of processes, methods, knowledge and skills to achieve the project objectives; the distractors describe operational and portfolio work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: When explaining project management to stakeholders unfamiliar with the discipline, which description would be the most accurate to give?
o: The selection of investments to balance the organisation's limited resources
The coordination of several related projects to achieve one strategic change
The routine oversight of established services to keep them running smoothly
The application of processes and skills to deliver a project's objectives
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is the application of processes and skills to deliver the project's objectives; the remaining options describe operations, programme and portfolio management respectively.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Within the wider hierarchy of managing change, which statement best defines what 'programme management' actually involves?
o: The selection of all organisational investments to reflect strategic priorities
The routine supervision of continuing operational services and business functions
The management of a single temporary endeavour to produce one defined output
The coordinated management of related projects to deliver benefits not achievable separately
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates related projects to deliver benefits beyond what individual projects could achieve alone; the distractors describe a single project, portfolio management and operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: When an organisation talks about 'portfolio management', which statement best captures what that discipline is concerned with?
o: The selection, prioritisation and control of projects and programmes to meet strategic goals
The delivery of a group of related projects to achieve a single change outcome
The day-to-day control of one project's scope, cost, schedule and quality
The coordination of routine business activities to sustain steady operational performance
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls the organisation's projects and programmes to align them with strategy; the others describe a programme, a single project and operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: An organisation groups related projects under one change initiative and separately reviews all initiatives for strategic fit. Which two disciplines are described?
o: Programme management then portfolio management
Programme management then project management
Project management then programme management
Portfolio management then programme management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Grouping related projects to deliver a shared change is programme management; reviewing the whole collection for strategic fit is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why might an organisation choose to manage several related projects together as a programme rather than entirely separately?
o: To guarantee that each project finishes strictly within its own isolated budget
To achieve coordinated benefits that the individual projects could not deliver alone
To remove the need for any individual project to have its own objectives
To convert temporary project work into permanent operational business activity
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme coordinates related projects so that combined, aligned benefits are realised that separate projects could not deliver individually.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A learner is confused between a programme and a portfolio. Which statement correctly distinguishes one from the other?
o: A portfolio always contains related projects, whereas a programme contains only unrelated ones
A portfolio delivers a single output, whereas a programme balances strategic investment
A portfolio's projects need not be related, whereas a programme's projects share a common objective
A portfolio is temporary, whereas a programme continues indefinitely as business as usual
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme's projects share a common objective, while a portfolio groups projects and programmes that need not be related, selected to meet strategic goals.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: How do project management, programme management and portfolio management typically relate to one another within an organisation?
o: A project may stand alone, or sit in a programme and/or a portfolio
Projects, programmes and portfolios are independent and never interact
Programmes and portfolios are just other names for very large projects
Portfolios sit within programmes, which sit within individual projects
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project may stand alone, sit within a programme, and/or sit within a portfolio. Programmes coordinate related projects for benefits; portfolios prioritise change against strategy and capacity.

n.1: They interact closely: programmes coordinate projects and portfolios prioritise both.
n.2: Programmes and portfolios are distinct ways of managing change, not just big projects.
n.3: This reverses the relationship; portfolios are the highest level, not the lowest.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A director reviews the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes to decide which to fund, pause or stop. Which discipline is this?
o: Programme management
Project management
Portfolio management
Operational management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Selecting, prioritising and controlling the whole collection of projects and programmes for strategic value is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A change initiative coordinates a new system, revised processes and staff training so that together they transform customer service. What is this?
o: Project management
Programme management
Portfolio management
Benefits realisation management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Coordinating related projects so that combined they deliver a shared transformation is programme management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Within the project, programme and portfolio hierarchy, which level is most directly concerned with aligning investment to organisational strategy?
o: Programme management
Portfolio management
Project management
Work package management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management is the level most directly focused on aligning the organisation's investment in projects and programmes with its strategy.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why do organisations apply project management to unique, time-limited pieces of work?
o: To guarantee that the work encounters no risks or unexpected events
To ensure the work continues indefinitely as part of routine operations
To achieve the defined objectives within agreed time, cost and quality constraints
To keep the project team occupied until a permanent role becomes available
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: The key purpose of project management is to achieve the project objectives within the agreed constraints, typically time, cost and quality.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A sponsor asks what project management is fundamentally there to accomplish on their initiative. What is the best reply?
o: To keep the initiative running indefinitely as a routine service
To guarantee the initiative faces no risks or changes whatsoever
To deliver the initiative's objectives successfully within the agreed constraints
To maximise the number of tasks the team completes each week
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: The key purpose of project management is the successful delivery of the initiative's objectives within its agreed constraints.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A firm keeps starting change initiatives that overrun and drift from their aims. Introducing project management would primarily help by:
o: increasing the number of deliverables produced each month
eliminating the possibility of any future change being requested
converting the initiatives into permanent operational functions
controlling the work so objectives are met within agreed constraints
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management brings control and structure so that objectives are delivered within agreed constraints rather than drifting.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: What does project management chiefly enable an organisation to do that ad hoc working does not?
o: Continue the same activities indefinitely with no completion point
Avoid ever having to make trade-offs between competing constraints
Guarantee that every stakeholder will be satisfied with the outcome
Deliver defined objectives in a controlled way within set constraints
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: The purpose of project management is the controlled delivery of defined objectives within agreed constraints, not the avoidance of trade-offs.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: How is the purpose of project management best distinguished from simply completing tasks?
o: It concentrates solely on cost, disregarding time and quality entirely
It assigns tasks randomly and reviews the results only at closure
It coordinates work purposefully to meet objectives within agreed limits
It focuses only on producing outputs, ignoring objectives and constraints
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management purposefully coordinates work to meet objectives within agreed constraints, going beyond merely finishing individual tasks.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project board wants assurance that a new initiative will meet its aims without exceeding budget or deadline. Which discipline directly serves this purpose?
o: Project management, which delivers objectives within agreed constraints
Facilities management, which maintains the organisation's physical assets
Business-as-usual management, which sustains ongoing repeatable services
Operational supervision, which oversees continuous daily production
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Delivering objectives within the agreed constraints of time and cost is the defining purpose of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project manager is preparing to advise the board whether to launch a new venture. Why include a PESTLE analysis?
o: To show the external factors that could shape or threaten the venture's success
To record the detailed costs of each deliverable in the budget
To confirm the internal reporting lines within the project's governance
To allocate individual work packages to named members of the team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE reveals the external factors that could shape or threaten success, informing the launch decision.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project manager wants to anticipate how the wider environment might influence a new venture. Which analysis best serves this purpose?
o: A PESTLE analysis of political, economic, social and other external factors
A responsibility assignment matrix mapping tasks to team roles
A risk register listing only internal delivery threats
A work breakdown structure decomposing the project's deliverables
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE is used to scan the external environment, whereas the other tools address internal work, roles or logged threats.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A retailer plans to enter an unfamiliar overseas market. How would a PESTLE analysis help the project manager assess this move?
o: By revealing external influences in that market that could create risks or opportunities
By recording the internal costs of each project deliverable
By defining the acceptance criteria for the finished product
By allocating the project's work packages to named team members
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE examines the external environment, exposing market-specific risks and opportunities the project must plan for.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A charity plans a major national campaign. Why might its project manager use PESTLE rather than rely on internal information alone?
o: Because it surfaces external forces that internal planning would otherwise overlook
Because it sets out the quality tolerances for each deliverable
Because it decomposes the campaign into manageable work packages
Because it records lessons learned from earlier campaigns
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE looks beyond the organisation, revealing external factors that internally focused planning tends to miss.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which outcome would a project manager most reasonably expect from completing a PESTLE analysis?
o: A finalised critical path for the project schedule
A complete list of the project's internal stakeholders
A clearer view of the external context influencing the project
A signed-off configuration baseline for all deliverables
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE produces an understanding of the external context; the other outputs come from scheduling, configuration and stakeholder work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project manager reviews economic, legal and environmental trends affecting a new facility. What is the purpose of examining these together?
o: To build a rounded picture of external influences on the project
To confirm the internal budget allocation for the facility
To measure the quality of the facility's finished components
To assign responsibilities to the facility's construction team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Considering these factors collectively, as in PESTLE, gives a rounded view of the external environment shaping the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: According to the APM, a project is best understood as a unique, transient endeavour undertaken primarily to achieve which of the following?
o: Coordinated benefits realised across several linked projects
Steady outputs delivered through repeatable routine tasks
Balanced returns from a managed collection of investments
Planned objectives that bring about beneficial change
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to achieve planned objectives, defined in terms of outputs, outcomes or benefits.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which single feature is most fundamental to something being classed as a project rather than another type of organised work?
o: It continues indefinitely without a planned end point
It is managed by a permanently established department
It generates a recurring, predictable stream of income
It is unique, producing outputs not delivered before
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Uniqueness is a defining characteristic of a project; each project delivers something not produced in exactly that way before.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A council forms a temporary team to build a new leisure centre, disbanding it once the centre opens. Which characteristic marks this as a project?
o: The team and funding are permanent and ongoing
The output is identical to previous deliverables
The work repeats on a fixed monthly cycle
The endeavour is transient with a defined end point
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is transient, having a defined beginning and end, after which the temporary organisation is disbanded.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A colleague argues that assembling the same standard kitchen unit for the thousandth time is a project. Why is this description incorrect?
o: The task is too small to require any planning
The task is not managed by a project sponsor
The task is repetitive and lacks any uniqueness
The task carries no financial cost to complete
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Repetitive, routine work lacks the uniqueness that characterises a project and is better classed as business as usual.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project is defined as being undertaken to achieve planned objectives. In what terms are these objectives usually expressed?
o: Outputs, outcomes or benefits
Departments, functions or teams
Profits, dividends or returns
Routine, repeated daily tasks
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Planned objectives on a project are defined in terms of outputs, outcomes or benefits, distinguishing a project from operations, programmes and portfolios.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why does describing a project as 'transient' matter when defining what a project actually is?
o: It guarantees the work produces identical repeated outputs
It shows the work will never involve any external suppliers
It signals the work has a defined start and finish
It confirms the work will always exceed its planned budget
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Transience means a project has a defined beginning and end, unlike the continuous nature of operational business-as-usual work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A manager lists features of project work to contrast it with business as usual. Which feature genuinely applies only to projects?
o: Delivering a steady, repeatable stream of outputs
Continuing indefinitely with no planned closure
Being temporary, with a defined start and end
Being run by a permanent operational department
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is temporary, with a defined start and end, whereas business as usual is repetitive and ongoing.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A bank runs daily transaction processing and, separately, a one-off move to new premises. Which statement about these two activities is correct?
o: The processing is a project; the move is operations
Both are projects because both consume resources
The processing is operations; the move is a project
Both are business as usual because both are essential
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Repetitive daily processing is business as usual, whereas the unique, time-bounded office move is a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Compared with business as usual, project work is generally characterised by higher levels of which factor?
o: Uncertainty, because the outputs are unique
Repetition, because the tasks are standardised
Predictability, because the work is routine
Stability, because the team is permanent
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Because projects deliver unique outputs, they carry greater uncertainty and risk than the routine, repeatable work of operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: An operations manager notes their team's output rarely changes month to month. How does this contrast with a project team's work?
o: A project team also produces unchanging monthly output
A project team operates without any start or end date
A project team works towards a defined, finite objective
A project team has no need to manage any resources
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project pursues a defined objective within a finite timeframe, unlike the steady, continuous output of operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is a feature of business as usual that a project does not typically share?
o: It is undertaken to deliver a defined change
It is delivered by a temporary organisation
It continues on a steady, repeatable basis
It is disbanded once its objectives are met
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Business as usual is steady-state and repeatable, whereas a project is temporary and disbands once its objectives are achieved.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Midway through a busy period, a manager treats a unique system upgrade exactly like routine operations. Why is this approach likely to fail?
o: The upgrade's uniqueness and finite scope need project management
Routine operations demand far more governance than projects
Operations and projects require exactly the same controls
The upgrade cannot involve any of the operational staff
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A unique, time-bounded upgrade requires project management disciplines, which differ from the steady controls used for business as usual.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement best defines a project?
o: A temporary endeavour undertaken to deliver a unique, defined outcome
A permanent department within the organisation's structure
A standard procedure that is repeated continuously over time
An ongoing operation that supports routine business functions
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: APM defines a project as a unique, transient endeavour with a defined beginning and end, undertaken to achieve planned objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: How does project management differ from managing business-as-usual operations?
o: It manages repetitive work that continues indefinitely
It produces no deliverables of any kind
It manages unique, time-bounded work with a defined objective
It requires no resources to be committed to it
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management delivers unique, temporary work, whereas business-as-usual is ongoing and repetitive.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: An organisation must implement a new CRM system by December to improve sales tracking. Which term best describes this piece of work?
o: Project
Programme
Business-as-usual
Portfolio
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: It is a project: a unique, temporary undertaking with a defined end date and a specific deliverable.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A team runs the same server backups every day as part of normal operations. How is this work best classified?
o: Portfolio
Business-as-usual
Project
Programme
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Routine, repetitive and ongoing tasks such as daily backups are business-as-usual rather than a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: You must define, deliver and close a one-off initiative to build a new office. Which discipline should you apply?
o: Strategic management
Quality management
Operations management
Project management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is the discipline for planning and controlling unique, temporary work to achieve defined objectives.

Life Cycles.q: You are running a construction project with a linear life cycle and fully defined requirements. What is the correct sequence of phases?
o: Initiation, Development, Execution, Review
Concept, Feasibility, Development, Handover
Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition
Concept, Definition, Deployment, Closure
Life Cycles.w: The APM linear life cycle runs Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. Older material used implementation and handover and closure for the later phases.

n.0: These are not APM phase names for a linear life cycle.
n.1: Feasibility is an iterative phase name, Development and Handover are not BoK7 linear phase names, and Definition is missing.
n.3: The final linear phase is Transition, which includes handover and closure.

Life Cycles.q: In a linear project life cycle, in which phase are the detailed schedule, budget and project management plan normally finalised?
o: Definition
Concept
Deployment
Transition
Life Cycles.w: Definition is where requirements and detailed plans are developed, the project management plan is produced and the deployment baseline is set before the work begins.

n.1: Concept develops the idea and outline business case; detailed plans come later.
n.2: Deployment carries out the work against plans that were finalised in definition.
n.3: Transition hands over the outputs and closes the project.

Life Cycles.q: Which activity is most characteristic of the concept phase within a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Defining the business need and justification for change
Completing the post-project benefit reviews
Allocating detailed work packages to the delivery team
Producing and signing off the final test results
Life Cycles.w: The concept phase articulates the need, high-level options and justification for the project before detailed planning begins.

Life Cycles.q: A linear project has handed new equipment over to the operations team, who have accepted it, and project resources are now being released. Which phase is being completed?
o: Definition
Transition
Concept
Deployment
Life Cycles.w: Transition is where outputs are handed over to users and accepted, resources are released, and the project is closed with lessons captured.

n.0: Definition sets requirements and detailed plans before any work is delivered.
n.2: Concept develops the idea and outline business case at the start.
n.3: Deployment builds and delivers the outputs; handover and acceptance happen in transition.

Life Cycles.q: In a linear life cycle, which of the following is a main purpose of the transition phase?
o: Designing and building the project's outputs
Handing over outputs and closing the project
Developing and approving the outline business case
Setting the deployment baseline for the work
Life Cycles.w: Transition hands the outputs over to users and business as usual, gains acceptance, releases resources, and closes the project, including capturing lessons learned.

n.0: Designing and building outputs happens in deployment.
n.2: The outline business case is developed in the concept phase.
n.3: The deployment baseline is set at the end of definition.

Life Cycles.q: A team is building a new mobile app through short development cycles with regular end-user feedback. Which life cycle is most likely being used?
o: Extended
Hybrid
Iterative
Linear
Life Cycles.w: An iterative life cycle delivers in small increments and refines the product through repeated cycles of stakeholder feedback.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement best describes a core feature of an iterative project life cycle?
o: The full scope is fixed upfront and delivered in one release
Formal reviews are avoided throughout the delivery period
The product is released in increments with frequent reassessment
Benefits are only realised once the final delivery is complete
Life Cycles.w: Iterative life cycles release the product in successive increments, reassessing and adapting the plan after each one.

Life Cycles.q: In an iterative life cycle, what term is commonly used for the short, time-boxed development cycles the team works in?
o: Milestones
Gateways
Phases
Sprints
Life Cycles.w: Sprints are the short, time-boxed iterations used to deliver increments of the product in iterative and agile approaches.

Life Cycles.q: A delivery model of successive product iterations shaped by stakeholder input is best suited to what kind of requirements?
o: Fixed by contract and legally constrained
Simple, repetitive and well understood
Evolving, uncertain or likely to change
Stable and fully defined from the outset
Life Cycles.w: Iterative life cycles suit evolving or uncertain requirements because feedback between iterations allows the product to be refined.

Life Cycles.q: In an iterative project life cycle, what typically happens at the end of each development iteration?
o: The final product is signed off and the project closes
Stakeholder feedback is gathered to shape later iterations
All remaining risks are transferred to suppliers
The business case is rewritten from scratch
Life Cycles.w: Each iteration ends with a review that gathers stakeholder feedback, informing and adapting the next iteration.

Life Cycles.q: Infrastructure must be delivered in a fixed sequence, while software features are released in cycles based on user feedback. Which life cycle is being used?
o: Iterative
Extended
Hybrid
Linear
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle combines a linear approach for predictable work with an iterative approach for work that benefits from feedback.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following statements best describes a typical hybrid project life cycle?
o: An adaptive model that uses only agile techniques
A combination of linear and iterative life cycle elements
An extended life cycle with additional benefit reviews
A series of fixed-scope deliveries with no overlap
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle blends predictive (linear) and adaptive (iterative) elements to suit the different parts of a project.

Life Cycles.q: A client wants a fixed upfront cost and schedule for deployment but also wants to evolve features after go-live. Which approach best fits?
o: Extended
Iterative
Hybrid
Linear
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid approach allows a predictable, planned deployment while retaining iterative flexibility to evolve features later.

Life Cycles.q: Which situation is the strongest reason for a project to adopt a hybrid life cycle?
o: Some parts are predictable while others need flexibility
All requirements are fixed and fully understood
The product is simple, small and repetitive
The customer has minimal involvement in delivery
Life Cycles.w: Hybrid life cycles are chosen when some components need firm, predictive control while others benefit from adaptive delivery.

Life Cycles.q: Infrastructure is delivered using a linear model while customer-facing features are developed and adjusted during delivery. What is this model called?
o: Extended
Agile
Hybrid
Waterfall
Life Cycles.w: Mixing sequential and iterative components within one project is the defining characteristic of a hybrid life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Months after a new CRM system was handed over and embedded in daily use, the team measures whether the expected benefits have been achieved. To which phase of an extended life cycle does this belong?
o: Transition
Evolutionary development
Benefits realisation
Adoption
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle adds adoption and benefits realisation after transition. Measuring whether the expected benefits have been achieved belongs to benefits realisation.

n.0: Transition is the handover itself, which the stem says has already happened.
n.1: Evolutionary development is a phase of the iterative life cycle, not of the extended life cycle.
n.3: Adoption is when users embed the outputs in their work, which the stem says is already done.

Life Cycles.q: In project management, what is the primary purpose of adopting an extended project life cycle?
o: To shorten the overall delivery timescale
To reduce resource usage during development
To manage post-project benefits and performance
To avoid further stakeholder engagement
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle continues beyond handover to ensure benefits are realised and performance is monitored over time.

Life Cycles.q: A document management system has been handed over to operations. Which activity would typically follow within the extended project life cycle?
o: Evaluating actual benefits against those forecast
Drafting the project initiation documentation
Holding the initial project kick-off workshop
Running performance tests on the old system
Life Cycles.w: Comparing benefits actually achieved against those forecast is a central activity of the extended life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Which activity is most closely associated with the extended project life cycle?
o: Monitoring benefit delivery over time
Defining the work breakdown structure
Procuring the development resources
Identifying the initial user requirements
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle focuses on tracking benefit delivery, often long after the deliverables have been handed over.

Life Cycles.q: After closure, the sponsor commissions periodic reviews to check whether the expected return on investment is being achieved. What does this indicate?
o: That extended life cycle activities are underway
That the project has re-entered development
That the original scope was left incomplete
That a formal change request has been raised
Life Cycles.w: Post-closure benefit reviews to confirm long-term value are part of the extended project life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: In a typical linear project life cycle, which phase immediately follows the concept phase?
o: Definition
Transition
Deployment
Operation
Life Cycles.w: A linear life cycle runs concept, definition, deployment then transition, so definition follows the concept phase.

Life Cycles.q: During which phase of a typical linear life cycle is the initial idea first tested for feasibility and strategic fit?
o: Transition
Deployment
Concept
Definition
Life Cycles.w: The concept phase tests the initial idea for feasibility and strategic fit before detailed planning begins.

Life Cycles.q: What principally happens during the transition phase of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: The high-level idea is assessed for viability and strategic fit
Detailed plans, schedules and budgets are produced and baselined
Outputs are handed over to users and the project is formally closed
The main deliverables are designed, built and progressively tested
Life Cycles.w: In the transition phase the outputs are handed over into use and the project is closed down.

Life Cycles.q: In which phase of a linear life cycle are the project's outputs actually built and tested?
o: Deployment
Transition
Concept
Definition
Life Cycles.w: The deployment phase is where the project management plan is executed and the outputs are created and tested.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the phases of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Optimisation
Definition
Concept
Deployment
Life Cycles.w: The four phases of a typical linear life cycle are concept, definition, deployment and transition; optimisation is not one of them.

Life Cycles.q: In a linear life cycle, moving from the definition phase into the deployment phase typically requires what?
o: Completion of user training and formal handover to operations
Approval at a decision gate confirming plans are ready for delivery
Realisation of the benefits set out in the business case
The first sprint retrospective to reprioritise the backlog
Life Cycles.w: Phase boundaries in a linear life cycle are controlled by decision gates that authorise progression once plans are ready.

Life Cycles.q: Which sequence correctly orders the deliverable focus across a linear life cycle?
o: Plans, then the concept, then handover, then the build
An idea, then detailed plans, then the build, then handover
Handover first, then build, then definition, then the concept
A working product, then plans, then an idea, then handover
Life Cycles.w: The linear life cycle progresses from concept (idea), to definition (plans), to deployment (build), to transition (handover).

Life Cycles.q: By the end of the concept phase in a linear life cycle, what is normally produced?
o: A signed acceptance certificate confirming benefits realised
An outline business case recommending whether to proceed
The fully tested product ready for operational handover
A detailed configuration management status report
Life Cycles.w: The concept phase concludes with an outline business case that supports the decision on whether to continue into definition.

Life Cycles.q: What is the defining feature of the way phases are arranged in a linear project life cycle?
o: All phases run in parallel from the very start of the project
Phases can be reordered freely according to team preference
Phases repeat in short cycles until the customer is satisfied
Each phase is largely completed before the next one begins
Life Cycles.w: A linear life cycle runs its phases sequentially, with each substantially finished before the next starts.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement best describes how the phases are arranged in a typical iterative project life cycle?
o: A single design phase followed by permanent operational running
A series of unrelated phases carried out by separate organisations
A fixed, once-only sequence of phases completed from start to finish
A set of activities repeated over successive cycles to refine the solution
Life Cycles.w: An iterative life cycle repeats a set of activities across successive cycles to develop the solution progressively.

Life Cycles.q: In a typical iterative life cycle, why are development activities repeated rather than completed only once?
o: To progressively evolve and improve the product through successive cycles
To remove the need for stakeholder involvement during delivery
To fix the full scope and budget before any work starts
To avoid producing any documentation until the final release
Life Cycles.w: Repetition lets the product evolve incrementally, incorporating feedback with each cycle.

Life Cycles.q: A team completes a cycle of planning, building and reviewing, then begins the same activities again. Which life cycle does this reflect?
o: An iterative life cycle
A hybrid life cycle
A linear life cycle
An extended life cycle
Life Cycles.w: Repeating the same set of activities over successive cycles is the defining feature of an iterative life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Within a single iteration of an iterative life cycle, which set of activities is typically carried out?
o: Procurement of all materials with no further planning needed
Planning, building and reviewing an increment of the solution
Closure and disbanding of the entire project team
A one-off concept phase followed by permanent operations
Life Cycles.w: Each iteration repeats a compact set of plan-build-review activities to produce an increment.

Life Cycles.q: Which feature most clearly distinguishes an iterative life cycle from a linear one in terms of its phases?
o: Its phases are repeated to develop the solution incrementally
Its phases exclude any form of review or feedback
Its phases are always carried out by external suppliers
Its phases are performed strictly once in a fixed order
Life Cycles.w: The defining difference is repetition of phases to build the solution incrementally rather than a single pass.

Life Cycles.q: During a typical iterative life cycle, when is stakeholder feedback most commonly gathered?
o: Never, because the scope is fixed at the outset
Only once, at the very end of the project
At the close of each iteration to shape later cycles
Only before the first iteration begins
Life Cycles.w: Iterative delivery seeks feedback at the end of each cycle so subsequent iterations can respond to it.

Life Cycles.q: Which sequence best represents how work flows through a typical iterative project life cycle?
o: Delivery carried out entirely before any planning takes place
Concept, definition, delivery and handover performed once only
A one-off design followed immediately by closure
Repeated cycles of build and review until the product is complete
Life Cycles.w: Iterative work progresses through repeated build-and-review cycles until the solution is complete.

Life Cycles.q: In an iterative life cycle, what is typically produced at the end of each cycle of work?
o: A complete business case covering the whole programme
The final, fully complete product ready for closure
A partial or improved increment of the overall solution
A fixed baseline that can never afterwards be revised
Life Cycles.w: Each iteration delivers an increment that adds to or improves the evolving solution.

Life Cycles.q: Why might an organisation choose an iterative life cycle for a project with uncertain requirements?
o: Because it fixes all requirements permanently before delivery
Because repeating cycles allow requirements to be refined as understanding grows
Because it guarantees a lower overall cost than any alternative
Because it removes the need for any project reviews
Life Cycles.w: Iterative cycles let requirements be clarified and refined progressively, suiting projects where they are not fully known upfront.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement most accurately describes what a hybrid project life cycle brings together within a single project?
o: A single linear sequence repeated so the team can refine the output twice
Linear phases for stable, well-understood work alongside iterative cycles for evolving requirements
Continuous iterations throughout, with no predefined phases fixed in advance
Two consecutive linear life cycles, each producing a separate final deliverable
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle blends a plan-driven (linear) approach for defined work with an adaptive (iterative) approach for evolving elements within one project.

Life Cycles.q: What is the main advantage of adopting a hybrid life cycle on a project with mixed requirements?
o: It removes the need for any change control because everything is planned upfront
It guarantees the project will finish earlier than a purely linear approach
It applies predictable planning where requirements are stable and flexibility where they evolve
It allows the team to avoid producing a deployment baseline at any stage
Life Cycles.w: The hybrid approach matches the method to the work, giving predictability to stable elements and adaptability to uncertain ones.

Life Cycles.q: A construction firm pours foundations in a fixed sequence but develops the building's smart controls in short cycles. Which life cycle is this?
o: Iterative life cycle
Extended life cycle
Linear life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
Life Cycles.w: Combining a linear sequence for fixed work with iterative cycles for evolving elements within one project is a hybrid life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: In a hybrid life cycle, which type of work is typically handled through the linear, plan-driven element?
o: Experimental elements where the final solution is still unknown
Stable components with well-defined, unlikely-to-change requirements
Any work the customer wishes to review after every short iteration
Features whose requirements are expected to change repeatedly during delivery
Life Cycles.w: The linear element suits stable, well-understood work that can be fixed and planned in advance without frequent change.

Life Cycles.q: Within a hybrid approach, which work is best suited to the iterative element of the life cycle?
o: Foundational elements whose design is settled before delivery begins
Evolving features that benefit from repeated user feedback and refinement
Fixed infrastructure that must be installed in a strict, unchanging order
Regulatory documentation that cannot be altered once it is approved
Life Cycles.w: The iterative element suits uncertain, evolving requirements that improve through successive cycles of feedback and refinement.

Life Cycles.q: How does a hybrid life cycle mainly differ from a purely iterative life cycle?
o: A hybrid is always shorter and cheaper than an iterative approach
A hybrid keeps predefined linear phases for part of the work, unlike a fully iterative approach
A hybrid abandons all upfront planning in favour of continuous change
A hybrid never gathers stakeholder feedback during delivery
Life Cycles.w: Unlike a purely iterative life cycle, a hybrid retains fixed linear phases for the parts of the work that are stable.

Life Cycles.q: Midway through planning, a team realises part of the scope is fixed and part is unclear. Why might a hybrid life cycle suit them?
o: It replaces the need for a project manager to coordinate the work
It combines predictable planning with adaptive delivery within one project
It lets them skip defining any requirements until the very end
It ensures no changes will ever be requested during delivery
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle accommodates both fixed and evolving work by combining plan-driven and adaptive approaches in one project.

Life Cycles.q: A colleague asks what 'hybrid life cycle' means. Which explanation is correct?
o: Blending linear and iterative approaches within one project's delivery
Handing the project between two organisations at the halfway point
Delivering the entire project through a single fixed sequence of phases
Running the same iterative cycle continuously until funding is exhausted
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle blends linear and iterative methods so each part of the work uses the most suitable approach.

Life Cycles.q: Which characteristic best distinguishes a hybrid life cycle from other project life cycles?
o: It follows one rigid sequence with no scope for iteration
It postpones all delivery until every requirement is agreed
It deliberately combines plan-driven and adaptive methods in one approach
It relies solely on adaptive methods with no fixed structure
Life Cycles.w: The defining feature of a hybrid life cycle is its deliberate combination of plan-driven and adaptive methods within a single project.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by an 'extended project life cycle'?
o: A life cycle in which the concept and definition phases are merged into one
A life cycle whose deployment phase is lengthened to allow for more testing
A linear life cycle followed by adoption and benefits realisation phases
A life cycle repeated in short cycles until the customer accepts the product
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle adds adoption and benefits realisation phases after transition, so it continues until the benefits in the business case are realised.

n.0: Merging concept and definition does not describe any APM life cycle model.
n.1: Lengthening deployment for testing does not extend the life cycle beyond handover.
n.3: Repeating short cycles describes an iterative life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Compared with a standard linear life cycle, what does an extended life cycle mainly change?
o: It merges the definition and deployment phases into one continuous phase
It repeats the deployment phase in short cycles until stakeholders are happy
It shortens the concept phase so that deployment can start much sooner
It continues after transition until the business case benefits are realised
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle adds adoption and benefits realisation after transition, reflecting that benefits usually arrive after the outputs are handed over.

n.0: Definition and deployment stay as separate phases in an extended life cycle.
n.1: Repeating cycles of development describes an iterative life cycle.
n.2: The early phases are unchanged; the extension comes after transition.

Life Cycles.q: What is the main benefit of extending a project life cycle to include a benefits realisation phase?
o: It allows the requirements to be changed freely throughout the delivery phase
It reduces the number of governance decision gates the project must pass through
It confirms that the intended benefits are actually achieved once the outputs are in use
It fixes the delivery budget more tightly before any work is allowed to begin
Life Cycles.w: Adding a benefits realisation phase lets the organisation confirm the forecast benefits are delivered in operational use.

Life Cycles.q: Compared with a typical linear life cycle, which additional phases does an extended life cycle include?
o: Adoption and benefits realisation phases after transition
Concept and definition phases before deployment begins
Operations and asset disposal phases after the handover
Further testing and integration phases within the deployment
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle adds adoption and benefits realisation after transition, so the life cycle continues until the benefits promised in the business case are realised.

n.1: Concept and definition are already part of every linear life cycle.
n.2: Running operations and disposing of assets describe the wider product life, not the phases APM adds.
n.3: Testing and integration take place within deployment in any linear life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: In an extended life cycle, which phase follows transition and focuses on users embedding the new outputs into their everyday ways of working?
o: The foundations phase
The adoption phase
The deployment phase
The definition phase
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle adds adoption, where the outputs are embedded in business as usual, and then benefits realisation.

n.0: Foundations is a phase of the iterative life cycle, before any development.
n.2: Deployment comes before transition and is where the outputs are built.
n.3: Definition comes early and sets the requirements and plans.

Life Cycles.q: A sponsor wants the life cycle to continue after handover until the benefits in the business case have been realised. Which life cycle supports this?
o: Linear life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
Extended life cycle
Iterative life cycle
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle adds adoption and benefits realisation after transition, so it continues until the planned benefits are realised.

n.0: A standard linear life cycle ends at transition, when the outputs are handed over.
n.1: A hybrid life cycle combines linear and iterative approaches; it does not by itself extend beyond handover.
n.3: An iterative life cycle delivers in time boxes but ends with deployment of the solution.

Life Cycles.q: How does an extended project life cycle differ from a hybrid life cycle?
o: Extended blends linear and iterative delivery, whereas hybrid adds operational phases
Extended adds phases after handover, whereas hybrid blends linear and iterative approaches
Both fix scope at the outset, but hybrid allows benefits to be reviewed later
Both remove the closure phase, but extended repeats delivery in short sprints
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle lengthens the timeline to cover benefits and disposal, while a hybrid life cycle combines linear and iterative delivery approaches.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following activities would appear within an extended life cycle but not within a standard one?
o: Approving the deployment baseline before delivery begins
Reviewing whether forecast benefits have been realised in operational use
Defining the project's scope during the concept phase
Producing the detailed project management plan
Life Cycles.w: Reviewing realised benefits after handover is characteristic of the extended life cycle, which continues beyond delivery of the outputs.

Life Cycles.q: In an extended project life cycle, at what point does the life cycle normally come to an end?
o: When the outputs are handed over to the users
When the business case is first approved
When the planned benefits have been realised
When deployment has produced all the outputs
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle continues through adoption and benefits realisation until the benefits promised in the business case have been realised.

n.0: Handover ends transition, which is where a standard linear life cycle stops, not an extended one.
n.1: Approval of the business case happens early, at the start of the life cycle.
n.3: Producing the outputs ends deployment; transition, adoption and benefits realisation still follow.

Life Cycles.q: Which sequence best represents the phases of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Initiation, sprint, retrospective, closure
Forming, storming, norming, performing
Concept, definition, deployment, transition
Concept, iteration, review, release
Life Cycles.w: A linear life cycle runs sequentially through the concept, definition, deployment and transition phases.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement best describes how work progresses in a typical iterative project life cycle?
o: Repeated cycles of planning, building and reviewing that refine the product incrementally
Predictive up-front planning combined with a one-off handover
A feasibility study followed only by long-term operational support
A single sequential pass through fixed phases from concept to closure
Life Cycles.w: An iterative life cycle repeats build-and-review cycles, refining and adding to the product over successive iterations.

Life Cycles.q: A team plans the overall scope up front using a predictive approach, then builds the features in a series of iterative sprints. What life cycle is this?
o: Iterative life cycle
Extended life cycle
Linear life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle combines predictive (linear) planning with iterative delivery of the work.

Life Cycles.q: A project includes a feasibility phase before delivery and a period of operational support after handover. Which life cycle term describes this?
o: Hybrid project life cycle
Iterative project life cycle
Linear project life cycle
Extended project life cycle
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle adds pre-project and post-project phases, such as feasibility and operation, around the core life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: A team delivers a prototype, gathers feedback, refines it and repeats until it is approved. Which life cycle does this describe?
o: Iterative life cycle
Linear life cycle
Extended life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
Life Cycles.w: Using feedback loops to refine the product over successive versions is characteristic of an iterative life cycle.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: An executive secured the funding and holds overall accountability for delivering the project's benefits. Which role is being described?
o: End user
Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project sponsor owns the business case, secures funding and is accountable for the realisation of the benefits.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the project sponsor?
o: Writing the detailed work breakdown structure
Maintaining the day-to-day project issue log
Producing the project communication plan
Approving key decisions and owning the business case
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor provides direction, owns the business case and approves the major decisions and investment for the project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Having approved the business case and committed funding, what should be a project sponsor's next priority?
o: Monitoring task-level performance of the team
Issuing procurement requests to suppliers
Developing the detailed project schedule
Ensuring strategic alignment and effective governance
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A key sponsor responsibility is keeping the project aligned to strategic objectives and supporting sound governance.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between the project sponsor and the project manager?
o: The sponsor sets direction and governance while the manager delivers
The sponsor manages daily delivery while the manager sets strategy
The two roles operate independently with no formal relationship
The sponsor handles finance while the manager makes technical choices
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor provides strategic direction and governance, while the project manager delivers the project within those boundaries.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A change in organisational strategy puts a project at risk of cancellation. Who is responsible for deciding whether it should continue?
o: Project sponsor
Project manager
Product owner
Project planner
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor assesses continued strategic alignment and has the authority to continue or cancel the project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: You manage the day-to-day activities of a project, control its risks and ensure deliverables are completed on time. Which role are you performing?
o: Project team member
Project manager
Product owner
Project sponsor
