Planning.w: The business case justifies the investment by presenting the costs, benefits, risks and options, providing the basis for the decision to proceed.

Planning.q: When reviewing a colleague's draft business case, which of the following would you expect to be a core component?
o: The finalised test scripts to be used in verifying each deliverable
The detailed activity schedule and the resource histogram for every member of the team
The expected benefits, costs, timescales and risks of the proposed investment
The configuration item register and the version history of every product
Planning.w: A business case justifies the investment by setting out its expected benefits, costs, timescales and risks, usually comparing options, so the sponsor can decide whether it is worth doing.

n.0: Test scripts are quality control documents prepared later for verification, not business case content.
n.1: Detailed schedules and resource histograms belong to the project management plan, not the business case.
n.3: Configuration records track products and versions during delivery; they are not part of the justification.

Planning.q: A business case usually evaluates alternative ways of meeting the identified need. What is this particular section commonly called?
o: The options appraisal
The risk register
The responsibility matrix
The configuration log
Planning.w: Comparing alternative approaches, such as 'do nothing', 'do minimum' and 'do something', forms the options appraisal within the business case.

Planning.q: Beyond gaining initial approval, what continuing purpose does the business case serve as the project progresses through delivery?
o: It replaces the need to maintain a project schedule during delivery
It records the version history of each of the configuration items
It provides the reference for checking that the investment remains justified
It sets out the acceptance tests to be run on the final product
Planning.w: The business case is reviewed throughout delivery to confirm the investment remains viable and continues to justify the project's continuation.

Planning.q: Within a business case, the expected benefits are weighed against which two factors to justify proceeding with the investment?
o: The costs and the risks of the investment
The schedule bar chart and the communication plan
The test scripts and the recorded defect logs
The team structure and the individual reporting lines
Planning.w: A business case justifies the investment by weighing the expected benefits against its costs and risks; schedules, team structures and test records are not what the benefits are balanced against.

Planning.q: A sponsor wants one document setting out why the project is worth doing and what it will cost. Which document meets this need?
o: The quality plan
The communication plan
The business case
The risk register
Planning.w: The business case explains why the project is worthwhile, presenting its justification, costs, benefits and risks in a single document.

Planning.q: Throughout the life of a project, who holds overall ownership of the business case and its continued validity?
o: The project sponsor
The project team
The project manager
The end users
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for ensuring the investment remains justified throughout the project.

Planning.q: When a business case is being developed, what is the project manager's typical contribution to that process?
o: Providing analysis such as options, costs and risks to inform the case
Accepting personal accountability for the realisation of the benefits
Deciding whether the project aligns with the corporate strategy
Approving the funding and committing the organisation's resources
Planning.w: The project manager supplies delivery analysis, such as options, costs and risks, to help the sponsor develop and maintain the business case.

Planning.q: Why is the sponsor, rather than the project manager, held accountable for the business case throughout the project?
o: Because the sponsor produces the detailed cost estimates used in delivery
Because the sponsor owns the investment and is answerable for its benefits
Because the sponsor writes the technical specification of the product
Because the sponsor manages the project's day-to-day activities and tasks
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the investment and is accountable for realising its benefits, which is why the business case sits with them, not the project manager.

Planning.q: During initiation the project manager drafts cost and risk information while the sponsor decides on strategic justification. What does this show?
o: The two roles collaborate, with the manager informing and the sponsor owning the case
The two roles entirely duplicate each other's responsibilities and effort
The sponsor is responsible only for producing the detailed cost estimates
The project manager holds ultimate accountability for the whole investment
Planning.w: Developing the business case is collaborative: the project manager provides delivery information while the sponsor owns and justifies the investment.

Planning.q: Which of the following activities best reflects the sponsor's particular role in relation to the project's business case?
o: Maintaining the project's day-to-day risk and issue registers
Championing and defending the investment at senior decision-making levels
Producing the detailed schedule and resource plan for the delivery work
Testing the completed deliverables against their acceptance criteria
Planning.w: The sponsor champions and defends the business case at senior level; scheduling, testing and register maintenance are project manager or team responsibilities.

Planning.q: A sponsor asks the project manager to refresh the cost and benefit figures within the business case. Why is this appropriate?
o: The manager becomes accountable for the realisation of the benefits
The manager alone now decides whether the project should continue
The manager supplies delivery information so the sponsor can keep it current
The manager is taking over ownership of the case from the sponsor
Planning.w: The project manager provides updated delivery information to help the sponsor keep the business case current; ownership and accountability remain with the sponsor.

Planning.q: Why is it inappropriate for a project sponsor to delegate ownership of the business case entirely to the project manager?
o: The project manager already owns the project's risk and quality registers
The project manager is not permitted to view the business case at any stage
Ownership must remain with the sponsor, who is accountable for the investment's benefits
Delegating it would automatically cancel the project's approved funding
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case because they are accountable for realising the investment's benefits; that ownership cannot be handed to the project manager.

Planning.q: The project manager has supplied updated risk analysis for the business case. Who decides whether the case is formally revised?
o: The end users, as recipients of the benefits
The project manager, as author of the analysis
The project team, as producers of the work
The project sponsor, as owner of the business case
Planning.w: The project manager provides the analysis, but the sponsor owns the business case and decides whether it is formally revised.

Planning.q: When developing a business case, which pairing of responsibilities to roles is correct?
o: Producing the estimates — the sponsor; deciding strategic fit — the manager
Owning it — the manager; approving the funding — the sponsor
Owning and championing it — the sponsor; providing information to develop it — the manager
Approving it — the end users; writing it — the project team
Planning.w: The sponsor owns and champions the business case, while the project manager provides the information needed to develop it.

Planning.q: How does an early stakeholder analysis help a project manager anticipate potential opposition to a project?
o: By guaranteeing that no stakeholder will ever oppose the project's aims
By revealing which stakeholders may resist, so their concerns can be addressed early
By transferring responsibility for opposition to the project sponsor
By removing any need to communicate with opposing stakeholders
Planning.w: Analysis reveals which stakeholders may resist, allowing their concerns to be understood and addressed early in engagement.

Planning.q: Analysis places a senior regulator as high influence but low interest in day-to-day detail. How should they be engaged?
o: Kept satisfied with concise, high-level updates rather than routine detail
Left entirely uninformed until the project has been formally closed
Sent every operational report so nothing is ever withheld from them
Given full control over prioritising the project team's daily tasks
Planning.w: High-influence, low-interest stakeholders should be kept satisfied with proportionate, high-level information rather than routine detail.

Planning.q: A stakeholder group is assessed as low influence and low interest. What engagement approach does the analysis suggest?
o: Treat them as the primary audience for detailed reporting
Involve them in every decision to secure their formal approval
Monitor them with minimal effort, informing them only if needed
Escalate all issues to them before any action is taken
Planning.w: Low-influence, low-interest stakeholders are monitored with minimal effort, receiving information only when necessary.

Planning.q: Why does stakeholder analysis help a project manager use limited engagement time efficiently?
o: It transfers responsibility for engagement to the project sponsor
It replaces the need for a communication plan later in delivery
It highlights where to focus effort by ranking influence and interest
It confirms that all stakeholders require identical levels of contact
Planning.w: By ranking influence and interest, analysis shows where engagement effort will have most value, allowing resources to be focused.

Planning.q: Beyond identifying who the stakeholders are, what further insight does a stakeholder analysis provide to guide engagement?
o: The precise technical solution each stakeholder must build
The final acceptance date agreed for every project deliverable
Each stakeholder's likely attitude, expectations and level of support
The exact budget each stakeholder is willing to contribute
Planning.w: Analysis assesses stakeholders' attitudes, expectations and support, informing how each should be engaged.

Planning.q: Midway through delivery a previously minor stakeholder gains significant influence. What does this imply for stakeholder analysis?
o: It shows analysis is only ever useful before the project starts
It means engagement should stop until the project is closed
It should be revisited so engagement reflects their changed position
It should be ignored because the original analysis is now fixed
Planning.w: Stakeholder analysis is iterative; as positions change it is revisited so engagement remains effective.

Planning.q: How does understanding stakeholders' interests through analysis improve project communication?
o: It ensures only good news is ever shared with stakeholders
It enables messages to be shaped to each group's needs and concerns
It removes the need to consider how messages are received
It allows the same generic message to be issued to everyone
Planning.w: Knowing each group's interests allows communications to be shaped to their needs, supporting more effective engagement.

Planning.q: Stakeholder analysis identifies a sponsor as high influence and high interest. What engagement does this indicate?
o: Close, active engagement and full involvement throughout delivery
Contact limited strictly to the closure phase of the project
No direct contact, relying on others to relay information to them
Occasional, low-detail updates issued only at major milestones
Planning.w: High-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be actively engaged and closely managed throughout the project.

Planning.q: A team lists its stakeholders then rates each on power and interest. What does this rating enable them to do?
o: Confirm the exact final cost of the project to the last item
Remove any stakeholder who might disagree with the project
Record only the contact details needed to send invitations
Plan an engagement approach proportionate to each stakeholder's position
Planning.w: Rating power and interest lets the team plan engagement that is proportionate to each stakeholder's position.

Planning.q: Which of the following statements best defines the term 'benefits management' in a project context?
o: The production and testing of the project's outputs before handover
The control of changes to the project's approved scope baseline
The scheduling of tasks so the project finishes by its agreed deadline
The identification, planning, tracking and realisation of a project's benefits
Planning.w: Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of the benefits a project is intended to deliver.

Planning.q: Benefits management covers a benefit from its first identification through to which final point?
o: The completion of the project's detailed schedule
The approval of the project's initial business case
The moment the project's outputs are handed over
Its realisation and review once the outputs are in use
Planning.w: Benefits management spans from identification through to the realisation and review of benefits once outputs are in use.

Planning.q: How does benefits management differ from simply producing and delivering a project's outputs?
o: It focuses on realising the value the outputs are meant to create
It ends the moment the outputs are handed over to users
It concentrates only on producing the outputs to specification
It ignores the outcomes and measures only delivery on time
Planning.w: Outputs enable outcomes and benefits; benefits management focuses on realising the value rather than merely producing outputs.

Planning.q: A team defines the improvements expected, then tracks whether they materialise after go-live. Which discipline are they applying?
o: Critical path analysis
Benefits management
Quality control
Configuration management
Planning.w: Defining expected improvements and tracking their realisation is the essence of benefits management.

Planning.q: A sponsor asks what benefits management will contribute once the new system is operational. What is the best answer?
o: It will build and test the remaining system components
It will close the project's contracts with its suppliers
It will approve any further changes to the system's scope
It will track and confirm that the expected improvements are actually achieved
Planning.w: Benefits management tracks and confirms that the expected improvements are actually realised once the output is in use.

Planning.q: Within the discipline of benefits management, a 'benefit' is most accurately defined as what?
o: A measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, seen as advantageous
A tangible product created by the project's delivery work
A risk that has occurred and now requires resolution
A task that must be completed before another can begin
Planning.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement, arising from an outcome, that is perceived as advantageous by stakeholders.

Planning.q: Which three methods are recognised as typical estimating approaches within project planning?
o: Levelling, smoothing and crashing estimating
Predictive, iterative and hybrid estimating
Analytical, analogous and parametric estimating
Qualitative, quantitative and residual estimating
Planning.w: Analytical, analogous and parametric are the standard estimating methods identified in the APM Body of Knowledge.

Planning.q: Which estimating method relies on decomposing the work and estimating each component before summing the totals?
o: Analogous estimating
Parametric estimating
Delphi estimating
Analytical (bottom-up) estimating
Planning.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating breaks work into components, estimates each and aggregates the totals.

Planning.q: At which point in a project is analogous estimating typically most useful?
o: Early on, when little detail exists but similar past projects do
Late in delivery when every work package is fully specified
Only after the critical path has been finalised
Only once the product has been handed over to operations
Planning.w: Analogous estimating draws on similar completed projects, making it valuable early when detailed information is scarce.

Planning.q: Which estimating method would give the most accurate figure once detailed design information is available?
o: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating of each work package
Analogous estimating based on a past project
A high-level judgement made at the concept gate
A rough order-of-magnitude estimate
Planning.w: Bottom-up estimating uses detailed component information, so it is most accurate once that detail exists.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes the way parametric estimating is used to produce a project estimate?
o: Basing the whole estimate on one similar completed project
Adding up separate estimates for every individual work package
Reaching an estimate through the anonymous consensus of experts
Applying a measured rate to the number of units of work required
Planning.w: Parametric estimating multiplies a known rate per unit by the quantity of units required.

Planning.q: A project manager combines a per-square-metre rate with a similar building's actual cost to sense-check figures. Which two methods are being used?
o: Analytical and Delphi estimating
Bottom-up and comparative estimating
Qualitative and residual estimating
Parametric and analogous estimating
Planning.w: Applying a unit rate is parametric, while comparing against a similar building's actuals is analogous estimating.

Planning.q: What does the estimating funnel primarily illustrate about project estimates over time?
o: The number of estimates required reduces to a single figure at the start
Costs always fall steadily throughout the life cycle
Accuracy improves and tolerance ranges narrow as more becomes known
Estimates become less reliable as the project progresses
Planning.w: The estimating funnel shows that estimate accuracy improves and tolerance ranges narrow as more detailed information becomes available.

Planning.q: Why should an early-stage estimate be presented as a range rather than a single figure, according to the estimating funnel?
o: Because single-figure estimates are never permitted under APM guidance
Because the range will always prove more accurate than the final cost
Because presenting a range removes the need for any later estimates
Because limited information at that stage means the estimate carries wide uncertainty
Planning.w: At an early stage limited information means the estimate carries wide uncertainty, so the funnel shows it is best expressed as a broad range.

Planning.q: Why do estimates near the bottom of the estimating funnel carry tighter tolerances than earlier ones?
o: The sponsor insists later estimates match the first figure given
Fewer stakeholders remain involved to challenge them
Contingency has been deliberately stripped out of them
More detailed scope and information are available by that stage
Planning.w: As the project progresses, greater scope definition and information reduce uncertainty, allowing tighter estimate tolerances.

Planning.q: A sponsor is frustrated that the concept-stage estimate later changed. How does the estimating funnel explain this?
o: Estimates are fixed once given and any change indicates poor planning
The original estimate should never have been shared with the sponsor
Early estimates are broad and refine as project detail increases
Later estimates are always less reliable than earlier ones
Planning.w: The funnel shows that early estimates are indicative and legitimately refine as more detail emerges through the life cycle.

Planning.q: Which statement best characterises how estimate tolerance behaves as a project moves through the estimating funnel?
o: Tolerance stays constant from concept through to delivery
Tolerance widens steadily as the project progresses
Tolerance narrows progressively as knowledge and detail increase
Tolerance is only ever expressed as a single fixed value
Planning.w: Estimate tolerance narrows progressively through the funnel as increasing knowledge and detail reduce uncertainty.

Planning.q: How does the estimating funnel help justify revisiting cost estimates at each stage of a project?
o: It confirms estimates should only ever be produced at project closure
It shows that increasing knowledge legitimately allows estimates to be refined over time
It demonstrates that later estimates are inherently less trustworthy
It proves that the first estimate given should be treated as final
Planning.w: The funnel shows that greater knowledge at each stage legitimately allows estimates to be refined, justifying revisiting them.

Planning.q: What most clearly distinguishes a deployment baseline from an ordinary version of the project plan?
o: It records only the risks identified before delivery began
It has been formally approved and fixed as the reference for measuring delivery
It is an informal draft that the team may amend at any time
It lists the personal contact details of every project stakeholder
Planning.w: The deployment baseline is the approved, fixed version of scope, time and cost used as the reference against which delivery is measured.

Planning.q: What is the main purpose of a deployment baseline once a project moves into delivery?
o: To record the names and contact details of all project stakeholders
To provide a fixed reference against which progress and variance are measured
To capture the lessons learned for use on future similar projects
To list the recognised standards that the deliverables must comply with
Planning.w: The deployment baseline serves as the benchmark for monitoring performance and identifying variances during delivery.

Planning.q: A project manager compares actual cost and progress against the plan approved before delivery to identify variances. What are they comparing against?
o: The risk register
The deployment baseline
The quality plan
The stakeholder analysis
Planning.w: Variances are measured against the deployment baseline, the approved plan for scope, cost and schedule.

Planning.q: Which combination of elements is typically fixed within a project's deployment baseline?
o: Team roles, supplier contracts and lessons learned
Quality standards, audits and benefit reviews
Stakeholder interests, risks and communication channels
Scope, schedule and cost agreed for delivery
Planning.w: The deployment baseline captures the approved scope, schedule and cost that define what will be delivered.

Planning.q: How does the deployment baseline relate to the project management plan?
o: It is produced by operations after the outputs are handed over
It records only the risks and issues identified during planning
It is the approved reference set for scope, time and cost drawn from the plan
It replaces the plan once the project enters the delivery phase
Planning.w: The deployment baseline is the fixed, approved set of scope, time and cost derived from the project management plan and used to control delivery.

Planning.q: At what point should a project's deployment baseline normally be agreed and approved?
o: Before delivery begins, at the end of planning
During the concept phase, before any planning is done
After the project has been formally closed
Only when a change request is first raised
Planning.w: The baseline is set and approved once planning is complete and before delivery begins, so performance can be measured from that point.

Planning.q: Before work begins, a project manager agrees measurable success criteria with all parties. What does this primarily achieve?
o: It removes the need to produce a business case for the investment
It transfers accountability for the benefits to the operational teams
A shared, agreed definition of what success will look like for the project
It guarantees that the project will be delivered within its budget
Planning.w: Agreeing success criteria at the outset gives every party a common, agreed understanding of what the project must achieve.

Planning.q: Midway through delivery a project manager faces a trade-off between two options. How can the agreed success criteria help?
o: They remove the need to consult the project sponsor about the choice
They replace the change control process for that particular decision
They automatically approve whichever option costs the least money
They provide a reference to guide the decision towards the intended outcome
Planning.w: During delivery, success criteria act as a reference point that keeps decisions aligned with the project's intended outcomes.

Planning.q: At handover, the operations team asks how it will be judged whether the project met its goals. What should they be shown?
o: The project stakeholder map
The project communication plan
The project risk register
The agreed project success criteria
Planning.w: The agreed success criteria are the standard against which the project's achievement of its goals is judged at handover.

Planning.q: At handover a customer claims the product is unacceptable while the team believes it is complete. Which reference best resolves this dispute?
o: The procurement strategy
The communication plan
The risk register
The agreed success criteria
Planning.w: Pre-agreed success criteria give an objective standard against which acceptance at handover can be judged, resolving such disputes.

Planning.q: Why are success criteria considered at the start, during and at the handover of a project rather than only once?
o: To ensure they remain relevant and are used to steer and finally judge the project
To increase the number of governance gates the project must pass through
To transfer ownership of the criteria to a different stakeholder each time
To allow the project budget to be revised at each of the three points
Planning.w: Revisiting success criteria across the life cycle keeps them relevant and ensures they both guide delivery and provide the final measure of success.

Planning.q: During delivery, how can regularly checking work against the success criteria benefit the project manager?
o: It removes the requirement to report progress to the sponsor
It fixes the deployment baseline so that no change can occur
It confirms that delivery is still heading towards the agreed definition of success
It guarantees that all of the identified risks will not materialise
Planning.w: Comparing progress with the success criteria during delivery confirms the project remains on course to meet its agreed objectives.

Planning.q: A linear project fixes its deployment baseline once at the outset. How is the iterative equivalent best described by comparison?
o: Set only after the final product has been delivered
Re-baselined progressively as each iteration completes
Abandoned entirely because iterative work needs no baseline
Fixed once and never revisited after approval
Planning.w: In an iterative life cycle the deployment baseline evolves and is re-established as successive iterations refine the solution, unlike the single fixed baseline of a linear project.

Planning.q: A project manager explains why a linear deployment baseline feels more rigid than an iterative one. Which explanation is correct?
o: Both fix the baseline rigidly before any delivery starts
Linear fixes it early, while iterative refines it each iteration
Iterative fixes it early, while linear evolves over time
Both leave the baseline entirely open until closure
Planning.w: A linear life cycle establishes a firm baseline early, whereas an iterative life cycle refines the baseline across successive iterations.

Planning.q: A team switching from a linear to an iterative approach asks how their deployment baseline will now behave. What is the best answer?
o: It will be locked for the entire project duration
It will be signed off only at the concept stage
It will be removed because iterative work has no plan
It will be updated as requirements emerge each iteration
Planning.w: Iterative delivery updates the deployment baseline as requirements emerge and are prioritised in each iteration, rather than locking it once.

Planning.q: Why is a single, tightly controlled deployment baseline more workable in a linear life cycle than in an iterative one?
o: Linear projects have no stakeholders to satisfy
Linear projects never encounter any change requests
Linear projects deliver nothing until the very end
Linear requirements are defined and stable up front
Planning.w: Linear life cycles define requirements up front and expect them to remain stable, so a single controlled baseline is appropriate; iterative requirements evolve.

Planning.q: Which of the following best describes how the deployment baseline behaves within an iterative project life cycle?
o: A document produced only at project handover
A fixed reference set once and never changed
An evolving reference updated as the solution develops
A record that applies solely to linear projects
Planning.w: In iterative delivery the deployment baseline evolves, being revised as each increment develops the solution.

Planning.q: A sponsor of a linear construction project asks how often the deployment baseline will change during delivery. What is the most accurate reply?
o: Weekly, as part of routine iteration planning
Constantly, after every single working day
Never, even where formal changes are approved
Rarely, and only through formal change control
Planning.w: In a linear life cycle the baseline is fixed early and only altered through formal change control, so changes are infrequent.

Planning.q: Two projects run side by side: one linear, one iterative. Which difference in their deployment baselines should the project manager expect?
o: The linear baseline flexes weekly; the iterative stays fixed
The iterative baseline flexes; the linear stays largely fixed
Both baselines remain completely unchanged throughout
Neither project establishes a baseline at any point
Planning.w: The iterative project's baseline evolves with each iteration, while the linear project's baseline is largely fixed after early approval.

Planning.q: In which life cycle is the deployment baseline most likely to be established firmly at a single point early in delivery?
o: Any life cycle where requirements keep changing
An iterative life cycle using repeated increments
A linear life cycle with defined, stable requirements
A life cycle that omits planning altogether
Planning.w: A linear life cycle sets a firm baseline early because requirements are defined and stable, unlike the evolving baseline of iterative delivery.

Planning.q: Midway through an iterative project, stakeholders reprioritise features. What effect does this typically have on the deployment baseline?
o: It invalidates the baseline, so it must be deleted
It updates the baseline to reflect the revised priorities
It freezes the baseline until the project closes
It has no effect, as the baseline is permanently fixed
Planning.w: An iterative deployment baseline is expected to evolve, so reprioritised features are absorbed by updating the baseline for the next iterations.

Planning.q: The project management plan is agreed between the project manager and which party who approves it on behalf of the organisation?
o: The end users
The project team members
The project sponsor
The external suppliers
Planning.w: The PMP is owned by the project manager but approved by the sponsor, who represents the organisation's interests.

Planning.q: Which group of stakeholders should contribute to a project management plan to ensure the delivered output can be operated after handover?
o: End users and operational staff
Competitors within the same market sector
Regulatory auditors external to the organisation
Members of an unrelated project's team
Planning.w: End users and operational staff must contribute so the plan reflects requirements needed for successful operation and handover.

Planning.q: When agreeing a project management plan, why is it important to involve the stakeholders who will provide the project's resources?
o: So they can remove the need for a schedule
So they take over the project manager's daily duties
So the plan's resource assumptions are realistic and committed
So they can approve the sponsor's business case
Planning.w: Resource providers must be engaged so the plan's assumptions on availability and commitment are realistic and agreed.

Planning.q: Which of the following is least likely to be a genuine stakeholder in a project management plan?
o: The team members delivering the work packages
A supplier with no involvement in the project
The end users who will operate the output
The project sponsor authorising the plan
Planning.w: A stakeholder has an interest in or is affected by the project; a supplier with no involvement has no such stake in the plan.

Planning.q: Why should the project sponsor be actively involved as a stakeholder in agreeing the project management plan?
o: Because the sponsor performs the day-to-day delivery tasks
Because the sponsor tests each deliverable for quality
Because the sponsor owns the business case and provides direction
Because the sponsor writes each work package personally
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case and provides strategic direction, so their agreement ensures the plan aligns with the organisation's aims.

Planning.q: A project manager omits the senior user when producing the project management plan. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Delivery costs will automatically increase tenfold
The sponsor loses all accountability for benefits
The plan may not reflect genuine user requirements
The schedule will no longer require any milestones
Planning.w: The senior user represents those who will use the output; omitting them risks a plan that does not reflect real user needs.

Planning.q: During delivery, what does regular progress reporting mainly allow a project manager to compare?
o: Team roles against Belbin behavioural profiles
Supplier prices against the wider market
Actual performance against the agreed baseline
The business case against the risk register
Planning.w: Progress reporting chiefly compares actual performance against the agreed baseline so variances can be identified and managed.

Planning.q: Midway through delivery, a steering group relies on progress reports to make decisions. Which benefit of reporting does this best illustrate?
o: It replaces the project's governance arrangements
It enables informed, timely decision-making
It guarantees the project finishes ahead of time
It removes all risk from the project entirely
Planning.w: Progress reporting gives stakeholders timely, accurate information, enabling informed decisions and effective control.

Planning.q: Which of the following is a genuine benefit of regular progress reporting to the project manager?
o: It provides early warning of emerging variances
It removes the requirement to hold a baseline
It guarantees stakeholders will never raise issues
It eliminates the need to manage project risks
Planning.w: Regular reporting highlights variances early, allowing corrective action before problems escalate.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes the way in which regular progress reporting supports effective control of a project?
o: It fixes the deployment baseline permanently in place
It records lessons only after the project has closed
It transfers accountability from the sponsor to users
It measures progress so deviations can be corrected
Planning.w: By measuring progress against plan, reporting exposes deviations so the project manager can take corrective action, supporting control.

Planning.q: A sponsor complains they only hear about problems once they are severe. Which reporting improvement would most directly address this?
o: Reporting progress regularly with early variance alerts
Reporting exclusively on completed deliverables
Reporting only when the sponsor formally requests it
Reporting only at the project's closure stage
Planning.w: Regular reporting with timely variance information gives early warning, preventing problems from being discovered only when severe.

Planning.q: Beyond control, what wider benefit does transparent progress reporting bring to a project's stakeholders?
o: It builds stakeholder confidence and trust
It removes the sponsor from the governance chain
It abolishes the need for a communication plan
It ensures no changes are ever requested
Planning.w: Open, accurate reporting builds stakeholder confidence and trust in the project's management and direction.

Planning.q: In an iterative life cycle, how is the deployment baseline usually treated for each time box?
o: Scope and quality are fixed, while time and cost flex
Time and cost are fixed, while the scope flexes
Scope and cost are fixed, while the time flexes
Time and scope are fixed, while the cost flexes
Planning.w: In an iterative life cycle time and cost are fixed for each time box and scope flexes, with lower-priority requirements deferred. Quality standards are protected, not traded away.

n.0: This reverses the iterative approach: scope is what flexes, and time and cost are fixed.
n.2: Time is fixed in a time box; the end date does not move.
n.3: Scope is not fixed in an iterative life cycle, and cost is fixed rather than flexing.

Planning.q: An iterative project's time box is ending and two lower-priority 'Could have' features will not be finished. What should normally happen?
o: Extend the time box until every feature is complete
Add funds and people so that all features are finished
Defer the unfinished features and keep the end date
Lower the acceptance standards to finish all features
Planning.w: Time and cost are fixed in a time box and scope flexes, so lower-priority features are deferred and the end date is kept. Quality standards are not traded away.

n.0: The time box end date is fixed; extending it breaks the iterative approach.
n.1: Cost and resources are fixed for the time box; scope flexes instead.
n.3: Agreed acceptance standards are protected; quality is not traded to fit more scope in.

Planning.q: How does the deployment baseline typically differ between a linear and an iterative life cycle?
o: Linear fixes time and cost; iterative fixes scope and quality
Linear has no baseline at all; iterative baselines the whole project
Both fix scope at definition and control it with change control
Linear fixes scope for the whole project; iterative lets it flex
Planning.w: In a linear life cycle the baseline is set for the whole project at the end of definition, with scope fixed and changes formally controlled. In an iterative life cycle time and cost are fixed and scope flexes, with detailed baselines set time box by time box.

n.0: This reverses the iterative approach, where time and cost are fixed and scope flexes.
n.1: Linear projects set a full deployment baseline at the end of definition.
n.2: Only the linear life cycle fixes scope at definition; iterative scope is refined and re-prioritised.

Planning.q: What is meant by a deployment baseline?
o: The initial list of stakeholders identified for the project
The approved reference for scope, schedule and cost against which performance is measured
The final approved budget figure for the project
The agreed schedule of all the project's meetings
Planning.w: The deployment baseline is the approved version of the plan against which actual progress and performance are measured.

Planning.q: How do deployment baselines typically differ between linear and iterative life cycles?
o: Linear baselines cover only scope, whereas iterative baselines cover only cost
Linear baselines change daily, whereas iterative baselines never change
Linear baselines are largely fixed, whereas iterative baselines are revisited each iteration
Linear baselines are optional, whereas iterative baselines are mandatory
Planning.w: A linear life cycle sets the baseline once, while an iterative life cycle re-baselines regularly as each iteration is planned.

Planning.q: A project manager decides which documents to fix as the reference for measuring future performance. What is being established?
o: Stakeholder register
Risk register
Communication plan
Deployment baseline
Planning.w: Fixing the agreed scope, schedule and cost documents as the reference point creates the deployment baseline.

Planning.q: Before any work begins the sponsor wants a document justifying the investment through its costs, benefits and risks. Which document is this?
o: Work breakdown structure
Risk register
Business case
Quality plan
Planning.w: The business case justifies the project by setting out its benefits, costs, risks and options to support the investment decision.

Planning.q: How does carrying out a stakeholder analysis support effective stakeholder engagement?
o: It schedules every meeting the stakeholders will attend
It identifies each stakeholder's interest, influence and communication needs
It sets the final approved budget for the project
It produces the project's detailed technical specification
Planning.w: Stakeholder analysis reveals stakeholders' interests, influence and needs, so engagement and communication can be tailored to each.

Scope Management.q: Which process ensures that a project delivers only the work required to meet its objectives?
o: Cost management
Change control
Stakeholder management
Scope management
Scope Management.w: Scope management defines and controls the work included in the project so that it delivers only what is necessary to meet its objectives.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best defines scope management?
o: Monitoring project progress and reporting on the outcomes achieved
Identifying and controlling what is included in and excluded from the project
Tracking budget expenditure and producing financial forecasts
Communicating the project's requirements to external suppliers
Scope Management.w: Scope management is concerned with identifying and controlling what the project will and will not deliver.

Scope Management.q: In a linear life cycle, in which phase is the project scope defined in detail and baselined?
o: The concept phase
The definition phase
The deployment phase
The transition phase
Scope Management.w: Definition is where requirements are defined in detail, the project management plan is produced and the deployment baseline (including scope) is set. From then on, scope is controlled through change control.

n.0: Concept develops the idea, the outline business case and feasibility. Scope is only outlined at a high level, not defined in detail or baselined.
n.2: Deployment delivers the work against the baseline set earlier. Scope is controlled here, not first defined.
n.3: Transition hands the outputs over to users and closes the project. Scope was fixed long before this point.

Scope Management.q: A review finds a project failed to deliver key elements because scope was poorly controlled. Which process should have prevented this?
o: Scope management
Resource scheduling
Communication planning
Risk analysis
Scope Management.w: Scope management ensures that all required deliverables are identified, defined and controlled throughout the project.

Scope Management.q: Why is effective scope management essential to the success of a project?
o: It defines and controls what the project will and will not deliver
It removes the need for any configuration management on the project
It ensures the project will always be delivered within its budget
It guarantees that every project risk will be completely eliminated
Scope Management.w: Scope management establishes and controls the boundaries of the work, helping to prevent scope creep and ensuring the agreed outputs are delivered.

Scope Management.q: A linear project fixes all deliverables before work starts, while an iterative project adapts them over time. What does this show about scope management?
o: Iterative projects carry out no planning before delivery
Linear projects are inherently less reliable than iterative ones
Iterative projects manage scope incrementally as understanding grows
Iterative projects fail to define their scope at all
Scope Management.w: Iterative projects manage scope in increments, refining it as understanding of the requirements improves.

Scope Management.q: A linear project finalised its scope during the concept phase. What is the likely consequence when new requirements emerge during delivery?
o: The change will be managed through strict change control
The scope will be re-planned freely at every stage
The change will be absorbed into the work automatically
The team will simply reprioritise its next sprint
Scope Management.w: Linear projects fix scope early, so new requirements arising later are handled through a formal, strictly controlled change process.

Scope Management.q: An agile team reviews scope at the start of each sprint and updates priorities from user feedback. How does this reflect iterative scope management?
o: The deliverables are set upfront and reviewed only monthly
The product evolves through ongoing review and stakeholder input
The team proceeds without defining any scope at all
The scope is fixed at the start and is never revisited
Scope Management.w: In iterative projects the scope evolves as work progresses, guided by continual review and stakeholder feedback.

Scope Management.q: Which statement best describes how scope is managed differently in linear and iterative projects?
o: Linear projects fix scope early, whereas iterative projects adapt it over time
Linear projects define scope late, whereas iterative projects define it early
Both linear and iterative projects fix their scope only at project closure
Iterative projects rely on strict change control, whereas linear projects stay flexible
Scope Management.w: Linear projects establish scope early in the life cycle, whereas iterative projects refine it throughout delivery.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor wants the flexibility to refine requirements as user needs emerge. Which life cycle is better suited, and why?
o: Linear, because it freezes the scope right from the start
Iterative, because it removes the need for any planning
Iterative, because it supports evolving scope through continuous feedback
Linear, because it copes best with high levels of uncertainty
Scope Management.w: An iterative life cycle is designed to accommodate changing requirements, allowing scope to evolve through continuous feedback.

Scope Management.q: In a linear project with scope locked at the concept phase, a client requests a significant change during delivery. How is this typically handled?
o: It is implemented without review to avoid delay
It is added straight into the next delivery sprint
It is deferred until the benefits realisation phase
It is assessed through a formal change control process
Scope Management.w: Linear projects manage changes to a fixed scope through a formal change control process to maintain control of the project.

Scope Management.q: An agile team adapts its backlog regularly throughout delivery. What does this indicate about scope management on the project?
o: Scope is left undefined until testing begins
Scope is adapted continuously as the project evolves
Scope is fixed and unchanged after the concept phase
Scope is fully defined at the start and then locked
Scope Management.w: Regular backlog refinement reflects iterative scope management, in which scope adapts to evolving priorities and feedback.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of scope management in a linear project?
o: Frequent reprioritisation of user stories each cycle
Continuous negotiation of scope with the stakeholders
Formal control of changes once the initial scope is defined
Dynamic delivery of requirements as they evolve
Scope Management.w: Linear projects define scope early and rely on formal change control to evaluate and manage any changes thereafter.

Scope Management.q: An IT team delivers in two-week sprints, and the client requests changes after each review. What does this indicate about scope?
o: Scope is tightly fixed at the beginning of the project
Scope is determined only at the close of the project
Scope is evolving continuously through collaboration
Scope is restricted to the original deliverables only
Scope Management.w: This is iterative scope management, in which requirements evolve through continuous collaboration, review and feedback.

Scope Management.q: Why is change control generally less rigid in an iterative life cycle?
o: Because iterative projects avoid producing any documentation
Because scope is expected to evolve throughout delivery
Because testing takes place only at project closure
Because the project budget is fixed from the outset
Scope Management.w: Iterative life cycles anticipate that scope will be refined continuously, so change is handled more flexibly than in linear projects.

Scope Management.q: A team uses a product breakdown structure (PBS) to represent the end product. What is its primary purpose in scope management?
o: To allocate costs to individual project activities
To estimate the overall schedule for the project
To define the deliverables that make up the final product
To assign team members to each project task
Scope Management.w: A PBS breaks the end product down hierarchically to define the deliverables that make up the final product.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between a PBS and a WBS?
o: The PBS defines the deliverables and the WBS defines the work to create them
The PBS defines the risks and the WBS defines the risk responses
The PBS sets the budget and the WBS sets the time limits
The PBS defines the costs and the WBS defines the people involved
Scope Management.w: The PBS identifies the product's deliverables, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

Scope Management.q: How do a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure support scope definition when used together?
o: They set out the project's risks and outstanding issues
They identify the communication channels and reporting lines
They link the deliverables to the work required to produce them
They record the financial transactions made for the stakeholders
Scope Management.w: Together the PBS and WBS connect what must be delivered to the work required to deliver it, giving a complete view of scope.

Scope Management.q: Why might a project manager create a product breakdown structure before a work breakdown structure?
o: To create a baseline budget for the project
To determine the cost of the individual tasks first
To assign team members to their roles early on
To establish a shared understanding of the product to be delivered
Scope Management.w: The PBS clarifies the deliverables required, giving a shared understanding of the product so that the WBS can be built around it.

Scope Management.q: A work breakdown structure contains items such as 'code user interface' and 'test module'. What does this structure help to define?
o: The procurement process for the external suppliers
The financial framework underpinning the project
The structure of the client's own organisation
The work required to produce each project deliverable
Scope Management.w: The WBS breaks the scope into the work required to complete each deliverable, expressed as manageable work packages.

Scope Management.q: A product breakdown structure sets out the main product, its subassemblies and its components. Why is this useful to the project manager?
o: It identifies which work packages are behind schedule
It clarifies exactly what the project must deliver
It shows who is responsible for each delivery
It allocates team members to each activity
Scope Management.w: The PBS defines and visualises all elements of the final product, clarifying exactly what the project must deliver.

Scope Management.q: What is the main difference between a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure?
o: The PBS shows the deliverables and the WBS shows the work to create them
The PBS sets the deadlines and the WBS sets the budgets
The PBS shows the work and the WBS shows the associated costs
The PBS supports communication and the WBS supports risk management
Scope Management.w: The PBS defines what the project must produce, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

Scope Management.q: A work breakdown structure is being developed for a software deployment project. What level of detail should it provide?
o: A breakdown of all the work packages needed to complete the deliverables
The roles and responsibilities of each team member
Only the financial costs linked to each task
Only the task names together with their durations
Scope Management.w: The WBS should decompose the total scope into smaller, manageable work packages that capture all the work required.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best explains how a product breakdown structure supports scope definition?
o: It lists all stakeholders and their communication preferences
It defines the product deliverables in a structured hierarchy
It records the planned and actual cost of each activity
It organises the reporting structure of the project team
Scope Management.w: The PBS sets out the product's deliverables in a structured hierarchy, giving a clear understanding of the required scope.

Scope Management.q: A team uses a work breakdown structure to define tasks and a product breakdown structure to define deliverables. What is a key benefit of using both?
o: They remove the need to maintain a stakeholder register
They reduce the need for a procurement process
They provide a legal framework for engaging suppliers
They link the work required to the outputs that are expected
Scope Management.w: Using both structures ensures the planned work is directly connected to the agreed outputs the project must deliver.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is developing a cost breakdown structure (CBS) for a project. What is the main purpose of this structure?
o: To record the issues and lessons learned during delivery
To break the deliverables down into manageable packages of work
To set out the reporting lines that exist between team members
To identify and track the costs of the project's individual components
Scope Management.w: A CBS breaks the project's costs down against its components, giving the project manager a structured basis for budgeting and cost control.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes how a cost breakdown structure (CBS) supports effective budget control on a project?
o: By setting out the project's overall decision-making structure
By showing the cost associated with each part of the project
By categorising the project's scope into functional units
By assigning named individuals to each of the project tasks
Scope Management.w: By attributing costs to each project element, the CBS lets the project manager monitor and control spending against the budget.

Scope Management.q: Why is a cost breakdown structure (CBS) usually derived from the work breakdown structure (WBS) on a project?
o: Because the WBS identifies the work that then needs to be costed
Because the CBS defines the thresholds for approving scope change
Because the WBS controls how stakeholders are communicated with
Because the CBS sets the reporting line for each work package
Scope Management.w: The WBS defines the work to be done, and the CBS attributes cost estimates to those components, so the two structures align.

Scope Management.q: How does a cost breakdown structure (CBS) help a project manager with tracking project costs?
o: By allocating a named team member to each individual task
By linking a cost to each element of the project's scope
By listing the decision gates set throughout the project
By recording the lessons learned from earlier projects
Scope Management.w: The CBS links costs to defined elements of scope, allowing the project manager to track actual spending against the budget.

Scope Management.q: A cost breakdown structure (CBS) most directly supports which of the following financial activities on a project?
o: Setting out the responsibilities held by each stakeholder
Assigning individual tasks to named members of the team
Estimating, budgeting and monitoring the project's costs
Monitoring the project's risks and its open issues
Scope Management.w: A CBS provides a structured breakdown of cost that underpins estimating, budgeting and ongoing cost monitoring for control.

Scope Management.q: A project manager creates an organisational breakdown structure (OBS). What is the main purpose of this tool?
o: To record the project's detailed work breakdown structure
To show the reporting relationships and lines of authority
To define the project's risks and their planned responses
To set out the methods used to communicate with stakeholders
Scope Management.w: An OBS sets out the project's organisational hierarchy, showing roles, reporting relationships and lines of authority.

Scope Management.q: How does an organisational breakdown structure (OBS) support role clarity within a project team?
o: By setting out the project's configuration control procedures
By identifying the deliverables that the project must produce
By showing how responsibilities are distributed through the organisation
By detailing the project's individual financial cost centres
Scope Management.w: The OBS clarifies who holds responsibility and who reports to whom, improving transparency of roles across the team.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following statements best describes the function of an organisational breakdown structure (OBS)?
o: It sets out the required packages of work in a hierarchy
It assigns a specific cost to each member of the team
It shows the structure of roles and reporting within the project
It defines the sequence in which tasks are to be delivered
Scope Management.w: An OBS is a hierarchical view of how the project is organised, showing roles and who reports to whom.

Scope Management.q: A senior stakeholder wants to understand how reporting will work across the project's several teams. Which structure should the project manager refer them to?
o: The product breakdown structure (PBS)
The organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
The work breakdown structure (WBS)
The cost breakdown structure (CBS)
Scope Management.w: The OBS shows reporting lines and how roles fit within the project's organisation, which is exactly what the stakeholder is asking about.

Scope Management.q: How does an organisational breakdown structure (OBS) contribute to the successful delivery of a project?
o: It sets out the risk responses required to address external threats
It clarifies reporting relationships and lines of management control within the project
It defines the sequence in which project activities will be performed
It assigns costs to each of the project’s deliverables and work packages
Scope Management.w: An OBS depicts the project’s reporting lines and accountabilities, supporting governance and management control of the work.

Scope Management.q: A project manager uses a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM). What is the key benefit of using this tool?
o: It tracks the financial cost incurred against each project phase
It allocates the packages of work to their related deliverables
It shows who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed
It breaks the project schedule down into its individual tasks
Scope Management.w: A RAM, often using RACI, maps who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task, giving clear role accountability.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is true of a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)?
o: It defines the physical components of the final product
It determines the order of the project's activities
It links organisational roles to the project's tasks
It sets the level of influence held by each stakeholder
Scope Management.w: A RAM matches roles from the OBS to the tasks in the WBS, ensuring each activity has clearly assigned responsibility.

Scope Management.q: A project team uses the RACI model to assign responsibilities. Which type of tool are they using?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A work breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) is a common form of responsibility assignment matrix used to clarify roles.

Scope Management.q: How does a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) help to reduce duplication of effort on a project?
o: By ranking the project's activities in their order of criticality
By defining the communication channels between the stakeholders
By assigning each member of the team to a specific budget code
By clarifying who is responsible and accountable for each task
Scope Management.w: By assigning clear responsibility and accountability, the RAM prevents overlap and confusion about who should do each task.

Scope Management.q: When is a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) most useful during a project?
o: When defining the project's overall scope and its schedule
When conducting the project's lessons learned review at closure
When assigning clear ownership of deliverables and decision-making
When establishing the communication channels with stakeholders
Scope Management.w: The RAM is most valuable when ownership and accountability for deliverables and decisions must be made explicit.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best defines configuration management in the context of a project?
o: Measuring the project's performance against its agreed baselines
Planning the allocation of resources across the packages of work
Estimating the level of budget reserve the project should hold
Identifying, controlling and tracking the project's products and their changes
Scope Management.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative activity of identifying, controlling, accounting for and verifying a project's products throughout their life.

Scope Management.q: What is the primary purpose of change control within project scope management?
o: To adjust the project's budget in line with the latest forecasts
To allow changes to proceed without approval to maintain momentum
To develop the initial scope statement at the start of the project
To assess and then approve or reject proposed changes to scope
Scope Management.w: Change control is the formal process for assessing proposed changes and deciding whether to approve or reject them before implementation.

Scope Management.q: Testing reveals a flaw and the team wants to modify a deliverable. Which process ensures the change is formally evaluated and approved?
o: Risk assessment
Benefits management
Change control
Schedule control
Scope Management.w: Change control ensures any alteration to scope or a deliverable is formally reviewed and authorised before it is implemented.

Scope Management.q: In configuration management, what does the term 'configuration item' typically refer to?
o: A stakeholder's preferred method of receiving communication
A deliverable or document that is placed under version control
A resource that has been assigned across several tasks
A task that lies on the project's overall critical path
Scope Management.w: A configuration item is any product, deliverable or document that is identified and controlled through the configuration management process.

Scope Management.q: How does configuration management help to maintain the integrity of project deliverables?
o: By approving or rejecting each change request that stakeholders raise
By allocating individual team members to specific project tasks
By identifying each item and controlling and recording its versions
By removing change restrictions so the team can work more flexibly
Scope Management.w: Configuration management identifies the configuration items and controls and records their versions and status, so everyone works from the correct, current version and only authorised changes are made.

n.0: Deciding whether a change is approved or rejected is the job of change control, not configuration management.
n.1: Allocating people to tasks is resource management, often shown in a responsibility assignment matrix.
n.3: Configuration management tightens control over changes to items; it does not remove restrictions.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes the role of a change control board on a project?
o: A group authorised to review and approve or reject scope changes
An external panel appointed to audit the project's accounts
A board that owns the business case and secures project funding
A team that implements approved changes and updates configuration items
Scope Management.w: A change control board is the body with the authority to evaluate change requests and decide whether they are approved, rejected or deferred.

n.1: Auditing the accounts is an independent assurance activity, not the evaluation of change requests.
n.2: Owning the business case and securing funding is the sponsor's role, not the change control board's.
n.3: Implementing changes and updating configuration records is done by the project team after a decision; the board makes the decision.

Scope Management.q: A deliverable is altered without going through the change control process. What is the most likely outcome?
o: More efficient approval of the change by the control board
Reduced cost and improved satisfaction among stakeholders
Stronger compliance with the project's quality standards
Increased risk of scope creep and unplanned rework
Scope Management.w: Unauthorised changes bypass assessment of their impact, leading to scope creep, misalignment with the baseline and likely rework.

Scope Management.q: What does version control help to ensure within the configuration management process?
o: That outdated documents are clearly identified and replaced
That the project's tasks are placed in the correct sequence
That the project's procurement rules are properly followed
That the entries in the risk register are correctly prioritised
Scope Management.w: Version control ensures that only the latest approved versions of documents and products are in use, and older versions are withdrawn.

Scope Management.q: Which process ensures that changes to scope are formally approved so they do not adversely affect quality or budget?
o: Risk escalation
Resource allocation
Team briefing
Change control
Scope Management.w: Change control assesses, authorises and integrates proposed changes so the impact on quality, cost and time is controlled.

Scope Management.q: Why are both change control and configuration management needed together in scope management?
o: To evaluate and approve changes and then maintain them in the outputs
To prevent any changes at all from being made to the project
To provide the project's budget approval and procurement sign-off
To handle only the external modifications made to contracts
Scope Management.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures those approved changes are correctly applied and maintained.

Scope Management.q: During testing a stakeholder suggests altering the interface, and the team updates the prototype without formal approval. What risk does this pose?
o: It reduces the project's reliance on captured lessons learned
It improves team morale but delays the realisation of benefits
It helps the team to finalise the configuration log early
It may cause scope creep and misalignment with the baseline
Scope Management.w: Changing a product without change control means the impact is not assessed, risking scope creep and divergence from the agreed baseline.

Scope Management.q: A supplier requests a change to a component because of a manufacturing constraint, so the project manager raises a change request. Which process decides whether the change is accepted?
o: Change control
Scheduling optimisation
Risk escalation
Scope definition
Scope Management.w: Change control is the formal process used to evaluate a change request and decide whether the change to scope should be accepted.

Scope Management.q: While reviewing the configuration log, a project support officer finds two conflicting versions of a technical specification. Which configuration process has most likely failed?
o: Resource levelling
Risk mitigation
Benefits tracking
Version control
Scope Management.w: Version control ensures a single current, approved version is in use, so conflicting versions point to a failure of this control.

Scope Management.q: Midway through delivery a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Submit a formal change request so the impact can be assessed and reviewed
Add the changes into the next stage of work in order to save time
Amend the configuration records directly to reflect the new requirements
Update the work breakdown structure and begin the changes straight away
Scope Management.w: Under change control, a formal change request must be raised and its impact assessed and approved before any change is implemented.

Scope Management.q: A proposed change is rejected because it would create inconsistencies with existing components. Which process supported this decision?
o: Risk assessment
Schedule management
Quality assurance
Configuration management
Scope Management.w: Configuration management maintains the integrity and consistency of the product, so it can identify a change that would conflict with existing items.

Scope Management.q: A client requests a change to a configured product, and it must be assessed and approved before work begins. Which process provides this formal evaluation?
o: Stakeholder engagement
Risk management
Change control
Scope definition
Scope Management.w: Change control provides the formal route for assessing and approving or rejecting a change before it affects any configuration items.

Scope Management.q: What is the role of configuration management once a scope change has been formally approved?
o: To carry out the approval of the original change request
To redefine the project's chosen life cycle for delivery
To ensure the approved change is applied and documented correctly
To communicate the approved change out to the stakeholders
Scope Management.w: After change control approves a change, configuration management ensures it is implemented, recorded and reflected in the controlled products.

Scope Management.q: A project manager notices discrepancies between the latest deliverable and the configuration baseline. Which process should be reviewed first?
o: Procurement management
Scheduling control
Communication planning
Configuration management
Scope Management.w: Configuration management keeps deliverables aligned with the current approved baseline, so it should be reviewed when discrepancies appear.

Scope Management.q: Why must configuration management and change control operate together on a project?
o: To assign the members of the team to their delivery roles
To allow the project to eliminate the use of baselines
To ensure changes are properly evaluated, approved and implemented
To remove the need for any formal documentation of change
Scope Management.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures they are consistently applied and documented.

Scope Management.q: Midway through a project a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Add the changes to the next iteration in order to save time
Submit a formal change request for the change to be reviewed
Update the work breakdown structure and proceed with the changes
Amend the entries in the configuration log to reflect the changes
Scope Management.w: The first step is to raise a change request so the change can be logged and its impact assessed before any implementation.

Scope Management.q: A senior stakeholder questions whether recent product updates were properly authorised. Which combination of processes evidences both approval and controlled implementation?
o: Change control and configuration management
Scheduling and stakeholder management
Benefits management and procurement
Risk management and issue tracking
Scope Management.w: Change control provides the record of approval, while configuration management shows the change was applied and tracked correctly.

Scope Management.q: A developer implements a software change from an informal request, and it later proves incompatible with existing modules. Which process breakdown occurred?
o: Stakeholder mapping was not kept properly up to date
Change control was bypassed and configuration was not enforced
Quality control was applied too heavily to the work
Risk escalation was skipped during the delivery phase
Scope Management.w: The change was not authorised through change control and was not verified or integrated through configuration management, so both controls failed.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best explains the distinction between change control and configuration management?
o: Change control evaluates proposed changes, and configuration management ensures approved changes are correctly implemented
Change control tracks scheduling milestones, and configuration management carries out product testing
Change control plans the use of resources, and configuration management defines the project team's roles
Change control manages procurement, and configuration management handles the project's budget reporting
Scope Management.w: Change control is the gatekeeper that assesses and approves changes; configuration management ensures approved changes are applied and maintained.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor asks for proof that recent product updates match the approved changes. Which configuration management records should be provided?
o: The version history and the configuration log
The stakeholder matrix and the project's RAID log
The updated work and organisational breakdown structures
The lessons learned report and the project audit plan
Scope Management.w: Version histories and the configuration log evidence that approved changes were tracked and correctly implemented in the product.

Scope Management.q: What does configuration management rely on to determine whether a proposed update can be safely implemented?
o: Approval given through the change control process
The project's overall work breakdown structure
The procedures used for escalating project risks
The project's stakeholder map and analysis
Scope Management.w: Configuration management only applies changes that have first been formally assessed and approved through change control.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder submits a formal request to alter a key deliverable. What is the first step in the change control process?
o: Escalate the matter straight to the project board
Implement the requested change to the deliverable immediately
Log the change request and assess its likely impact
Update the configuration baseline before any review
Scope Management.w: The first stage of change control is to log the request and assess its impact on time, cost, quality and risk before any decision.

Scope Management.q: What must happen before a change can be applied to a project's baseline?
o: Declaration of a change freeze across the project
Renegotiation of the relevant supplier contract
Deletion of the affected configuration item
Formal approval through the change control process
Scope Management.w: No change should be applied to a baseline until it has been formally assessed and approved through change control.

Scope Management.q: A developer implements a requested change without anyone first analysing its effect on scope, time, cost, quality and risk. Which change control stage should have carried out that analysis?
o: Post-implementation review
Benefits review
Configuration audit
Detailed evaluation
Scope Management.w: Detailed evaluation assesses the impact of a proposed change on scope, time, cost, quality, risk and benefits so that a recommendation can be made.

n.0: A post-implementation review is not a stage of the change control process, and it would come too late.
n.1: A benefits review checks whether planned benefits are being realised, usually after the project.
n.2: A configuration audit checks items against their requirements and records; it does not assess proposed changes.

Scope Management.q: Which sequence correctly shows the last four stages of the change control process?
o: Detailed evaluation, recommendation, implement, update plans
Recommendation, detailed evaluation, update plans, implement
Detailed evaluation, update plans, recommendation, implement
Detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans, implement
Scope Management.w: After the change request and initial evaluation, the change is evaluated in detail, a recommendation (decision) is made, the plans are updated, and then the change is implemented.

n.0: Plans are updated before the change is implemented, so work proceeds against the revised baseline.
n.1: A recommendation cannot be made until the detailed evaluation has assessed the impact.
n.2: Plans are only updated once a decision to approve the change has been made at recommendation.

Scope Management.q: In the APM change control process, which stage comes last, directly after the plans have been updated?
o: Carry out a detailed evaluation of it
Make a recommendation to the sponsor
Implement the change and communicate it
Raise a fresh change request for review
Scope Management.w: The six stages are change request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans and implement. Implementing (and communicating) the change is the final stage, once the baseline and plans reflect it.

n.0: Detailed evaluation is the third stage, assessing impact before any decision is made.
n.1: Recommendation is the fourth stage, where the change is approved, rejected or deferred before plans are updated.
n.3: Raising a change request is the first stage. An approved change does not go back round the process.

Scope Management.q: A client requests an urgent change to a critical deliverable. What should the project manager do first?
o: Implement the change straight away to meet expectations
Include the change within the next routine progress report
Email the project team and proceed with it immediately
Raise and assess a change request through the formal procedure
Scope Management.w: Every change, however urgent, is raised and assessed through the formal change control procedure so its impact is understood before any decision.

Scope Management.q: Which document typically captures the details of a proposed scope change before it is formally reviewed?
o: Change request form
Stakeholder matrix
Configuration item log
Communication plan
Scope Management.w: A change request form initiates the process, recording the proposed change and its rationale so it can be assessed and a decision made.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor approved a change, then discovered its full effect on cost and schedule had never been analysed. Which change control stage was missed?
o: Logging the change request
Detailed evaluation
Updating the plans
Implementing the change
