Scope Management.w: Detailed evaluation is the stage that analyses the full impact of a change on scope, time, cost, quality, risk and benefits, and it must come before the recommendation.

n.0: Logging records the request at the start; it does not analyse its impact.
n.2: Updating the plans happens after approval and reflects the decision; it does not analyse the impact beforehand.
n.3: Implementing is the final stage and applies the change once plans are updated.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the stages of the APM change control process?
o: Initial evaluation of the request
Post-implementation review
Updating the plans and baseline
Recommendation on the change
Scope Management.w: The six stages are change request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans and implement. A post-implementation review is not one of them.

n.0: Initial evaluation is the second stage: a quick check of whether the request merits a full assessment.
n.2: Update plans is the fifth stage: the baseline, plan and configuration records are updated before implementation.
n.3: Recommendation is the fourth stage: the change is approved, rejected or deferred by the appropriate authority.

Scope Management.q: A project board rejects a change after assessment shows high cost for limited benefit. What does this demonstrate about change control?
o: It speeds up delivery through early implementation
It removes the need for any stakeholder input
It ensures that only beneficial changes are implemented
It supports uncontrolled changes to the project scope
Scope Management.w: Change control applies formal evaluation so the project is protected from changes that are unnecessary or harmful to its objectives.

Scope Management.q: Which configuration management activity defines how items will be controlled and versioned throughout a project?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Scope Management.w: Configuration planning sets out the framework, roles and procedures for how configuration items will be managed across the project.

Scope Management.q: A configuration management plan is produced during initiation. What does this plan typically include?
o: A list of the approved external procurement providers
Roles, responsibilities, item tracking methods and audit schedules
The benefits realisation strategy for the whole project
A detailed cost breakdown of each individual task
Scope Management.w: The configuration plan defines the framework for managing items, including who is responsible, how items are tracked, and when audits occur.

Scope Management.q: A team identifies all the key deliverables that must be placed under version control. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Scope Management.w: Configuration identification determines which items are to be controlled and labels them so they can be managed.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder asks whether the latest test script represents the most current version. Which configuration activity provides the answer?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting records the version history, current status and location of each controlled item, allowing such questions to be answered.

Scope Management.q: The design specification is uniquely labelled and changes to it are authorised, but nobody has kept a record of its current version or change history. Which configuration management activity has failed?
o: Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting records and reports the current status, version and change history of each configuration item. Without it, nobody can tell which version is current.

n.1: A verification audit checks that items match their requirements and records; it does not keep the records itself.
n.2: Identification uniquely labels the items, and the stem says the specification is already labelled.
n.3: Planning decides how items will be identified, controlled, recorded and audited; the failure here is in the recording itself.

Scope Management.q: Which configuration management activity ensures that only approved changes are made to configuration items?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Configuration control
Scope Management.w: Configuration control ensures that changes to controlled items follow the correct review and approval process before being made.

Scope Management.q: After a change, the team confirms that the new deliverable matches the approved configuration. Which activity is this?
o: Configuration planning
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration identification
Scope Management.w: Verification and audit confirm that items conform to their approved configuration and that changes were made correctly.

Scope Management.q: A configuration audit finds that several different versions of the same document are in active use. Which activity has failed?
o: Configuration identification
Configuration control
Verification audit
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Configuration control should prevent unauthorised or duplicate versions from being released and used across the project.

Scope Management.q: A project sets up a version-controlled folder with controlled access for all configuration items. Which activity does this address?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration control
Scope Management.w: Configuration control includes the procedures that govern controlled access and the storage of approved item versions.

Scope Management.q: A configuration log records the current status of each controlled item. Which configuration management activity does this represent?
o: Status accounting
Configuration control
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting keeps a traceable record of the status of every configuration item and the changes made to it.

Scope Management.q: An audit confirms that versioning rules were followed and only approved changes were made. What does this outcome confirm?
o: That all of the planned benefits have been realised
That the stakeholder requirements have changed
That the agreed project baseline has since changed
That configuration control and verification were effective
Scope Management.w: A satisfactory audit demonstrates that changes were properly controlled and that items conform to their approved configuration.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is not normally an activity within the configuration management process?
o: Status accounting
Configuration procurement
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Procurement is not part of configuration management; the recognised activities include planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification.

Scope Management.q: What is the purpose of configuration verification within the configuration management process?
o: To confirm that configuration items match their approved specifications
To redefine the project budget once the baseline has been agreed
To approve the protocols used for stakeholder communication
To review supplier invoices submitted during the delivery phase
Scope Management.w: Verification and audit confirm that configuration items conform to their approved specification and that records accurately reflect their status.

Scope Management.q: Why is it important to carry out regular configuration audits during a project?
o: To speed up the procurement processes used by the project
To reduce the number of team members the project requires
To confirm that only authorised changes have been implemented and recorded
To ensure that all project work is completed ahead of schedule
Scope Management.w: Configuration audits verify that only authorised changes have been made and that the deliverables and records match the approved configuration.

Scope Management.q: Scope management is often said to have two core activities. Which pair best describes them?
o: Defining the required work, then controlling changes to it
Identifying the risks, then assigning owners to each
Scheduling the work, then levelling the resources across it
Estimating the budget, then reporting the actual spend
Scope Management.w: Scope management first defines the work required and then controls changes to it; the distractors describe scheduling, cost and risk activities.

Scope Management.q: When a project team lists what is 'in scope' and 'out of scope', which discipline are they applying?
o: Procurement management
Risk management
Quality management
Scope management
Scope Management.w: Defining what is in and out of scope sets the boundaries of the project's work, which is a core part of scope management.

Scope Management.q: Uncontrolled additions to the agreed work are steadily expanding a project beyond its plan. Which discipline is intended to prevent this?
o: Scope management
Resource management
Risk management
Quality management
Scope Management.w: Controlling additions to the agreed work, and so preventing scope creep, is a core purpose of scope management.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes what scope management is chiefly concerned with?
o: The tolerances that are applied to the project's cost estimates
The outputs, outcomes and benefits, and the work to produce them
The methods and channels used to communicate with stakeholders
The behavioural roles adopted by the individual members of the team
Scope Management.w: Scope is the totality of the outputs, outcomes and benefits and the work needed to produce them. Scope management identifies, defines and controls that whole.

n.0: Tolerances on cost estimates relate to estimating and cost control, not to what is in or out of scope.
n.2: Methods and channels for reaching stakeholders belong in the communication plan.
n.3: Behavioural team roles are described by models such as Belbin, which is about leadership and teamwork.

Scope Management.q: A learner confuses scope management with schedule management. Which statement correctly explains how the two disciplines differ?
o: Scope management controls cost, while schedule management controls quality
Scope management defines the work required, while schedule management sequences it in time
Both are simply identical processes operating under two different names
Scope management sequences the work, while schedule management defines what is required
Scope Management.w: Scope management defines what work is required, whereas schedule management arranges that work in time; they are distinct disciplines.

Scope Management.q: A colleague asks you to complete the sentence 'scope management is the process whereby...' using APM terminology.
o: ...threats and opportunities to the objectives are identified and managed
...people and equipment are allocated to the project's planned activities
...progress is reported regularly to the sponsor and other stakeholders
...outputs, outcomes and benefits are identified, defined and controlled
Scope Management.w: APM describes scope management as the process whereby outputs, outcomes and benefits are identified, defined and controlled. Doing this well prevents scope creep.

n.0: Identifying and managing threats and opportunities describes risk management, not scope management.
n.1: Allocating people and equipment to activities is resource management and scheduling.
n.2: Regular reporting to the sponsor and stakeholders is progress reporting and communication.

Scope Management.q: A responsibility assignment matrix is typically created by combining which two structures?
o: The communication plan and the procurement strategy
The product breakdown structure and the benefits map
The cost breakdown structure and the risk register
The work breakdown structure and the organisational breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: A RAM maps the work packages of the WBS against the people or teams in the OBS to assign responsibilities.

Scope Management.q: Team members are unsure who is accountable for each work package, causing duplicated effort. Which tool should the project manager use?
o: A risk breakdown structure
A critical path network
A responsibility assignment matrix
A cost breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: A RAM clarifies who is responsible and accountable for each work package, reducing gaps and duplication.

Scope Management.q: A project manager wants to show how the project's work is distributed across the organisation's departments and teams. Which tool suits this?
o: A product breakdown structure
An organisational breakdown structure
A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
Scope Management.w: An OBS structures the project's people resources into the organisational units responsible for the work.

Scope Management.q: A project manager wants to organise estimated costs into a hierarchy of categories for budgeting. Which structure suits this?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
A cost breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: A cost breakdown structure organises project costs into a hierarchy of categories, supporting budgeting and cost control.

Scope Management.q: Which statement correctly matches a breakdown tool to its use?
o: The CBS structures project costs, while the OBS structures the teams
The CBS assigns responsibilities for each project work package
The RAM aggregates all project costs into reportable categories
The OBS lists the risks that could affect project delivery
Scope Management.w: The CBS organises costs and the OBS organises the people resources, each serving a distinct planning purpose.

Scope Management.q: In a RACI responsibility assignment matrix, what does designating a person as 'accountable' for a task signify?
o: They are ultimately answerable for the task's completion, though others may do the work
They are merely kept informed once the task has been completed
They physically carry out every element of the task themselves
They are consulted for an opinion but hold no further involvement
Scope Management.w: In RACI, the accountable person is ultimately answerable for the task, even though responsible parties may perform the work.

Scope Management.q: In a linear project, when is the scope of work normally fixed?
o: Only after the product has been handed over
Continuously throughout each delivery cycle
Early on, and then controlled through formal change control
At the very end, once all work is complete
Scope Management.w: Linear projects define scope early and thereafter manage any changes through formal change control.

Scope Management.q: How is scope typically handled in an iterative project compared with a linear one?
o: It is refined progressively as each iteration is reviewed
It is set by suppliers rather than the project team
It is defined only after delivery finishes
It is frozen at the outset and never revisited
Scope Management.w: Iterative scope is refined cycle by cycle in response to review and feedback, unlike a fixed linear baseline.

Scope Management.q: A linear project treats a scope change as an exception requiring formal approval. Why does this differ from an iterative approach?
o: Because linear projects have no defined scope at all
Because iterative projects expect scope to evolve cycle by cycle
Because iterative projects fix all requirements upfront
Because iterative projects never allow any scope changes
Scope Management.w: Iterative delivery anticipates evolving scope, so change is routine rather than an exception.

Scope Management.q: Two teams run the same product, one linearly and one iteratively. What difference in scope management should be expected?
o: Both teams leave scope entirely undefined until handover
The linear team changes scope daily; the iterative team never alters it
Neither team applies any control over scope changes
The linear team fixes scope early; the iterative team reprioritises it each cycle
Scope Management.w: Linear fixes scope early, while iterative reprioritises it repeatedly as the solution develops.

Scope Management.q: In an iterative project, which mechanism is most commonly used to manage what gets built next?
o: A locked scope baseline signed at initiation
A single change request covering the whole project
A fixed work breakdown never revisited after concept
A prioritised, evolving backlog reviewed each cycle
Scope Management.w: Iterative scope is managed through a prioritised backlog that is reviewed and reordered each cycle.

Scope Management.q: Why is scope in a linear project usually captured in a detailed baseline agreed before delivery starts?
o: So that scope can be decided only after the product is built
So that the team can alter deliverables freely without any record
So that any later change can be measured against an agreed, approved reference
So that stakeholders need not be consulted during planning
Scope Management.w: A fixed scope baseline gives an agreed reference so later changes can be assessed and controlled against it.

Scope Management.q: Which characteristic of scope management is more typical of iterative than linear projects?
o: Complete avoidance of stakeholder involvement in scope
A detailed scope baseline agreed once and rarely altered
Flexibility to adjust deliverables in response to regular feedback
A single formal acceptance of scope at project handover
Scope Management.w: Iterative scope management is characterised by flexibility to adjust deliverables as feedback arrives.

Scope Management.q: Why does a linear life cycle generally require tighter scope control than an iterative one?
o: Because scope is only ever agreed after delivery has ended
Because its baseline is fixed early, so change disrupts the plan
Because it has no defined deliverables that need protecting
Because it welcomes unlimited change at any point in delivery
Scope Management.w: A linear baseline is set early, so uncontrolled change threatens the plan and demands rigorous control.

Scope Management.q: A team switches from a linear to an iterative approach. What should they expect to change about scope management?
o: Scope will now be locked permanently at the start
Scope will no longer need any prioritisation
Scope will be decided solely by the project sponsor
Scope will now be reviewed and adjusted each cycle
Scope Management.w: Moving to iterative delivery means scope is reviewed and reprioritised in each cycle rather than fixed once.

Scope Management.q: In the context of scope management, how is 'change control' best defined?
o: The process for identifying and recording all project stakeholders
The process for levelling resources across the project schedule
The process for closing risks once they no longer apply
The process for formally requesting, assessing and approving changes to scope
Scope Management.w: Change control is the process by which changes to scope are formally requested, evaluated and authorised.

Scope Management.q: A project manager must define 'configuration management' for a new starter. Which description is correct?
o: The formal process for requesting and approving changes to scope
The technical and administrative control of a project's deliverables and their versions
The identification and engagement of the project's stakeholders
The evening out of resource demand across the schedule
Scope Management.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative control of deliverables, their status and their versions.

Scope Management.q: A project logs each deliverable, tracks its versions and controls access to it. Which discipline does this describe?
o: Benefits management
Configuration management
Change control
Quality assurance
Scope Management.w: Identifying, versioning and controlling deliverables is configuration management.

Scope Management.q: Which term describes the process that ensures every alteration to scope is evaluated before it is accepted or rejected?
o: Stakeholder analysis
Configuration management
Change control
Resource smoothing
Scope Management.w: Change control ensures each proposed alteration to scope is assessed before a decision is made.

Scope Management.q: What is the primary focus of configuration management within scope management?
o: Approving or rejecting individual requests for change
Selecting the most suitable procurement route
Maintaining the integrity and consistency of the project's products
Estimating the total cost of each work package
Scope Management.w: Configuration management maintains the integrity and consistency of the project's products and their versions.

Scope Management.q: A team both authorises a requested change and then updates the version record of the affected deliverable. Which two disciplines have they used?
o: Quality assurance, then benefits management
Change control, then configuration management
Change control only
Configuration management only
Scope Management.w: Authorising the change is change control; updating the deliverable's version record is configuration management.

Scope Management.q: A diagram breaks a new aircraft into fuselage, wings and avionics, then into their sub-parts. Which structure is this?
o: Product breakdown structure
Cost breakdown structure
Work breakdown structure
Organisational breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: A product breakdown structure decomposes the final output into its major products and their component parts.

Scope Management.q: A chart divides a project into 'design', 'build' and 'test', each split into smaller work packages. Which structure is this?
o: Product breakdown structure
Work breakdown structure
Cost breakdown structure
Responsibility assignment matrix
Scope Management.w: A work breakdown structure decomposes the total work of a project into progressively smaller, manageable work packages.

Scope Management.q: Once a work breakdown structure is complete, which subsequent planning activity does it most directly enable?
o: Approving the project's business case
Estimating and scheduling the identified work packages
Selecting the project's governance board
Realising the project's long-term benefits
Scope Management.w: The WBS defines manageable work packages that can then be estimated, scheduled and assigned for control.

Scope Management.q: How does starting scope definition with a product breakdown structure help ensure completeness?
o: It removes the need to produce a work breakdown structure
It fixes the project budget before any products are known
It ensures all required deliverables are identified before the work is planned
It confirms who will approve changes to the schedule
Scope Management.w: Identifying all deliverables in the PBS first ensures the work needed to create them can be planned completely, reducing missed scope.

Scope Management.q: A team lists activities like 'write code' and 'run tests' but never identifies the deliverables these produce. Which structure is missing?
o: A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
An organisational breakdown structure
A product breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: The product breakdown structure identifies the deliverables; without it the team risks planning work without confirming what it must produce.

Scope Management.q: A project manager derives the work breakdown structure directly from the product breakdown structure. What benefit does this bring?
o: It fixes the responsibilities of each team member
It ensures the planned work aligns with the required deliverables
It guarantees the project finishes ahead of schedule
It removes the need for any change control process
Scope Management.w: Deriving the WBS from the PBS ensures the work planned maps directly to the deliverables required, reducing the chance of missed scope.

Scope Management.q: At its lowest level, what does a work breakdown structure typically break the work down into?
o: Work packages that can be assigned, estimated and controlled
Individual products and their raw materials
High-level phases only, without further detail
Departments responsible for the project
Scope Management.w: A WBS decomposes work to the level of manageable work packages that can be assigned, estimated, scheduled and controlled.

Scope Management.q: When comparing the two, which pairing correctly matches each structure to what it represents?
o: PBS = deliverables; WBS = the work to create them
PBS = activities; WBS = products
PBS = costs; WBS = timescales
PBS = responsibilities; WBS = risks
Scope Management.w: A PBS represents the deliverables (products), whereas a WBS represents the work required to create those deliverables.

Scope Management.q: Before delivery, a sponsor and team use a product breakdown structure to agree exactly what will be produced. What does this most help avoid?
o: Misunderstandings about which deliverables are in scope
The need to schedule any of the work
The requirement to assign any responsibilities
The production of a project management plan
Scope Management.w: Agreeing the deliverables via a PBS creates a shared understanding of scope, reducing later disputes about what is in or out.

Scope Management.q: A change request has just been logged on a project. What is the next stage in a typical change control process?
o: Close the project's business case
Assess the impact of the proposed change
Update the risk register and take no further action
Immediately implement the change to save time
Scope Management.w: After a change is logged, its impact on time, cost, scope and quality is assessed before any decision to authorise it.

Scope Management.q: A change request has just been approved at the recommendation stage. Which stage of the change control process comes next?
o: Update the plans and baseline
Carry out a detailed evaluation
Implement the change straight away
Log the original change request
Scope Management.w: After the decision, the plans, baseline and configuration records are updated. Only then is the change implemented, so the work is controlled against the revised baseline.

n.1: Detailed evaluation happens before the recommendation, not after it.
n.2: Implementation is the final stage and follows updating the plans, not the decision itself.
n.3: Logging the change request is the first stage and was completed before evaluation began.

Scope Management.q: During the change control process, what is the main purpose of the impact assessment stage?
o: To close any related issues automatically
To remove the change from the register permanently
To implement the change as quickly as possible
To understand the effect on time, cost, scope and quality before deciding
Scope Management.w: Impact assessment evaluates the consequences on time, cost, scope and quality so an informed authorisation decision can be made.

Scope Management.q: At which stage of the change control process is a change formally approved, rejected or deferred?
o: Before the change request is logged
Only once the change has been implemented
At recommendation, after the evaluation
During the transition phase exclusively
Scope Management.w: At the recommendation stage, once the change has been evaluated, the sponsor or appropriate authority decides to approve, reject or defer it.

n.0: Nothing can be decided before the request exists and has been logged.
n.1: The decision must come before implementation; otherwise the change is uncontrolled.
n.3: Change requests can arise and be decided at any point once the baseline is set, not only at transition.

Scope Management.q: Why are the plans and baseline updated after a change is approved but before it is implemented?
o: So that the change no longer needs a formal decision by anyone
So progress is measured against the agreed, current baseline
So that no further change requests can be raised on the project
So that the original change request record can then be deleted
Scope Management.w: Updating plans comes before implementation so that the work, and the measurement of progress, are controlled against a baseline that already reflects the approved change.

n.0: The decision has already been made at the recommendation stage; updating plans does not replace it.
n.2: Further change requests can be raised at any time and go through the same process.
n.3: Change records are kept as an audit trail; they are not deleted once a change is approved.

Scope Management.q: A team implemented a change straight after it was requested. Which stage should have evaluated its full effect on cost, time and quality?
o: Logging the initial change request
Closing the completed project
Implementing the approved change
Detailed evaluation of the change
Scope Management.w: Detailed evaluation assesses the impact of the change on cost, time, quality, scope, risk and benefits, so the appropriate authority can make an informed decision.

n.0: Logging captures the request; it does not evaluate its effects.
n.1: Closure is not a stage of change control and comes far too late to evaluate a change.
n.2: Implementation is what the team did too early; it does not evaluate the change.

Scope Management.q: How do change control and configuration management typically work together when a change is proposed?
o: Both processes independently decide whether the change should proceed
Configuration management approves the change and change control disposes of old items
Change control authorises the change and configuration management records the resulting versions
Change control tracks version history while configuration management judges the request
Scope Management.w: Change control decides whether a change is authorised; configuration management then records and controls the versions that result.

Scope Management.q: How does configuration management support the change control process when a request is being assessed?
o: By selecting the supplier who will implement the change
By setting the overall budget available for changes
By identifying which configuration items the proposed change would affect
By deciding whether the change should be approved or rejected
Scope Management.w: Configuration records show which items a change would affect, informing the impact assessment that supports the change control decision.

Scope Management.q: A change board has approved a deliverable change. Which process now ensures the new version is recorded and the old one withdrawn?
o: Configuration management
Change control
Benefits management
Risk management
Scope Management.w: Once a change is authorised, configuration management records the new version and controls withdrawal of the superseded one.

Scope Management.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between change control and configuration management?
o: Both processes apply only after the project has been formally closed
Configuration management authorises changes; change control audits the schedule
Change control governs whether changes happen; configuration management maintains records of items and versions
They are the same process operating under two different names
Scope Management.w: Change control decides on changes while configuration management keeps the record of controlled items and their versions; the two are complementary.

Scope Management.q: If change control operated without any configuration management, what problem would most likely arise?
o: No change could ever be authorised because there would be no approval route
The project would be unable to identify any of its stakeholders
Approved changes might be made without the resulting versions being recorded or traceable
The business case could not be written before delivery began
Scope Management.w: Without configuration management, authorised changes would not be recorded, so version control and traceability of items would be lost.

Scope Management.q: Why does the combined use of change control and configuration management help prevent unauthorised versions of a deliverable?
o: Version records replace the need to assess the impact of any change
Approval authority is delegated to whoever raises the change request
Changes are implemented immediately and reviewed only at project closure
Only approved changes are made, and every resulting version is recorded and traceable
Scope Management.w: Together they ensure changes are authorised before implementation and that every version is controlled and traceable, preventing uncontrolled copies.

Scope Management.q: How does the timing of change control differ from that of configuration management on a project?
o: Both operate only after the outputs have been handed over to operations
Both operate only once, during the concept phase, and then stop
Change control runs continuously, whereas configuration management acts only at project closure
Change control acts when a change is requested, whereas configuration management runs continuously to keep records current
Scope Management.w: Change control is triggered by each change request, while configuration management is an ongoing activity keeping item records up to date.

Scope Management.q: How do change control and configuration management together protect the integrity of a project's deliverables?
o: One identifies risks; the other transfers them to a supplier
One trains the users; the other reviews the benefits realised
One fixes the budget; the other sets the delivery schedule
One ensures changes are properly authorised; the other keeps items consistent and correctly versioned
Scope Management.w: Change control ensures only authorised changes proceed, while configuration management keeps deliverables consistent and correctly versioned.

Scope Management.q: How do change control and configuration management jointly relate to a project's baseline?
o: Configuration management authorises baseline changes; change control archives the previous plan
Neither of the two processes has any bearing on the project's baseline
Change control authorises amendments to the baseline; configuration management records the updated, controlled baseline
Both freeze the baseline permanently so that it can never be altered
Scope Management.w: Change control governs whether the baseline may be amended; configuration management maintains the record of the controlled, updated baseline.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following correctly lists the main activities of a typical configuration management process?
o: Concept, definition, deployment, transition and benefits
Identification, analysis, response, review and closure
Planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit
Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and closure
Scope Management.w: A typical configuration management process comprises planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit.

Scope Management.q: During configuration management, which activity assigns a unique reference to each item so that it can be tracked individually?
o: Configuration control
Verification audit
Identification
Status accounting
Scope Management.w: Identification defines the configuration items and gives each a unique reference so it can be tracked throughout the project.

Scope Management.q: Which configuration management activity maintains records of each item's current state and its history of changes?
o: Verification audit
Identification
Configuration planning
Status accounting
Scope Management.w: Status accounting keeps the records showing the current status and change history of each configuration item.

Scope Management.q: An auditor physically checks delivered products against the configuration records to confirm they match. Which activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Status accounting
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: A verification audit confirms that the recorded configuration matches the actual products, checking the records are accurate.

Scope Management.q: At the start of a project a team decides the naming conventions, tools and responsibilities for managing controlled items. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Identification
Status accounting
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Configuration planning establishes how items will be managed, including conventions, tools and responsibilities.

Scope Management.q: How does configuration identification differ from status accounting within the configuration management process?
o: Identification records change history; status accounting assigns each item a reference
Identification defines and references the items; status accounting records their state and history
Both assign references, but only one audits the schedule
Both record change history, but only one plans the budget
Scope Management.w: Identification defines and labels the configuration items, whereas status accounting maintains the ongoing record of their status and changes.

Scope Management.q: What is meant by scope management?
o: Selecting and managing the project's suppliers
Preparing and controlling the project's overall budget
Defining and controlling what is, and is not, included in the project
Scheduling the sequence in which tasks are carried out
Scope Management.w: Scope management defines the totality of the outputs and work required, and controls what is and is not included.

Scope Management.q: How does scope management typically differ between iterative and linear project life cycles?
o: Iterative and linear life cycles both fix all scope before any work begins
Iterative life cycles fix scope early, whereas linear life cycles refine scope each phase
Iterative life cycles refine scope each cycle, whereas linear life cycles baseline scope early
Iterative life cycles ignore scope, whereas linear life cycles define it repeatedly
Scope Management.w: Iterative life cycles progressively elaborate scope across cycles, whereas linear life cycles baseline the scope once, early on.

Scope Management.q: Which structure decomposes a project's final output into its major products and their component parts?
o: Product breakdown structure (PBS)
Cost breakdown structure (CBS)
Organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
Work breakdown structure (WBS)
Scope Management.w: A product breakdown structure hierarchically decomposes the end product into its major components and sub-components.

Scope Management.q: Which structure decomposes the total work of a project into manageable work packages?
o: Work breakdown structure (WBS)
Product breakdown structure (PBS)
Cost breakdown structure (CBS)
Organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
Scope Management.w: A work breakdown structure breaks the project's deliverables down into a hierarchy of manageable work packages.

Scope Management.q: Which process ensures that only formally evaluated and approved changes are added to a project's scope?
o: Issue management
Configuration management
Quality control
Change control
Scope Management.w: Change control evaluates, approves or rejects, and documents proposed changes before any adjustment to scope is made.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of scheduling within a project?
o: To track the project's risks and open issues
To confirm that the business case is financially viable
To identify the key stakeholders of the project
To sequence activities and allocate time for their completion
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling sequences activities and assigns durations so the project can be planned and delivered within an agreed timeframe.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager prepares a Gantt chart to show when specific tasks will be carried out. Which aspect of scheduling does this support?
o: Financial and cost reporting
Task sequencing and time planning
Assignment of team roles
Identification of project risks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A Gantt chart is a scheduling tool that displays the order of tasks and when each is planned to take place.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What key benefit does effective scheduling provide to a project manager?
o: Improved levels of motivation across the project team
Easier negotiation with influential project stakeholders
Reduced financial risk within the project business case
Clarity on task dependencies and the overall project duration
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling makes dependencies visible and establishes how long the project will take, supporting sound planning and control.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A schedule shows that two activities must finish before testing can begin. What does this illustrate?
o: A task dependency
A work breakdown structure
A project benefits map
A scope verification check
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A dependency exists where one activity cannot start until another is complete; scheduling identifies these relationships.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is scheduling considered essential to managing the delivery of a project?
o: It defines the overall scope of the work the project will deliver
It establishes the cost breakdown structure for the whole project
It provides a framework to monitor progress and identify delays early
It removes the need for a project manager to oversee delivery
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A schedule sets out when activities occur, giving a baseline against which progress is monitored and delays identified and managed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the primary purpose of critical path analysis in project scheduling?
o: To identify the sequence of tasks that determines the project's duration
To define the overall scope of work for the project
To establish the stakeholder communication methods
To allocate team roles and responsibilities to members
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis identifies the longest chain of dependent tasks with zero float, which sets the minimum project duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager uses critical path analysis to find which tasks must finish on time to avoid delaying the project. What is being managed?
o: Critical path activities
The quality of project resources
The overall project budget
Formal stakeholder approval
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path activities have zero float, so they must be completed on time to prevent the project end date from slipping.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following is a key outcome of performing critical path analysis?
o: A detailed quality assurance plan for deliverables
An understanding of which tasks have scheduling flexibility
A stakeholder influence and interest chart
A revised procurement contract for the main suppliers
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis distinguishes tasks with float from those without, showing where the schedule has flexibility.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Critical path analysis shows a task that can be delayed without affecting the overall project timeline. What is this an example of?
o: Float
Budget slippage
Configuration drift
Scope creep
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Float, or slack, is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project's completion date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is identifying the critical path important to the success of a project?
o: It enables better control of time-sensitive tasks that affect the duration
It improves the project's overall stakeholder engagement strategy
It determines which procurement options the project will use
It ensures only the most skilled members are assigned to tasks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Knowing the critical path lets the project manager focus attention on the tasks that directly drive the completion date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a project milestone?
o: To track the unresolved risks within the project
To assign specific tasks to individual project team members
To measure product quality against the baseline specification
To mark a significant point or achievement within the schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones are zero-duration events that flag key points such as phase completions or major approvals within the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager uses a milestone to record the formal approval of the completed design phase. What does this milestone provide?
o: A checklist of quality requirements
An overview of team responsibilities
A schedule marker that shows progress
A register of the project stakeholders
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone marks a significant scheduled event, such as a phase completion or approval, providing a clear indicator of progress.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why are milestones useful when monitoring the ongoing performance and progress of a project?
o: They provide the deadlines by which supplier contracts must be signed
They reveal slippage by comparing planned and actual achievement dates
They remove the need for any formal progress reporting on the project
They allocate individual tasks to named members of the project team
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones mark key events, so comparing planned and actual dates highlights schedule slippage and emerging risk to delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A milestone marks the completion of system testing. What is its main purpose in the schedule?
o: To trigger a brand new stakeholder engagement plan
To give a checkpoint for monitoring and reporting progress
To move the project automatically into the final closure phase
To allow the risk register to be permanently archived
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone is a significant zero-duration event that acts as a checkpoint for monitoring and reporting progress and communicating key dates.

n.0: Reaching a milestone does not require a new stakeholder engagement plan.
n.2: Moving between phases is decided at a decision gate, not triggered automatically by a milestone.
n.3: The risk register is a living document kept up to date until the project closes.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does a milestone differ from an ordinary task within a project schedule?
o: Milestones must be repeated within every phase of the project life cycle
Milestones have zero duration and mark significant events, unlike tasks
Milestones consume project resources, whereas ordinary tasks do not
Milestones are used only within quality control activities on a project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone is a zero-duration marker of a significant event or decision point, whereas a task represents work that consumes time and resource.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is meant by the term 'time boxing' in project management?
o: Fixing the time allocated to an activity and allowing scope to vary within it
Assigning extra resources to the activities with the longest durations
Holding a reserve of unused time to draw on during emergencies
Extending the project deadline to accommodate additional scope changes
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing fixes the duration of an activity or phase, with the scope delivered varying to fit within the allotted time.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In which type of project life cycle is time boxing most commonly applied?
o: Linear
Iterative or Agile
Extended
Sequential
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing is a core practice of iterative and Agile approaches, where time is fixed and the scope delivered is flexible.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A team is given two weeks to complete as much as possible from a defined set of features. Which technique is being used?
o: Critical path calculation
Time boxing
Milestone tracking
Float analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: This is time boxing: the duration is fixed at two weeks while the scope achieved within it is allowed to vary.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key advantage of using time boxing in project delivery?
o: It ensures delivery is prioritised within a fixed timeframe
It guarantees that the full scope will always be delivered
It removes the need for configuration management activities
It extends deadlines to allow further stakeholder approval
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Fixing the time forces prioritisation and focus, improving predictability of delivery within the agreed period.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A sprint ends before all of its assigned tasks are finished. In a time-boxed approach, what happens next?
o: The team is formally penalised for missing the target
The sprint is extended until every task is complete
The incomplete tasks are permanently abandoned
The remaining work is re-prioritised for a future sprint
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing fixes the time, so unfinished work is reassessed and, if still needed, carried forward and re-prioritised.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager finds that a key resource is assigned to several tasks on the same day. Which technique should resolve this?
o: Milestone tracking
Scope definition
Earned value analysis
Resource levelling
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling reschedules activities to resolve over-allocation, accepting that the end date may be affected.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which statement best describes resource smoothing as a method of resource optimisation?
o: Adjusting activities within their available float to reduce peaks in resource demand
Cutting lower-priority activities in order to shorten the schedule
Adding extra staff directly to the activities on the critical path
Extending the schedule as required to remove all float from the plan
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing reschedules activities within their available float to even out peaks in demand without extending the project end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A team adjusts the start times of non-critical tasks to even out resource demand without delaying completion. Which technique is this?
o: Float analysis
Change control
Procurement scheduling
Resource smoothing
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing uses available float to reduce peaks in resource demand while keeping the project completion date unchanged.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key difference between resource levelling and resource smoothing?
o: Levelling adjusts quality, whereas smoothing adjusts the cost
Levelling may extend the end date, whereas smoothing does not
Levelling applies only to agile, whereas smoothing is linear
Smoothing adds team members, whereas levelling removes them
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling resolves over-allocation by delaying activities and may extend the end date. Smoothing moves activities only within their float, so the end date does not change.

n.0: Neither technique adjusts quality or cost; both reschedule activities against resource availability.
n.2: Both techniques can be used in any type of life cycle.
n.3: Neither technique is about adding or removing people; both move activities in time.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the main purpose of applying resource optimisation techniques when planning a project schedule?
o: To set the thresholds at which changes must be formally approved
To define how the project team will communicate with its stakeholders
To forecast how inflation will affect the overall project budget
To use resources efficiently and avoid periods of over- or under-allocation
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource optimisation adjusts the schedule so that resource demand is balanced, avoiding overloads and idle periods.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A schedule is revised to delay a task by three days so a shared specialist can finish another job first. Which technique is this?
o: Time boxing
Resource levelling
Resource smoothing
Risk transfer
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling resolves a resource conflict by moving task timings to match availability, even where this affects the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When applying resource smoothing to a schedule, which constraint must always be respected?
o: The risk register must be cleared of all entries before smoothing starts
The available float must not be exceeded, so the completion date is protected
The project sponsor must approve each individual resource change first
The stakeholder analysis must be fully revised before smoothing begins
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing works only within available float; the critical path and the project end date must remain unchanged.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When resource smoothing is applied and the project end date must not change, what typically happens to the schedule?
o: Non-critical tasks are rescheduled within their float to even out resource demand
All tasks are moved onto the critical path so delivery is faster
The scope of several tasks is reduced to lower overall resource demand
Additional staff are recruited so that the work can be shortened
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing keeps the end date fixed by rescheduling non-critical activities within their available float to level resource demand.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why might a project manager choose resource levelling rather than resource smoothing?
o: To reduce the number of stakeholders involved in the project
To remove the need for regular progress reporting during delivery
To keep the project's original end date fixed whatever the resource position
To resolve resource over-allocation even if the project end date must be extended
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling prioritises resolving resource over-allocation and may extend the schedule, unlike smoothing which protects the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a typical output of applying resource optimisation techniques to a project?
o: An updated communication plan for the project’s stakeholders
A revised schedule that balances resource demand against availability
A prioritised list ranking the project’s stakeholders by influence
An approved business case setting out the project’s justification
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource optimisation produces a revised schedule in which resource demand is balanced against the resources available.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the main purpose of a procurement strategy in project management?
o: To schedule the internal resources needed to complete project tasks
To identify and document the risks that face the project
To define how goods and services will be acquired from external suppliers
To assign roles and responsibilities to project team members
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy sets out how external products, services and resources will be obtained to support delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager decides to buy in specialist development work from an outside supplier. Which document guides this approach?
o: The change request log
The risk register
The work breakdown structure
The procurement strategy
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The procurement strategy defines whether work is delivered internally or bought externally, and the criteria for doing so.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following would you typically expect to find within a procurement strategy?
o: Preferred contract types and the criteria for evaluating suppliers
The models used to support development of the project team
The amount of float available on each of the project's tasks
The categories used to prioritise the identified project risks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy defines how suppliers will be chosen, including preferred contract types and evaluation criteria.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key benefit of agreeing a procurement strategy at the start of a project?
o: It removes the need to monitor suppliers once contracts are signed
It gives a structured, consistent approach to acquiring goods and services
It replaces the need to produce a business case for the project
It guarantees that internal resources are always selected in preference
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: An early procurement strategy provides a consistent, transparent framework for obtaining resources and services externally.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project needs a specialised system that only two suppliers can provide. What should guide the selection of a supplier?
o: The stakeholder communication plan
The lessons learned log
The project issue log
The procurement strategy
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The procurement strategy sets out the supplier selection criteria and contract preferences that inform such a decision.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the primary purpose of a milestone in a project schedule?
o: To mark the completion of a significant stage or deliverable
To calculate the total float available on the critical path
To allocate the project budget across its work packages
To record the daily effort logged by each team member
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone is a key point in the schedule, usually marking the completion of a significant deliverable or stage; it has zero duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following statements best describes a milestone?
o: A scheduled event marking a key point, with zero duration
An activity with a defined duration and assigned resources
A period of contingency added to protect the end date
A document that lists every risk facing the project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone is a significant point or event in the schedule and, unlike an activity, has no duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why might a project manager include milestones within a project schedule?
o: To remove the need for a formal project management plan
To guarantee that the project finishes ahead of schedule
To provide clear checkpoints for monitoring and reporting progress
To increase the total number of activities shown on the plan
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones give recognisable checkpoints against which progress can be monitored and reported to stakeholders.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project plan shows 'design approved' as a milestone. What does this most likely represent?
o: The list of resources assigned to the design work
The completion of a significant deliverable or decision point
The amount of effort required to produce the design
The total cost of the design phase of the project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone marks a significant achievement or decision point, such as an approval, rather than effort or cost.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Several workstreams must all reach a common checkpoint before integration testing begins. How is this checkpoint best represented in the schedule?
o: As the critical path
As a milestone
As a work package
As a resource histogram
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A shared checkpoint marking a key point that workstreams must reach is represented as a milestone; it has no duration itself.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How do milestones assist a project manager specifically when reporting the status of a project to its stakeholders?
o: They set out the communication methods to be used for each group
They record the full technical specification of each project deliverable
They list the individual costs of every one of the project's activities
They provide clear reference points showing whether delivery is on track
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones give clear, recognisable reference points against which achievement can be reported, showing stakeholders whether delivery is on track.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a supplier contract with staged deliverables, milestones are frequently used to trigger which of the following events?
o: Staged payments once agreed points are reached
The identification of new project-level risks
Automatic changes to the project's agreed scope
The levelling of over-allocated project resources
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones mark agreed points of achievement and are often used contractually to trigger staged payments on their completion.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager prepares a one-page summary schedule for executives showing only the key dates. What are these key dates called?
o: Work packages
Baselines
Milestones
Dependencies
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Key dates shown on a summary schedule are milestones, giving senior stakeholders a high-level view of progress.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During delivery a planned milestone is not achieved on its target date. What does this most usefully signal to the project manager?
o: That the risk register no longer needs to be maintained
That the project's scope has been formally reduced
That the project's budget has automatically been increased
That progress may be slipping and corrective action may be needed
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A missed milestone is an early signal that progress is slipping, prompting the project manager to consider corrective action.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is a milestone shown on a schedule with zero duration rather than as a bar spanning several days?
o: Because it can never appear anywhere on the critical path
Because it is the most expensive element in the schedule
Because it marks a single point in time and represents no work itself
Because it always has the most float of any scheduled item
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone marks a single point in time and involves no work, so it has zero duration, unlike an activity shown as a bar.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which underlying principle lies at the very heart of the time boxing scheduling technique?
o: The cost is fixed and the quality is reduced to meet it
The team size is fixed and the deadline moves to suit it
The time available is fixed and the scope is adjusted to fit it
The scope is fixed and the time is extended until it is complete
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing fixes the period and flexes the scope to fit, rather than extending time to complete a fixed scope.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In a delivery approach that uses time boxing, which element is deliberately held fixed throughout the work?
o: The duration of the period allotted to the work
The full set of features that are to be delivered
The total budget that is available to the project
The size of the team that is assigned to the work
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: In time boxing the time period is fixed; scope is the variable that flexes so the deadline is always met.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Because a time box cannot be extended, what is the likely fate of the lowest-priority items if time runs short?
o: They are delivered by lowering the required quality
The time box is lengthened until they are all finished
They automatically become the highest-priority items
They are dropped or deferred to a later time box
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: With the deadline fixed, the lowest-priority items are dropped or deferred to a later time box rather than the period being extended.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does working in fixed time boxes help a team guard against work expanding without limit?
o: The immovable deadline forces the work to be contained within the period
It removes the need to prioritise any of the work
It fixes the scope so that nothing can ever be added
It allows the deadline to move whenever more work appears
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The fixed, immovable deadline contains the work within the period, guarding against uncontrolled expansion or scope creep.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Short, fixed-length cycles such as sprints in an iterative delivery are an application of which scheduling technique?
o: Parametric estimating
Time boxing
Critical path analysis
Resource levelling
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Sprints are fixed-length cycles, a direct application of time boxing within iterative delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why does an approach based on time boxing depend heavily on clear prioritisation of the work to be done?
o: Because prioritisation removes the need to set any deadline at all
Because the period is simply extended to accommodate all of the work
Because the scope is fixed and therefore cannot ever be reduced
Because only the highest-priority items can be guaranteed within the fixed period
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: With time fixed, prioritisation ensures the most valuable items are completed first, as not all scope can be guaranteed in the period.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does a time-boxed activity differ from a conventionally scheduled activity in terms of what is fixed and what flexes?
o: Its end date is fixed and its scope flexes, rather than time flexing to fit scope
Both its scope and its end date are entirely fixed at the outset
Its scope is fixed and its end date flexes to suit the remaining work
Neither its scope nor its end date is ever actually defined
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: In time boxing the end date is fixed and scope flexes; conventional scheduling instead lets the timeline extend to fit the scope.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A client insists a release must launch on a fixed date, accepting that some lower-priority features may not be ready. Which technique fits?
o: Critical path analysis
Time boxing
Resource levelling
Analogous estimating
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Holding the launch date fixed while allowing lower-priority features to drop is time boxing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In project scheduling terms, what does the technique of time boxing primarily help a project team to control?
o: The elapsed time devoted to a piece of work
The quality standards applied to the outputs
The reporting format used for progress updates
The number of stakeholders that are consulted
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing controls the elapsed time given to a piece of work by fixing the period and flexing scope within it.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Resource levelling and resource smoothing are the two main examples of which scheduling activity?
o: Change control
Configuration management
Resource optimisation
Critical path analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling and smoothing are the two principal resource optimisation techniques used within scheduling.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When resource levelling is applied because resources are limited, what is the likely effect on the schedule?
o: The project cost is guaranteed to fall to its lowest level
The project end date may be extended to fit resource availability
The scope automatically expands to absorb the spare capacity
The critical path is removed from the schedule entirely
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling is resource-limited, so activities are rescheduled to available resources and the end date may move out.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Resource smoothing evens out resource peaks by rescheduling activities within which scheduling allowance?
o: The critical path duration
The project's cost baseline
Their mandatory dependencies
Their available float
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing reschedules activities within their available float, evening out demand without moving the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Resource levelling is most accurately described as which kind of scheduling technique?
o: Quality-limited, adjusting specifications to save resources
Resource-limited, adjusting the schedule to available resources
Scope-limited, deleting tasks until demand is affordable
Time-limited, never allowing the completion date to change
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling is resource-limited, adjusting the schedule to fit the resources available, which may extend the duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A deadline is fixed and cannot move, but resource peaks must be reduced. Which optimisation technique should the project manager apply?
o: Resource smoothing, using float without changing the end date
Crashing, adding cost to shorten the critical path
Fast tracking, overlapping activities to save time
Resource levelling, accepting a later completion date
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: When the end date must hold, smoothing evens out resource peaks using available float without delaying completion.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why might resource smoothing alone fail to resolve a serious over-allocation of resources?
o: Because it always pushes the completion date far into the future
Because it only moves tasks within float and cannot exceed the end date
Because it ignores the project's float when moving activities
Because it deletes tasks from the schedule to reduce demand
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing is constrained by the end date and float; where demand still exceeds capacity, levelling may be needed instead.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In the context of project management, how is a 'procurement strategy' best defined?
o: A matrix assigning internal team members to each work package
The overall approach to obtaining goods and services from suppliers
A record of the threats and opportunities affecting suppliers
A schedule showing when each supplier's work will take place
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy sets out the overall approach a project will take to acquiring the goods and services it needs.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which description best reflects the level and focus of a project's procurement strategy?
o: A high-level plan for how a project will source what it needs externally
A list of the internal skills the project team already possesses
A log of goods received and inspected against their specifications
A detailed cost estimate for every item the project will purchase
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy is the high-level approach to sourcing externally, not a detailed estimate, receipt log or skills list.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A procurement strategy sets out, among other things, decisions about which of the following?
o: Which project risks should be escalated to the sponsor
Whether the project makes items in-house or buys them externally
Which quality tests each deliverable must pass before handover
Which milestones will be used to monitor project progress
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Make-or-buy decisions are a core element of the procurement strategy's approach to sourcing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team documents its overall approach to using external suppliers before any contracts are signed. What have they produced?
o: A procurement strategy
A configuration management plan
A stakeholder engagement matrix
A benefits realisation plan
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Documenting the overall approach to sourcing from external suppliers is the procurement strategy.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does a procurement strategy differ from an individual supplier contract?
o: The strategy binds a named supplier; the contract only sets aims
The strategy lists internal roles; the contract lists project risks
The strategy records goods received; the contract sets the budget
The strategy sets the overall sourcing approach; the contract governs one agreement
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The procurement strategy is the overarching sourcing approach, whereas a contract is the specific agreement with a single supplier.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Deciding whether to use a single supplier or several competing suppliers is a decision captured within which document?
o: The communication plan
The risk register
The quality plan
The procurement strategy
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Supplier relationship decisions, including single versus multiple sourcing, form part of the procurement strategy.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Selecting the type of contract and reimbursement approach for external work forms part of which project document?
o: The responsibility assignment matrix
The issue log
The procurement strategy
The work breakdown structure
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Contract and reimbursement types are decisions set out within the procurement strategy.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following would a project's procurement strategy normally NOT be expected to address?
o: The types of contract to use with external suppliers
The approach to selecting and managing suppliers
The detailed test scripts for verifying each deliverable's quality
Whether to make items in-house or buy them externally
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Test scripts belong to quality control; a procurement strategy covers make-or-buy, contract types and supplier management.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Beyond simply naming suppliers, what does a well-considered procurement strategy aim to achieve for a project?
o: The detailed daily task schedule for the internal project team
Value for money and a sound, consistent approach to sourcing external work
A guarantee that no external suppliers will be needed at all
The elimination of every risk associated with using suppliers
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy aims to secure value for money through a sound, consistent approach to sourcing external work.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager sequences activities and sets their timings before delivery begins. Which project management activity is being carried out?
o: Quality control
Benefits management
Scheduling
Risk analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Determining the timing and sequence of activities, and the resources needed, is the purpose of scheduling.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants to know whether current progress is ahead of or behind plan. Which tool most directly supports this?
o: The business case
The stakeholder matrix
The schedule
The risk register
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The schedule provides the time baseline against which actual progress is measured, showing whether work is ahead of or behind plan.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following statements best describes what a schedule provides to those delivering a project?
o: A time-based plan of activities, dependencies and resources
A record of quality standards the outputs must meet
A list of stakeholders and their communication needs
A justification of why the project should be funded
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A schedule is a time-based plan showing activities, their dependencies, durations and required resources.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is producing a realistic schedule important before a project moves into delivery?
o: It guarantees the project will finish under budget
It replaces the requirement for a project sponsor
It removes the need to identify any project risks
It provides a basis for coordinating resources and tracking progress
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A realistic schedule allows resources to be coordinated and progress to be measured against a time baseline throughout delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Without any schedule, a team is unsure which tasks to start and when. Which core purpose of scheduling is being demonstrated by its absence?
o: Recording configuration items under version control
Establishing the sequence and timing of activities
Defining the acceptance criteria for quality
Approving the project's overall business case
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling establishes the order and timing of activities; without it, the team cannot know what to do when.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following is a direct purpose of scheduling in a project?
o: To forecast when the project is likely to complete
To record issues that have already occurred
To decide which supplier should win a contract
To define the behavioural balance of the team
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: By setting out activity durations and dependencies, the schedule forecasts completion dates and supports planning of resources.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A planner links dependent activities to find the longest path through the network. What are they determining?
o: The minimum time in which the project can be completed
The number of stakeholders needing consultation
The total cost of all the project's resources
The quality standards for each deliverable
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities, which determines the shortest possible project duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is knowing the critical path valuable when managing a project's timescale?
o: Because activities on it can slip without any effect
Because it removes the need to monitor other activities
Because it lists every risk recorded in the register
Because delay to any of its activities delays the whole project
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Activities on the critical path have no float, so any delay to them directly delays the project completion date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In critical path analysis, what is true of the activities that lie on the critical path?
o: They are optional and can be removed if needed
They have zero float and cannot be delayed
They may be delayed freely without consequence
They each hold generous amounts of spare float
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path activities have zero float; delaying any of them extends the overall project duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants to know where to focus attention to protect the completion date. Which analysis best supports this?
o: PESTLE analysis
Cost-benefit analysis
Critical path analysis
Stakeholder analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis reveals the activities that must not slip, showing the project manager where to focus to protect the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Critical path analysis shows a non-critical task has five days of float. What does this tell the project manager?
o: The task must be finished five days earlier than planned
The task can slip up to five days without delaying completion
The task lies directly on the project's critical path
The task should be removed from the schedule entirely
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Float is the time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project end date; five days of float means that much slippage is tolerable.
