Quality.q: A construction project introduced quality procedures early and monitored them regularly; what benefit does this bring?
o: It removes the need to obtain stakeholder approval
It increases the likelihood that deliverables meet their specifications
It guarantees that no changes will occur during delivery
It reduces the amount of planning the team must do
Quality.w: Applying quality management consistently helps ensure deliverables meet agreed specifications and reduces the likelihood of rework.

Quality.q: A team defines, plans and controls its processes so that outputs satisfy customer expectations; what is the purpose of this?
o: To provide the cheapest possible product to the customer
To shorten the overall project life cycle
To ensure deliverables meet stakeholder-defined standards
To transfer quality responsibility across to the suppliers
Quality.w: The purpose of quality management is to define the agreed quality requirements and ensure they are met throughout the project.

Quality.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of quality management within a project?
o: To avoid the need for any configuration control
To provide contingency against any time overruns
To remove every single risk that the project might face
To ensure outputs and processes are fit for purpose
Quality.w: Quality management ensures that the outputs, benefits and the processes that deliver them meet stakeholder requirements and are fit for purpose.

n.0: Configuration management is still needed; quality management does not replace it.
n.1: Contingency against overruns is a reserve of time or money set through risk management.
n.2: No process can remove every risk; that is not the purpose of quality management.

Quality.q: A project manager works with stakeholders to agree the quality requirements before delivery begins; which process is this?
o: Change control of the scope
Quality control of the outputs
Quality planning for the project
Progress reporting to sponsors
Quality.w: Quality planning identifies the quality requirements and determines how they will be met before execution begins.

Quality.q: What is the main output produced by the quality planning process on a project?
o: A project closure report
A project risk register
A change control log
A quality management plan
Quality.w: The quality management plan sets out how quality will be defined, managed and verified throughout the project.

Quality.q: During quality planning, a team agrees to follow recognised industry standards to guide development; what does this represent?
o: Selecting the quality measures for the project
Avoiding risk by outsourcing the work
Assigning the procurement roles for the team
Reducing project cost through standardisation
Quality.w: Choosing standards during quality planning helps define the measures used to verify that deliverables meet requirements.

Quality.q: A team specifies acceptance criteria for the appearance, function and durability of a new product. Which quality management activity is this?
o: Quality planning
Quality assurance
Quality control
Continuous improvement
Quality.w: Quality planning takes the defined scope and specifies the acceptance criteria used to validate that outputs are fit for purpose, along with the standards and quality activities.

n.1: Quality assurance gives confidence that the agreed processes and standards are being followed.
n.2: Quality control inspects and tests outputs against the criteria; it does not set them.
n.3: Continuous improvement looks for ways to improve processes over time, not to set acceptance criteria.

Quality.q: Why is carrying out quality planning during the early stages of a project so important?
o: It guarantees the fastest possible project delivery
It removes the need to communicate with stakeholders
It reduces the budget the project will require
It defines how outputs will be verified against requirements
Quality.w: Quality planning establishes clear verification criteria, reducing rework and increasing confidence in delivery.

Quality.q: On a software project the team decides all deliverables must comply with a recognised standard; which aspect of quality planning is this?
o: Creating the change control procedures
Selecting the relevant quality standards
Defining the overall budget baseline
Documenting the lessons learned so far
Quality.w: Quality planning includes selecting the standards that will guide development and testing of deliverables.

Quality.q: A plan is being produced to set out how requirements will be confirmed throughout delivery; which process does this describe?
o: Quality control of outputs
Quality assurance of processes
Change control of the scope
Quality planning for the project
Quality.w: This is quality planning, which decides how quality will be measured and verified before work is carried out.

Quality.q: Which of the following is a typical activity carried out during quality planning?
o: Monitoring the changing attitudes of the project’s stakeholders
Approving the procurement contracts entered into by the project
Defining the acceptance criteria that deliverables must meet
Identifying the residual risks remaining after responses are applied
Quality.w: Quality planning determines the standards and acceptance criteria that deliverables must meet and how quality will be achieved.

Quality.q: Before construction starts, a manager identifies standards, reviews specifications and outlines inspection procedures; which process is this?
o: Quality control of outputs
Quality assurance of processes
Quality planning for delivery
Issue management activity
Quality.w: Defining standards, requirements and inspection methods before execution is the essence of quality planning.

Quality.q: Which of the following best defines 'quality planning' in the context of a project?
o: Controlling any slippage against the schedule
Determining how quality requirements will be defined and met
Documenting the risk responses that were chosen
Inspecting the finished deliverables to find defects
Quality.w: Quality planning determines the quality standards required and how they will be achieved across the project.

Quality.q: A team inspects completed deliverables to confirm they meet the agreed requirements; which process are they performing?
o: Quality planning of outputs
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Stakeholder management work
Quality.w: Quality control involves inspecting and testing deliverables to verify they meet the agreed quality requirements.

Quality.q: What is the primary purpose of quality control within a project?
o: To document the interests of the stakeholders
To confirm outputs conform to specifications through inspection
To produce a detailed and costed business case
To manage the contracts held with suppliers
Quality.w: Quality control verifies outputs through inspection, measurement and testing to confirm they meet requirements.

Quality.q: After a prototype is built it undergoes several tests to confirm it meets the client's requirements; which process is this part of?
o: Risk management activity
Quality assurance of processes
Quality control of outputs
Change management activity
Quality.w: Quality control includes testing outputs to confirm they meet the required standards and client expectations.

Quality.q: Which activity is most closely associated with quality control on a project?
o: Defining the quality standards the project will need to meet
Inspecting completed deliverables against their agreed acceptance criteria
Conducting the post-project review once delivery is complete
Planning how the quality assurance processes will be carried out
Quality.w: Quality control inspects, tests or reviews completed deliverables against defined acceptance criteria to confirm they conform.

Quality.q: A defect is discovered while the final product is being tested; which process is responsible for detecting it?
o: Change control process
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Issue resolution activity
Quality.w: Quality control detects defects through the inspection and testing of deliverables.

Quality.q: Which statement best defines quality control in a project setting?
o: Training the team members in various quality methods
Planning how the required quality will be assured
Monitoring results to check they comply with standards
Identifying lessons learned from earlier quality issues
Quality.w: Quality control monitors and inspects project outputs to confirm they meet the specified requirements.

Quality.q: A team regularly reviews the work completed so far, checking each output against its specification; which process is this?
o: Risk assessment activity
Resource optimisation activity
Communication planning work
Quality control of outputs
Quality.w: Quality control includes regular reviews and inspections to ensure deliverables meet their agreed specifications.

Quality.q: Which of the following techniques is most commonly used to carry out quality control?
o: A formal lessons learned report
Inspection and testing procedures
The work breakdown structure
Critical path analysis of tasks
Quality.w: Inspection and testing are key techniques in quality control, confirming that outputs meet requirements.

Quality.q: How does quality control contribute to the successful delivery of a project?
o: By communicating agreed changes to the project’s stakeholders
By verifying that outputs meet defined standards before they are accepted
By selecting the most appropriate project delivery methodology
By ensuring that the plans align closely with the users’ needs
Quality.w: Quality control checks outputs against defined standards before acceptance, reducing rework and helping ensure deliverables are fit for purpose.

Quality.q: A quality control check finds that several components fail to meet the specification; what should happen next?
o: Ignore the failures because most components passed
Adjust the original scope to match the output
Change the requirements to suit the output
Report the failure and decide on corrective action
Quality.w: Non-conformance found in quality control should be reported so that corrective action can be taken to meet the standard.

Quality.q: A manager arranges a peer review of the team's process to confirm agreed procedures are being followed; what is this an example of?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Scope verification activity
Change control process
Quality control of outputs
Quality.w: Quality assurance confirms that project processes are being followed correctly so that quality outputs are produced.

Quality.q: What is the primary purpose of quality assurance within a project?
o: To ensure the processes used are effective and followed
To assign the available resources to tasks
To control and monitor the project budget
To inspect and test the final outputs
Quality.w: Quality assurance confirms that the quality processes used to produce deliverables are effective and being applied.

Quality.q: An audit is carried out to assess whether the project's quality procedures are being applied correctly; which process is this?
o: Project scheduling activity
Quality assurance of processes
Requirements gathering work
Risk assessment activity
Quality.w: Audits are a form of quality assurance used to confirm that established quality procedures are being followed.

Quality.q: Which of the following best describes quality assurance within a project?
o: Identifying the risks that the project faces
Monitoring adherence to the quality processes used
Checking finished deliverables against the standards
Defining the acceptance criteria for outputs
Quality.w: Quality assurance ensures that the quality management processes are being followed and remain effective.

Quality.q: A sponsor asks how the team ensures their processes consistently produce quality outputs; which process is most relevant?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Procurement planning work
Quality control of outputs
Stakeholder analysis activity
Quality.w: Quality assurance focuses on the processes used to ensure that quality outputs are consistently produced.

Quality.q: Which of the following is a common tool used to carry out quality assurance?
o: Product inspections of the deliverables
Change request logs for the project
Issue registers maintained by the team
Peer reviews of the processes used
Quality.w: Peer reviews of processes support quality assurance by verifying that agreed procedures are being applied.

Quality.q: A quality assurance review shows that a key process is not being applied consistently; what should happen next?
o: The findings should be ignored by the team
The project should be closed down immediately
Corrective actions should be identified and implemented
The product should be delivered without change
Quality.w: Quality assurance identifies process shortfalls so that corrective actions can realign work with quality standards.

Quality.q: How does quality assurance differ from quality control in the delivery of a project?
o: Assurance checks that processes are followed, while control inspects the outputs
Assurance happens after delivery, while control happens before planning begins
Assurance applies only to iterative projects, while control applies to linear ones
Assurance inspects the deliverables, while control defines the standards
Quality.w: Quality assurance provides confidence that the correct processes are being followed, while quality control checks the resulting deliverables against standards.

Quality.q: A project has quality procedures in place but never reviews whether the team follows them; what is missing?
o: Risk management activity
Scope management activity
Issue control activity
Quality assurance of processes
Quality.w: Without checks to verify process adherence, quality assurance is not being properly implemented.

Quality.q: What is quality assurance primarily intended to prevent during the delivery of a project?
o: Disagreements arising between the project’s various stakeholders
The need for any change requests to be raised during delivery
The approval of the project’s final outputs at each decision gate
Defects in deliverables, by ensuring the correct processes are followed
Quality.w: By giving confidence that appropriate processes are being followed, quality assurance helps prevent defects arising in project deliverables.

Quality.q: In a linear life cycle, a board reviews whether the project should move into its next phase; what is this review called?
o: A stakeholder review
A decision gate
A post-project review
A formal quality audit
Quality.w: A decision gate is a review point used to decide whether a project should proceed to the next phase.

Quality.q: What is the main purpose of a decision gate within project governance?
o: To approve the contracts held with suppliers
To assess whether the project should continue
To carry out the lessons learned sessions
To delegate new work packages to the team
Quality.w: Decision gates provide control points where continuation of the project is reviewed against performance and objectives.

Quality.q: A project fails to meet its key success criteria at a gate review; what is the likely outcome?
o: New scope is added without any assessment
The project may be paused or stopped
The project budget is increased without review
The team proceeds automatically to the next stage
Quality.w: Decision gates allow the organisation to pause, redirect or stop a project based on its current performance and alignment.

Quality.q: At a decision gate review, who typically decides whether the project proceeds to the next phase?
o: An external team of auditors
The project manager acting alone
The governance board or sponsor
The project team collectively
Quality.w: Gate decisions are made by the governance board or sponsor to provide objective oversight and strategic alignment.

Quality.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of decision gates?
o: They let the sponsor decide whether the project continues
They replace all other assurance and quality control activities
They ensure that only the final output is ever reviewed
They remove the need to engage with the stakeholders
Quality.w: Decision gates are points between phases where the sponsor or governance board decides whether the project continues, reviewing the business case, progress and readiness.

n.1: Gates complement assurance and quality control; they do not replace them.
n.2: Gates occur between phases throughout the life cycle, not only at the end.
n.3: Stakeholder engagement continues throughout; gates do not remove the need for it.

Quality.q: What is the main purpose of holding a post-project review once delivery is complete?
o: To assess the morale of the members of the project team
To allocate the project’s resources to the next planned project
To capture lessons learned and evaluate how the project performed
To gain approval for the final budget submitted by the project
Quality.w: A post-project review evaluates performance and captures lessons learned so that future projects can benefit from the experience.

Quality.q: After a challenging delivery, an organisation holds a structured session on what went well and what could improve; what is this?
o: A post-project review
A risk assessment
A quality control check
A cost benefit analysis
Quality.w: A post-project review allows the team and stakeholders to reflect on and learn from the project experience.

Quality.q: Which of the following would typically be discussed during a post-project review?
o: Lessons learned and performance against objectives
Plans for procuring brand new suppliers
Estimates for the costs of a new product
Detailed technical rework of the product
Quality.w: Post-project reviews cover overall performance, stakeholder feedback and lessons learned to inform future projects.

Quality.q: Who should ideally take part in a post-project review to make it effective?
o: The finance department only, reviewing the project’s final costs
Key stakeholders, project team members and project leadership together
The project manager alone, without input from any other party
External consultants only, engaged specifically for the review
Quality.w: A broad group of those involved in the project should contribute so that the review provides a balanced and comprehensive evaluation.

Quality.q: A post-project review finds that weak stakeholder engagement led to missed requirements; what should be done with this insight?
o: Ignore it because the project has now closed
Use it to place blame on the stakeholders
Delete it to protect the project's reputation
Document it as a lesson learned for future projects
Quality.w: Lessons learned should be captured and shared so that stakeholder engagement improves on future projects.

Quality.q: A benefit review is scheduled some months after a project completes; what is its primary purpose?
o: To close down all of the procurement contracts
To assign new tasks to the former project team
To begin a fresh change control process
To determine whether planned benefits have been realised
Quality.w: Benefit reviews assess whether the expected outcomes and benefits have actually been delivered after implementation.

Quality.q: Why are benefit reviews often carried out well after a project has finished?
o: To give the project team time to recover
To reduce the overall costs of the project
To allow benefits time to emerge and be measured
To avoid any pressure coming from the sponsors
Quality.w: Some benefits take time to materialise, so reviews after implementation assess whether those outcomes were achieved.

Quality.q: A benefit review finds that only part of the forecast savings were achieved; what should the organisation do?
o: Analyse why the benefits were not fully realised
Treat the whole project as a complete failure
Cancel all future benefit reviews entirely
Ignore the results because the project has closed
Quality.w: The gap between expected and actual benefits should be analysed and captured as lessons learned for future projects.

Quality.q: Following project handover, who is normally accountable for tracking whether the intended benefits are actually realised?
o: The project sponsor or designated benefits owner
The finance administrator who managed the budget
The lead supplier who provided the deliverables
The project manager who led the delivery work
Quality.w: Benefits are usually realised after the project has closed, so accountability passes to the sponsor or a designated benefits owner identified in the business case.

Quality.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of carrying out a benefit review on a project?
o: An evaluation of whether the expected business benefits have been delivered
A discussion of scope changes held with the project’s suppliers
A report on the availability of the team once the project ends
An internal audit of the time-tracking systems used by staff
Quality.w: A benefits review assesses whether the anticipated benefits set out in the business case have actually been realised.

Quality.q: A project audit examines whether the team followed agreed processes. What is the main purpose of carrying one out?
o: To assess adherence to agreed policies, procedures and governance
To assign blame to individuals for the project's problems
To plan the scope of work for the next project phase
To approve the final invoice submitted by the suppliers
Quality.w: A project audit checks whether project activities have complied with internal and external standards and governance requirements.

Quality.q: Why might an organisation choose to conduct a project audit while the project is still being delivered?
o: To test the completed deliverables for technical faults
To confirm compliance and highlight improvements while action is still possible
To cancel the project before any more money is committed
To sign off the final benefits review with the sponsor
Quality.w: A mid-project audit can surface issues early, allowing corrective action to be taken while the project is still underway.

Quality.q: What best distinguishes a project audit from a post-project review carried out after closure?
o: Audits are informal discussions, whereas reviews are formal inspections
Audits apply only to iterative projects, whereas reviews apply to linear ones
Audits assess benefits, whereas reviews assess only the schedule
Audits check compliance and governance, whereas reviews capture performance and lessons
Quality.w: Audits examine whether the project complied with organisational processes and governance, while post-project reviews focus on results and lessons learned.

Quality.q: A senior manager commissions a check on whether a project complies with corporate governance requirements. Which process is this?
o: Conducting a project audit
Planning the project's risk responses
Realising the project's benefits
Carrying out quality control
Quality.w: A project audit is the formal assessment of a project's compliance with governance, processes and policies.

Quality.q: Which of the following is the most likely outcome of a project audit?
o: Recommendations to improve governance and process adherence
The immediate release of all the project's resources
A revised business case approved by the sponsor
A new procurement strategy for future contracts
Quality.w: Audits are intended to produce recommendations that strengthen process compliance and governance for the current or future projects.

Quality.q: Quality control is often described as a 'detective' activity. What does carrying it out actually involve?
o: Inspecting and testing outputs to find any that do not meet requirements
Auditing whether the correct processes are being followed consistently
Setting the quality standards and tolerances before the work begins
Planning how quality will be managed across the whole project
Quality.w: Quality control is detective: it inspects and tests outputs to find non-conformances, unlike planning or assurance which are preventive.

Quality.q: Of quality planning, assurance and control, which is the only one performed on the finished or in-progress deliverables themselves?
o: Quality governance
Quality assurance
Quality planning
Quality control
Quality.w: Quality control is performed on the deliverables themselves through inspection and testing; planning and assurance act on standards and processes.

Quality.q: In quality management, which activity examines the product itself rather than the process that created it?
o: Quality control
Continuous improvement
Quality assurance
Quality planning
Quality.w: Quality control examines the product, that is the deliverable, whereas quality assurance examines the process used to create it.

Quality.q: A team measures completed components against their tolerances and rejects those that fail to conform. Which quality activity is this?
o: Quality control
Quality assurance
Quality planning
Configuration control
Quality.w: Measuring completed outputs against tolerances and rejecting non-conforming items is quality control.

Quality.q: Which of the following is a typical output of the quality control process on a project?
o: Records of inspections and test results for the deliverables
The schedule of independent process audits to be carried out
The quality management plan produced for the whole project
The list of quality standards the project will adopt
Quality.w: Quality control produces inspection and test records for deliverables; the other items are outputs of quality planning or assurance.

Quality.q: At what point during project delivery does the quality control process principally take place?
o: Before any work starts, when standards are being set
Only after the project has been formally closed down
When deliverables have been produced and can be inspected or tested
Continuously, by auditing the management processes in use
Quality.w: Quality control takes place once deliverables exist and can be inspected or tested against their requirements.

Quality.q: A client asks what calling their deliverable 'quality' actually guarantees about it. What is the best answer?
o: That it conforms to its agreed requirements and is fit for its purpose
That it was delivered faster than originally scheduled
That it includes every possible additional feature
That it is the most advanced and expensive option available
Quality.w: Quality means conformance to agreed requirements and fitness for purpose, not maximum cost, features or speed.

Quality.q: How does the term 'quality' differ from the term 'grade' in a project context?
o: Quality always requires the most expensive materials available
Quality is meeting requirements; grade is a category of features
Grade measures conformance, while quality ranks features by luxury
Quality means a higher grade; the two terms are identical
Quality.w: Quality is conformance to requirements, while grade categorises features or characteristics; a low grade can still be high quality.

Quality.q: A team assumes a 'quality' product must be the most expensive and feature-rich option. Why is this view mistaken?
o: Quality is only ever judged by the project's total cost
Quality has no connection to the customer's stated needs
Quality means meeting the agreed requirements, not maximising features
Quality requires deliberately exceeding every stated requirement
Quality.w: Quality is about meeting the agreed requirements and fitness for purpose, not about cost or maximising features.

Quality.q: A deliverable performs exactly the job it was intended to do. In quality terms, this makes it what?
o: Non-conforming, and therefore automatically defective
Low grade, and therefore of poor quality
Over-specified, and therefore inherently wasteful
Fit for purpose, and therefore of good quality
Quality.w: A deliverable that does exactly the job intended is fit for purpose, which is the essence of quality.

Quality.q: A modest, low-cost component performs exactly as its specification demands. How should its quality be judged?
o: Impossible to judge without knowing its market price
Good, because it meets its requirements and is fit for purpose
Poor, because it lacks additional premium features
Poor, because it is inexpensive and simply designed
Quality.w: Because it meets its requirements and is fit for purpose, the component is of good quality regardless of cost.

Quality.q: Against what standard should a project deliverable's quality ultimately be judged in practice?
o: The total budget that was spent on producing it
The requirements and needs it was created to satisfy
Its ranking against rival products in the marketplace
The number of premium features it happens to contain
Quality.w: Quality is judged against the requirements and needs the deliverable was created to satisfy, not cost or market position.

Quality.q: Why is delivering far beyond the agreed requirements not necessarily a sign of quality?
o: Quality is unrelated to the requirements set for the deliverable
Quality always improves whenever more features are added
Quality is about meeting requirements, so over-delivery can waste resources
Quality is measured solely by how much is delivered
Quality.w: Since quality means conformance to requirements, delivering beyond them (gold plating) adds no quality and can waste resources.

Quality.q: One product is basic but meets every requirement; another is elaborate but misses several. Which better demonstrates quality?
o: The elaborate product, because it offers more features
Neither, because quality cannot be compared between products
The elaborate product, because it clearly cost more to build
The basic product, because it conforms to its requirements
Quality.w: Quality is conformance to requirements, so the basic product that fully meets its requirements demonstrates quality.

Quality.q: Why can two stakeholders usually agree on whether a deliverable has quality when its requirements are clear?
o: Because quality is judged objectively against the agreed requirements
Because quality always means the highest specification possible
Because quality is decided solely by the deliverable's price
Because quality depends only on each person's individual taste
Quality.w: With clear requirements, quality can be judged objectively against them rather than by subjective opinion.

Quality.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of quality assurance on a project?
o: Providing confidence that the processes can deliver the required quality
Inspecting and correcting individual defective deliverables
Giving objective, independent evidence about how the work is done
Checking that the agreed processes are being followed
Quality.w: Inspecting and correcting individual deliverables is quality control; assurance is process-focused and provides confidence.

Quality.q: Quality assurance is often described as 'process-focused'. What does this mean in practice?
o: It concentrates on ensuring the methods used can produce quality, rather than checking each output
It focuses only on controlling the project's overall budget
It records risks and issues as they arise during delivery
It inspects every finished output and rejects those that fail
Quality.w: Being process-focused, quality assurance ensures the methods used are capable of producing quality rather than inspecting each output.

Quality.q: Why is quality assurance often carried out by people independent of the delivery team?
o: So that the delivery team is relieved of all quality responsibility
So that the schedule can be shortened by removing reviews
So that inspection of the final product can be skipped entirely
So that confidence in the processes is objective and unbiased
Quality.w: Independence gives quality assurance objectivity, providing unbiased confidence that processes are sound.

Quality.q: A sponsor wants assurance that the methods being used are capable of producing acceptable outputs. Which activity provides this?
o: Quality assurance, by evaluating whether processes are sound
Quality control, by inspecting each finished item
Risk management, by logging threats to delivery
Configuration management, by controlling document versions
Quality.w: Quality assurance evaluates whether the processes are capable of delivering acceptable outputs, giving the sponsor confidence.

Quality.q: A reviewer evaluates whether the design procedure in use will reliably yield acceptable results. Is this assurance or control?
o: Assurance, because it counts the number of finished items produced
Assurance, because it examines the process rather than a finished output
Control, because it inspects a completed deliverable against its specification
Control, because it corrects a defect found in the product
Quality.w: Examining whether a process will reliably yield acceptable results is quality assurance, which is process-focused.

Quality.q: During delivery a team reviews whether its agreed working procedures are being applied consistently across all workstreams. Which process is this?
o: Benefits management
Change control
Quality control
Quality assurance
Quality.w: Reviewing whether agreed processes and procedures are being applied is a quality assurance activity.

Quality.q: In a project, what is quality management fundamentally intended to ensure about the deliverables?
o: That they are delivered before the agreed schedule
That they are produced at the lowest possible cost
That they involve the fewest possible team members
That they are fit for purpose and meet the agreed requirements
Quality.w: Quality management ensures deliverables meet agreed requirements and are fit for purpose.

Quality.q: Quality management is best understood as an umbrella covering which combination of activities?
o: Quality planning, assurance, control and continuous improvement
Estimating, scheduling, procurement and resource optimisation
Identifying, analysing, responding to and closing project risks
Concept, definition, deployment and transition of the outputs
Quality.w: Quality management is made up of quality planning, quality assurance, quality control and continuous improvement.

n.1: These are planning and resourcing activities, not the parts of quality management.
n.2: These are the stages of the risk management process.
n.3: These are the phases of a linear life cycle.

Quality.q: Why does a project adopt quality management rather than relying on inspection alone?
o: To build quality in through planning, assurance and control
To guarantee the project finishes ahead of schedule
To eliminate the need for any project documentation
To remove the sponsor's involvement in the project
Quality.w: Quality management builds quality in through planning, assurance and control rather than depending on end inspection.

Quality.q: What is a likely consequence of a project running no quality management at all?
o: Deliverables may fail to meet requirements and prove unfit for purpose
The project's scope becomes permanently fixed
Stakeholder communication is no longer required
All of the project's risks are automatically eliminated
Quality.w: Without quality management, deliverables risk failing requirements and being unfit for purpose.

Quality.q: A project manager wants confidence that both the process and the product will meet requirements. Which discipline provides this?
o: Quality management
Risk management
Configuration management
Benefits management
Quality.w: Quality management addresses both process and product, giving confidence that requirements will be met.

Quality.q: How does quality management contribute to overall project success?
o: By removing the need to manage project risks
By ensuring outputs meet the standards stakeholders expect
By fixing the scope so it can never be changed
By shortening the critical path automatically
Quality.w: By ensuring outputs meet expected standards, quality management directly supports acceptance and success.

Quality.q: Which outcome would a well-run quality management approach be expected to deliver?
o: A guarantee that no risks will ever materialise
A permanent freeze on the project's approved budget
Deliverables that reliably conform to their specifications
An automatic increase in the size of the project team
Quality.w: Effective quality management produces deliverables that reliably conform to their specifications.

Quality.q: At what point during a project should quality management activities be applied?
o: Only if a defect is reported by the customer
Throughout the life cycle, from planning through to delivery
Only before any planning has begun
Only at the very end, once the product is finished
Quality.w: Quality management runs throughout the life cycle, building quality in rather than checking only at the end.

Quality.q: A sponsor asks how the project will make sure quality is managed, not just checked at the end. What is the best response?
o: Quality will be measured solely by the final cost
Quality will be left entirely to the supplier to judge
Quality will be planned, assured and controlled throughout delivery
Quality will only be inspected once the product is finished
Quality.w: Quality management spans planning, assurance and control throughout delivery, not just a final check.

Quality.q: Which of the following is the range of outcomes a decision gate can authorise for a project?
o: Only continue, since a gate can never stop a project
Continue to the next phase, amend the plan, or stop the project
Only stop, since a gate cannot allow continuation
Reassign the entire project team to other work
Quality.w: A decision gate can decide to proceed, amend or stop, not merely authorise continuation.

Quality.q: Which review is specifically concerned with confirming whether the intended benefits have actually materialised?
o: A benefit review
A decision gate
A project audit
A post-project review
Quality.w: A benefit review checks whether the forecast benefits have actually been realised, usually after closure.

Quality.q: Which review focuses mainly on capturing lessons learned to improve future projects?
o: A benefit review
A post-project review
A decision gate
A configuration audit
Quality.w: A post-project review captures lessons learned so future projects can benefit from them.

Quality.q: Why is a project audit usually carried out by people independent of the delivery team?
o: So the assessment of compliance with processes is objective and unbiased
So the next phase is automatically authorised
So the benefits can be measured long after handover
So the delivery team can approve its own results
Quality.w: Independence lets a project audit assess process compliance objectively, free from the delivery team's bias.

Quality.q: What does passing through successive decision gates help to confirm about a project during its life?
o: That its scope can never again be altered
That it remains viable and justified before further resources are committed
That the delivery team has followed every process correctly
That all of its benefits have already been realised
Quality.w: Decision gates repeatedly confirm the project remains viable and justified before more resources are committed.

Quality.q: A sponsor wants independent confirmation, during delivery, that governance and processes are being followed. Which mechanism serves this best?
o: A project audit
A post-project review
A benefit review
A decision gate
Quality.w: A project audit gives independent assurance that governance and processes are being applied correctly.

Quality.q: What does the quality planning process mainly set out to establish before delivery of a project begins?
o: The market price of each project deliverable
The behavioural roles within the project team
The quality standards required and how they will be met
The defects found in completed deliverables
Quality.w: Quality planning determines the relevant quality standards and requirements and defines how they will be achieved during the project.

Quality.q: Quality planning is best described as which type of activity within quality management?
o: An activity limited to auditing supplier processes
A proactive activity that sets standards before delivery
An activity concerned only with closing the project
A reactive activity carried out only after defects appear
Quality.w: Quality planning is proactive, establishing the standards and approach to quality before delivery begins.

Quality.q: Before delivery begins, a project manager defines the standards the outputs must meet and how conformance will be checked. Which process is this?
o: Quality assurance
Quality planning
Configuration management
Quality control
Quality.w: Setting the required standards and how conformance will be checked, ahead of delivery, is quality planning.

Quality.q: Which of the following statements most accurately captures the central focus of the quality planning process?
o: Escalating issues that exceed the manager's authority
Reviewing whether agreed procedures are being applied
Measuring completed products against their specification
Identifying the quality criteria and the means to satisfy them
Quality.w: Quality planning focuses on defining the quality criteria to be met and the methods and resources used to satisfy them.

Quality.q: Which of the following outputs would typically result from the quality planning process?
o: A register of risks and their owners
A quality plan defining standards and responsibilities
A signed contract with a chosen supplier
A completed post-project review report
Quality.w: Quality planning produces a quality plan setting out the standards, methods and responsibilities for achieving quality.

Quality.q: A team agrees, at the outset, the tolerances and acceptance criteria their deliverables must satisfy. This activity is an example of what?
o: Quality assurance auditing the applied processes
Benefits management forecasting the project's value
Quality planning defining those criteria upfront
Quality control checking against those criteria
Quality.w: Defining tolerances and acceptance criteria in advance is part of quality planning, which sets the requirements to be met.

Quality.q: In the context of a project, how is the term 'quality' best defined?
o: The degree to which the deliverables meet the agreed requirements
The speed at which the project's activities are completed
The number of features included within the final deliverables
The total amount of budget spent on producing the deliverables
Quality.w: Quality is the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics of the deliverables fulfils the agreed requirements.

Quality.q: What is the main purpose of quality assurance on a project?
o: To inspect each finished deliverable against its acceptance criteria
To provide confidence, by auditing the processes, that requirements will be met
To plan the sequence and timing of the project's activities
To define the agreed boundaries of the project's scope of work
Quality.w: Quality assurance audits processes and methods to give confidence that the project will meet its quality requirements.

Quality.q: A deliverable fails to meet its acceptance criteria during inspection. Which quality activity has identified this?
o: Quality planning
Quality control
Change control
Quality assurance
Quality.w: Quality control inspects and tests deliverables against their acceptance criteria to confirm whether they conform.

Quality.q: The project management office carries out an audit of whether the agreed processes are being followed. Which activity is this?
o: Quality control
Quality planning
Risk analysis
Quality assurance
Quality.w: Quality assurance uses audits of processes to verify that they are being applied correctly and meet the required standards.

Quality.q: After the project's outputs are delivered, the team meets to capture lessons learned. Which review is being carried out?
o: A post-project review
A configuration audit
A benefits review
A decision gate
Quality.w: A post-project review evaluates overall performance and captures lessons learned so that future projects can improve.

Communication.q: Which of the following statements best defines communication in the context of a project?
o: The process of completing and filing project documentation
A control activity used only during the planning phase
The exchange of information between people to reach shared understanding
The transfer of technical data solely to the project sponsor
Communication.w: Communication in projects is the exchange of information to achieve shared understanding and alignment among those involved.

Communication.q: What is regarded as the primary objective of communication within a project?
o: To remove the need for formal project documentation
To ensure that all identified project risks are mitigated
To support shared understanding among the project's stakeholders
To reduce the total number of meetings that are held
Communication.w: The purpose of communication is to ensure that everyone involved understands the relevant information and expectations.

Communication.q: Which of the following is most likely to support effective communication on a project?
o: Delaying all project updates until the project reaches closure
Engaging stakeholders and delivering consistent, timely messages
Changing the communication approach at frequent intervals
Giving the delivery team only verbal instructions
Communication.w: Effective communication depends on engaging stakeholders and sharing consistent, timely information.

Communication.q: A manager defines communication as sending a message from sender to receiver 'with feedback'. Why is the feedback element important?
o: It confirms the receiver has received and understood the message
It formally records the message within the communication plan
It sets out the agreed scope for the project's deliverables
It introduces the technical terminology the team will use
Communication.w: Feedback confirms that the message has been received and understood, which is central to effective communication.

Communication.q: Why is effective communication considered critical to success within a project environment?
o: It allows the project manager to avoid engaging with stakeholders
It removes the need for any project documentation to be produced
It ensures all decisions are made solely by the project sponsor
It enables collaboration and alignment between the project’s stakeholders
Communication.w: Effective communication keeps stakeholders informed and aligned, enabling collaboration and supporting project success.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of face-to-face communication on a project?
o: It removes any need for written follow-up or documentation
It reduces the travel and scheduling costs for the team
It permits immediate feedback and the reading of body language
It guarantees that stakeholders will agree with the message
Communication.w: Face-to-face communication conveys non-verbal cues and allows misunderstandings to be clarified immediately.

Communication.q: What is a major benefit of using virtual communication tools on a project?
o: They guarantee strong cohesion among all team members
They prevent technical problems from disrupting the project
They enable collaboration across different locations and time zones
They remove the need to engage with project stakeholders
Communication.w: Virtual communication allows geographically dispersed teams to collaborate effectively regardless of location.

Communication.q: What is an advantage of using physical, paper-based communication in certain project environments?
o: It prevents any form of miscommunication from occurring
It gives a tangible, lasting record that does not depend on technology
It is always the quickest way to distribute project information
It guarantees that recipients will actually read the information
Communication.w: Physical communication provides a reliable, permanent record in environments where technology access is limited.

Communication.q: A project holds a face-to-face kick-off meeting with key stakeholders. What is a genuine advantage of this approach?
o: It removes the need for any later follow-up communication
It lowers the travel and venue costs for the project
It speeds up the project's procurement decisions
It helps build trust and stronger relationships early on
Communication.w: Face-to-face interaction helps build relationships, trust and alignment at the start of a project.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using instant-messaging platforms within a project team?
o: They support fast, informal exchanges that aid quick decisions
They remove the need for the team to hold any meetings
They create a formal, legally binding record of decisions
They eliminate the difficulties caused by differing time zones
Communication.w: Instant messaging enables rapid, informal collaboration, which is useful for fast-moving issues.

Communication.q: How can virtual meetings benefit a project team spread across different countries?
o: They reduce clarity by removing the body language of participants
They delay project updates because of the technology involved
They remove the need to keep any written record of decisions
They allow real-time collaboration between teams in different locations
Communication.w: Virtual communication lets geographically dispersed teams collaborate in real time without the delay and cost of travel.

Communication.q: Which communication method best allows immediate two-way feedback and interpretation of tone and body language?
o: Posting to a shared online drive
Holding a face-to-face meeting
Distributing a printed newsletter
Exchanging threads of email
Communication.w: Face-to-face communication is the richest method, providing direct dialogue and non-verbal cues.

Communication.q: In which situation is a physical, printed communication method likely to be most beneficial?
o: When real-time collaborative editing is required
When rapid decisions must be reached within the team
When stakeholders are remote and rely on mobile devices
When working with non-digital audiences or in technology-restricted settings
Communication.w: Printed documents ensure accessibility where technology access is unreliable or absent.

Communication.q: What advantage does video conferencing offer when compared with a voice-only call?
o: It removes the possibility of any technical problems arising
It is more formal and removes the need for a meeting agenda
It guarantees that no message can ever be misinterpreted
It conveys visual cues such as facial expressions and gestures
Communication.w: Video adds non-verbal context to a conversation, helping to clarify tone and intent.

Communication.q: Which communication method is most effective for detailed discussions that need clarification and negotiation?
o: Holding a face-to-face meeting
Issuing a monthly written status report
Sending a one-way recorded video message
Circulating a general group email
Communication.w: Face-to-face meetings allow complex points to be discussed and clarified immediately through two-way dialogue.

Communication.q: Why can virtual tools such as shared whiteboards be advantageous for collaborative planning?
o: They remove the need to keep any project documentation
They are inherently more secure than meeting in person
They prevent disagreement between the project's stakeholders
They allow asynchronous contributions from remote participants
Communication.w: Shared online tools support collaboration even when participants are not all available at the same time.

Communication.q: What is a key benefit of summarising a verbal discussion in a follow-up email?
o: It guarantees the eventual success of the whole project
It removes the need for the original discussion to take place
It removes every possibility of the message being misread
It provides a record of what was agreed and the next steps
Communication.w: A written summary creates a record and reinforces shared understanding of what was agreed verbally.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using email for communication on a project?
o: It is always a fully secure and completely private channel
It provides a written trail that can be referred to later
It functions without any need for an internet connection
It removes the need to hold project meetings altogether
Communication.w: Email creates an auditable written record that is easy to store and refer back to throughout the project.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using several different communication methods on a project?
o: It removes the need to plan communication in advance
It reliably leads to information overload for stakeholders
It allows the project manager to reduce stakeholder engagement
Stakeholders receive information in the format that best suits them
Communication.w: Tailoring the method to each stakeholder's needs increases the likelihood that information is received and understood.

Communication.q: What is a common disadvantage of relying on face-to-face communication in a project?
o: It can incur higher costs through travel and scheduling
It is too formal to be used in iterative environments
It limits the opportunities for participants to give feedback
It reduces the level of trust between team members
Communication.w: Although effective for building trust, face-to-face communication can be costly and time-consuming to arrange.

Communication.q: What is a key limitation of using email as a communication method?
o: It is the most suitable channel for urgent decision-making
It is not actually a written form of communication
It lacks tone and non-verbal cues, so it can be misread
It always ensures an immediate two-way exchange of views
Communication.w: Emails can be misinterpreted because they carry no tone of voice or body language.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a potential drawback of virtual communication methods?
o: They provide the same rich body-language cues as meeting in person
They remove every difficulty associated with differing time zones
They always ensure the confidentiality of shared information
They can suffer technical problems and reduced personal connection
Communication.w: Virtual tools can create barriers through technical limitations and weaker non-verbal engagement.

Communication.q: What is a recognised disadvantage of physical, paper-based communication on a project?
o: It promotes instant feedback between the sender and the recipient
It is difficult to update and distribute quickly when things change
It is the most secure communication option in every situation
It is ideally suited to sending urgent updates at short notice
Communication.w: Paper-based communication is slow to amend and circulate, which is a disadvantage in a fast-changing project environment.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of video conferencing in projects?
o: Prolonged calls can cause fatigue and reduced concentration
It cannot be recorded for those unable to attend
It is always more effective than meeting in person
It guarantees that every participant contributes equally
Communication.w: Extended video calls can cause fatigue, which reduces attention and engagement.

Communication.q: What is a downside of relying too heavily on informal verbal communication?
o: It guarantees that information is always communicated accurately
Agreements may go undocumented and be misunderstood later
It removes the need for any defined escalation routes
It substantially increases the volume of project documentation
Communication.w: Informal verbal communication relies on memory, so agreements can be forgotten or misunderstood unless confirmed in writing.

Communication.q: Why can face-to-face communication be less effective in certain project delivery environments?
o: It provides too much written documentation for the team
It can be impractical for dispersed teams or tight schedules
It excludes body language from the exchange of information
It removes the need to consider cultural sensitivities
Communication.w: For geographically dispersed or fast-moving projects, arranging in-person meetings can be costly and time-consuming.

Communication.q: What is a risk of overusing group email threads on a project?
o: They always deliver clear and unambiguous decisions
They can overwhelm recipients and dilute the key messages
They reduce the amount of information that is shared
They create an instant and reliable feedback loop
Communication.w: Excessive group emails can cause important information to be overlooked and reduce overall clarity.

Communication.q: What is a limitation of virtual communication methods when engaging project stakeholders?
o: It always guarantees full understanding of the message
It allows the physical handover of deliverables in person
It supports the same rich non-verbal cues as being present
It can reduce emotional connection and weaken rapport
Communication.w: Virtual settings can hinder relationship-building because of reduced physical presence and informal interaction.

Communication.q: What is a disadvantage of using physical noticeboards for communication on a project?
o: They provide real-time chat features for participants
They rely on people being present in person to see updates
They can be edited and updated remotely with ease
They automatically create a backup of their content
Communication.w: Physical noticeboards are static and only reach those who can access them in person.

Communication.q: What is a common issue with relying solely on virtual communication platforms?
o: They are vulnerable to internet outages or system failures
They remove the need for any project documentation
They function without issue in every geographic region
They require no training for people to use them
Communication.w: Poor connectivity or system failures can disrupt communication entirely when it depends only on virtual platforms.

Communication.q: What is a major drawback of using instant messaging to make project decisions?
o: It can scatter decisions so they are hard to trace
It ensures the team complies with governance requirements
It improves the clarity of the project's agreed scope
It enforces formal stakeholder approval of every decision
Communication.w: Virtual methods often create a record, but decisions spread across informal chats can be hard to find, trace and confirm, which weakens control and the audit trail.

n.1: Informal messaging tends to bypass governance rather than ensure compliance with it.
n.2: Fragmented chats tend to blur, not clarify, the agreed scope.
n.3: Instant messaging does not enforce any approval process.

Communication.q: What is a limitation of relying on phone calls as the main communication method?
o: Calls always provide detailed visual aids for the discussion
Calls remove every risk of a message being misinterpreted
Calls may not be recorded or documented easily
Calls are always the best fit for project governance
Communication.w: Unless recorded or followed up in writing, phone calls can leave no official record of what was said.

Communication.q: What is a risk of stakeholders relying solely on written communication such as reports?
o: Reports are the ideal channel for resolving emotional conflict
Reports encourage immediate two-way dialogue between parties
Reports may be misinterpreted or ignored without discussion
Reports remove all ambiguity as soon as they are issued
Communication.w: Written reports can be overlooked or misunderstood, particularly where there is no chance to seek clarification.

Communication.q: A project manager is drafting a communication plan. Which content should it include to ensure messages reach the right people?
o: The risk register, showing each risk owner and planned response
The work breakdown structure and the detailed activity schedule
Stakeholders, methods, frequency and communication responsibilities
The supplier evaluation criteria and the timetable for receiving tenders
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who receives information, what and why, how and how often it is shared, and who is responsible for sharing it, so messages reach the right people.

n.0: Risk owners and responses are recorded in the risk register, not the communication plan.
n.1: The WBS and activity schedule plan the work itself; they do not set out how information reaches stakeholders.
n.3: Supplier evaluation criteria and tender timetables belong in the procurement strategy.

Communication.q: Which of the following is most likely to be included in a project communication plan?
o: A list of the sponsors of previous, unrelated projects
The technical hardware specifications of the outputs
The individual salaries of the project team members
The frequency and method for each stakeholder group
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who needs what information, why, when and how often, by what method, who is responsible, and how feedback is gathered.

n.0: Sponsors of unrelated projects are not part of this project's audience.
n.1: Technical specifications belong in requirements documents, not the communication plan.
n.2: Salaries are confidential personnel data, not communication planning.

Communication.q: A stakeholder does not receive project updates because of a gap in the communication plan. What was most likely left out?
o: The earned value baseline agreed for the project
The storage location of the archived project data
The stakeholder's preferred method and required frequency
The project's formal change control process
Communication.w: A communication plan specifies who receives what information, when and how, so omitting these details can create gaps.

Communication.q: A team uses a RACI matrix and a stakeholder register to inform its communication plan. What benefit does this bring?
o: Roles and responsibilities are reflected in tailored communication
The overall project schedule is noticeably shortened
Procurement is then able to proceed without any oversight
The need to carry out risk assessments is removed
Communication.w: Drawing on a RACI matrix and stakeholder register ensures each communication is directed to the right person in the most appropriate way.

Communication.q: Which of the following best describes the typical contents of a project communication plan?
o: The system defects, their severity and current resolution status
The supplier contracts, payment terms and procurement schedule
The project's risks, their probabilities and planned responses
Stakeholders, communication methods, frequency and responsibilities
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who needs information, how and how often it will be provided, and who is responsible for providing it.

Communication.q: A communication plan states that weekly status reports go to the steering group, issued by the project coordinator. Which attributes does this define?
o: The audience, method, frequency and responsibility for the information
The probability, impact and response owner for a risk
The severity, priority and closure date for an issue
The supplier, contract value and delivery date for procurement
Communication.w: It specifies what is communicated, to whom, how often and by whom, all of which are standard contents of a communication plan.

Communication.q: External stakeholders report that they are not receiving relevant project information. Which document should the project manager review first?
o: The risk register's list of threats and their owners
The quality plan's checklists and acceptance criteria
The communication plan's stakeholder list and distribution schedule
The benefits register's expected outcomes and measures
Communication.w: The communication plan defines who should receive which information and when, so its stakeholder mapping and schedule are the first thing to check.

Communication.q: What does a well-structured communication plan help a project team to ensure during delivery?
o: That all identified project risks are resolved automatically
That every project meeting is cancelled to save time and cost
That the right people receive the right information at the right time
That only face-to-face meetings are used throughout the project
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who needs what information, when and how, so the right people are kept informed at the right time.

Communication.q: Before delivering a major milestone presentation, why would a project manager consult the communication plan?
o: To review the supplier's procurement performance
To approve an outstanding change request to scope
To confirm the audience, delivery method and timing of the update
To reassess the risk thresholds and escalation triggers
Communication.w: The communication plan defines the who, what, how and when of key information sharing, so it confirms how the milestone update should be delivered.

Communication.q: Which of the following would you least expect to find within a project communication plan?
o: The format and frequency of routine status reports
A record of decisions already taken on the project
The preferred communication channel for each stakeholder
The individuals responsible for issuing project updates
Communication.w: A communication plan is a forward-looking tool; a record of decisions already taken belongs in a separate decision log.

Communication.q: What is a key benefit of a communication plan to the project manager?
o: It prevents any conflict from arising within the team
It ensures consistent, structured messaging reaches the right people
It guarantees that the project will be delivered successfully
It removes the need to maintain any project documentation
Communication.w: A communication plan helps deliver the right message, to the right people, at the right time in a consistent format.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help to reduce misunderstandings on a project?
o: By reducing the amount of stakeholder engagement needed
By clarifying who communicates what, when and how
By transferring all communication tasks to suppliers
By restricting the team to informal conversations only
Communication.w: Clear responsibilities and defined channels support accurate, consistent communication throughout the project.

Communication.q: A new stakeholder joins mid-delivery and the project manager uses the communication plan to brief them. Which benefit does this demonstrate?
o: A reduction in the number of technical defects found
Faster processing of change requests through governance
Improved oversight of supplier procurement activities
Consistent onboarding of stakeholders into established communications
Communication.w: The communication plan ensures new stakeholders quickly receive timely, relevant information and understand existing communication arrangements.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help when several stakeholder groups with differing needs are involved?
o: It allows senior leadership to be left out of all updates
It restricts every communication to a single email channel
It requires the same message to be sent to every group
It lets the manager tailor messages to each audience's needs and influence
Communication.w: Communication plans support stakeholder-specific approaches, improving the relevance and effectiveness of engagement.

Communication.q: What is the benefit to the project manager of defining a communication frequency within the plan?
o: It ensures updates are delivered regularly and predictably
It guarantees that suppliers will meet their commitments
It allows decisions to be taken without any discussion
It removes the need to keep any project documentation
Communication.w: Scheduled updates create consistency and reduce ambiguity, helping to build stakeholder trust.

Communication.q: Two departments received different updates and the sponsor asks why. How does the communication plan help the project manager respond?
o: It requires every department to receive identical content
It prevents the two departments from working together
It removes the manager's need to answer such questions
It records how communications were tailored and the reasons why
Communication.w: The plan documents who receives which information and why, allowing variations in the communication approach to be justified.

Communication.q: What benefit does a communication plan provide when conflict arises from misunderstood expectations?
o: It provides an agreed record of communication responsibilities
It guarantees that every team member is satisfied
It delays resolving the matter until project closure
It removes the need to involve stakeholders at all
Communication.w: Documented communication methods and responsibilities reduce ambiguity and provide a reference point that supports conflict resolution.

Communication.q: Under the communication plan, status updates are issued every Monday by 10 a.m. What does this help the project manager achieve?
o: Freedom from attending project governance meetings
Predictable updates that build stakeholder confidence
Automatic generation of procurement requests
The removal of any need to produce progress reports
Communication.w: Predictable, scheduled updates keep stakeholders informed and build confidence in how the project is being controlled.

Communication.q: In a fast-paced project with several stakeholder groups, what benefit does a communication plan provide?
o: It removes the need to carry out any risk management
It maps who needs what, keeping communication relevant and manageable
It guarantees that all communication happens in real time
It automatically prevents any changes to project scope
Communication.w: A good plan helps the project manager manage the volume and relevance of communication across diverse stakeholder groups.

Communication.q: Why is a communication plan especially valuable when stakeholders change during a project?
o: It removes the need for any formal handover activity
It shows who needs what information, when and how
It allows new stakeholders to ignore past agreements
It prevents any future misunderstanding from occurring
Communication.w: The plan sets out who needs what information, when and how, so new stakeholders can quickly be brought into the right communication routine.

n.0: A communication plan supports handover; it does not replace it.
n.2: New stakeholders are still bound by agreed decisions; the plan does not change that.
n.3: A plan reduces misunderstanding but cannot prevent it completely.

Communication.q: How does having a documented communication plan give the project manager a consistent basis for project communications?
o: It records who receives what information, how and when, so messages stay consistent
It removes the need to identify the project's stakeholders at all
It guarantees the project will be delivered comfortably within its budget
It transfers responsibility for delivery across to the stakeholders
Communication.w: The plan records who receives what, how and when, giving the project manager a consistent, agreed basis for all communications.

Communication.q: Why does having an agreed communication plan actually save the project manager effort during the delivery of a project?
o: It removes the need to maintain a detailed underlying schedule
It automatically resolves all of the disagreements between stakeholders
Communication decisions are agreed once rather than repeated each time
It eliminates every one of the project's risks well in advance
Communication.w: With communications agreed in advance, the project manager avoids reconsidering who, what, when and how for each message, saving effort.

Communication.q: A communication plan helps the project manager manage stakeholder expectations during delivery mainly because it does which of the following?
o: It guarantees that all stakeholders will actively support the project
It sets out clearly what will be communicated, to whom and how often
It fixes the scope so that no further changes can ever occur
It removes the need to record any of the project's risks
Communication.w: By defining what is communicated, to whom and how frequently, the plan sets consistent expectations and reduces surprises for stakeholders.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help a project manager direct communication effort where it is most needed?
o: By removing the need to report progress to the sponsor at all
By matching the type and frequency of information to each audience's needs
By fixing the project scope so that no updates are required
By requiring every stakeholder to receive identical daily updates
Communication.w: The plan matches information type and frequency to each audience, so the project manager focuses communication effort where it is most needed.

Communication.q: In terms of stakeholder support, what benefit does a well-maintained communication plan bring to the project manager?
o: Well-informed stakeholders are more likely to remain engaged and supportive
Stakeholders no longer need to be consulted on any decisions
The project becomes exempt from its scheduled governance reviews
The project's approved budget is automatically increased in size
Communication.w: Timely, relevant communication keeps stakeholders informed and engaged, which helps sustain their support for the project.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help ensure stakeholders receive consistent information even when different team members send updates?
o: It replaces the need for a project schedule during delivery
It defines the agreed messages, channels and timing that everyone follows
It prevents team members from ever contacting stakeholders directly
It requires the project manager personally to send every single message
Communication.w: By defining agreed messages, channels and timing, the plan keeps information consistent regardless of which team member issues it.

Communication.q: Beyond simply sending information, what must effective project communication achieve between the parties involved?
o: A shared understanding confirmed through feedback between sender and receiver
The largest possible volume of messages distributed to everyone
A permanent written record stored for audit purposes only
A one-way flow of instructions requiring no response
Communication.w: Effective communication achieves shared understanding, confirmed through feedback between sender and receiver, not merely the sending of information.

Communication.q: On a project, what distinguishes genuine communication from merely transmitting information to a group of recipients?
o: The volume of information contained in the message
The seniority of the person sending the message
The choice of digital rather than printed channels
The receiver's feedback confirming the message is understood
Communication.w: Feedback that confirms the message has been understood turns one-way transmission into genuine, effective communication.

Communication.q: A communication model describes a sender, a message, a medium and a receiver. Which further element makes it effective?
o: A larger distribution list for the message
A more senior sender issuing the message
A longer, more detailed written message
Feedback confirming the message has been understood
Communication.w: Feedback closes the loop between sender and receiver, confirming shared understanding and making communication effective.

Communication.q: Two team members carried out a task differently after a briefing because neither confirmed what was meant. Which aspect of communication failed?
o: The wrong communication medium was chosen
There was no feedback to confirm shared understanding
The message was too short to be archived
The message was sent to too many recipients
Communication.w: Without feedback to confirm shared understanding, the message was interpreted differently, so the communication was not effective.

Communication.q: Which statement best captures what the process of communication actually involves during project delivery?
o: Issuing instructions that require no response
A two-way process of conveying and confirming meaning
Recording information for audit purposes only
Broadcasting updates to as many people as possible
Communication.w: Communication is a two-way process of conveying information and confirming that its meaning has been received and understood.

Communication.q: Which of the following is the weakest description of communication in a project setting?
o: An exchange of information involving feedback
A process aimed at building shared understanding
A two-way flow between sender and receiver
A one-off transmission that needs no confirmation
Communication.w: Communication requires feedback and shared understanding, so a one-way transmission needing no confirmation is the weakest description.

Communication.q: Which of the following would a communication plan typically specify about each message?
o: The exact cost of producing each report
The supplier's contractual penalties
The project's detailed technical specification
The intended audience for the message
Communication.w: A communication plan defines who each message is for, alongside its content, method, frequency and responsibility.

Communication.q: A communication plan entry reads: 'monthly, by email'. Which two attributes of the communication does this define?
o: Sender and audience
Audience and purpose
Frequency and medium
Purpose and frequency
Communication.w: 'Monthly' defines the frequency of the communication and 'by email' defines its medium.

Communication.q: Specifying that updates will be shared 'via video call' in a communication plan defines which attribute?
o: The frequency of the update
The owner of the update
The medium of the update
The audience of the update
Communication.w: Stating the channel, such as a video call, defines the medium or method of communication within the plan.

Communication.q: Naming the person accountable for issuing each project report is which part of a communication plan?
o: The frequency of the communication
The responsibility, or sender, for the communication
The medium of the communication
The purpose of the communication
Communication.w: Identifying who issues each message defines the responsibility, or sender, attribute of the communication plan.

Communication.q: A project manager lists each recipient, message, channel and timing in a communication plan. Which further detail should be added?
o: The full risk register scoring
The project's complete cost breakdown
The detailed critical path of the schedule
Who is responsible for issuing each communication
Communication.w: A communication plan should also record who is responsible for issuing each communication, alongside recipient, message, channel and timing.

Communication.q: A colleague expects the communication plan to contain the project's full risk scores. Why is this misplaced?
o: Risk scores are never recorded anywhere on a project
Risk scores must replace the audience details in the plan
Risk scores are the sole content of a communication plan
Risk scores belong in the risk register, not the communication plan
Communication.w: Risk scores belong in the risk register; a communication plan records audience, method, frequency and responsibility.

Communication.q: A plan lists the executive board against a monthly summary report. Which attribute of the communication is this defining?
o: The frequency
The medium
The sender
The audience
Communication.w: Naming the executive board as the group to receive the report defines the audience for that communication.

Communication.q: A communication plan records why each message is sent, such as 'to maintain sponsor confidence'. Which attribute is this?
o: The purpose of the communication
The frequency of the communication
The recipient of the communication
The medium of the communication
Communication.w: Recording the reason a message is sent defines its purpose within the communication plan.
