Communication.q: Beyond audience, method and frequency, which further detail strengthens a communication plan?
o: The detailed cost breakdown for each work package
The named owner of each risk in the risk register
A means of gathering feedback from recipients
The supplier's internal reporting lines
Communication.w: Including a feedback mechanism makes communication two-way, confirming that messages have been received and understood as intended.

n.0: The cost breakdown belongs to budgeting and the CBS, not the communication plan.
n.1: Risk owners are recorded in the risk register, not the communication plan.
n.3: A supplier's internal reporting lines are its own affair; the plan covers the project's audiences and channels.

Communication.q: Why is face-to-face communication often the most suitable method for delivering sensitive or difficult news to a stakeholder?
o: It reaches large, geographically dispersed audiences at the lowest cost
It removes the need to follow the conversation up afterwards
It allows tone, empathy and immediate reassurance to be conveyed in person
It creates a permanent written record of exactly what was said
Communication.w: Face-to-face communication conveys tone and body language and allows immediate, empathetic two-way response, suiting sensitive messages.

Communication.q: A contract must be signed and kept as lasting evidence of what both parties agreed. Which method best suits this?
o: An instant-messaging chat
A brief telephone call
A live video conference
A physical, printed document
Communication.w: A physical, printed document provides a durable, signable record, an advantage where formal evidence of agreement is required.

Communication.q: For a quick decision needing input from team members across three time zones, which method offers the greatest advantage?
o: A single face-to-face meeting at head office
A virtual meeting or video conference
A printed memo posted to each location
A physical noticeboard in the site office
Communication.w: Virtual methods connect geographically dispersed members quickly and cheaply, without the time and cost of bringing everyone together in person.

Communication.q: A project manager must brief forty stakeholders in different offices within an hour. Which method offers the strongest advantage here?
o: A briefing poster displayed on every office noticeboard
A printed newsletter posted out to each of the offices
A one-to-one face-to-face meeting with each person
A virtual broadcast or video conference to all of them
Communication.w: Virtual methods are fast and reach many dispersed people at once, so a broadcast or video conference can brief all forty stakeholders within the hour.

n.0: A poster is a physical method: it may not be seen in time and gives no chance for questions.
n.1: A printed newsletter is slow to produce and distribute, so it cannot reach everyone within an hour.
n.2: Forty one-to-one meetings in different offices cannot be held within an hour.

Communication.q: What advantage does a physical display board in a shared site office offer a co-located project team?
o: It provides constant, at-a-glance visibility of key information to everyone present
It captures the tone and body language of the author
It automatically notifies remote members of every update
It provides a searchable digital archive of all the messages
Communication.w: A physical display gives everyone in the shared space continuous, at-a-glance access to key project information.

Communication.q: Which advantage does a recorded virtual meeting offer that a face-to-face meeting usually does not?
o: It guarantees immediate emotional reassurance to all
It can be replayed later by those who could not attend
It always conveys body language much more clearly
It removes any possibility of a technical failure
Communication.w: A recorded virtual meeting can be stored and replayed, giving absent members access to the discussion later.

Communication.q: A dispersed team relies on email for a complex negotiation, which drags on for days. Which disadvantage of email does this illustrate?
o: It provides an instant, written audit trail
It automatically records the sender and time
It handles nuanced, back-and-forth discussion poorly
It reaches large numbers of recipients at once
Communication.w: Email is asynchronous and text-based, making it poorly suited to nuanced, real-time negotiation that benefits from immediate two-way dialogue.

Communication.q: Head office insists on face-to-face reviews, but the project team works across four countries. Which drawback does this most clearly expose?
o: It removes all ability to read tone and body language
It leaves no record whatsoever of any decisions taken
It can only ever reach a single person at a time
It is costly and impractical to gather everyone in one place
Communication.w: Face-to-face meetings require people to be co-located, which is costly and impractical for a geographically dispersed team.

Communication.q: A key decision made verbally in a corridor is later disputed because nobody wrote it down. Which drawback of informal verbal communication is shown?
o: It often leaves no permanent record
It relies entirely on stable technology
It reaches too many recipients at once
It is too slow for urgent matters
Communication.w: Informal verbal communication frequently leaves no documented record, making agreements hard to confirm later.

Communication.q: Halfway through a critical online review, the connection repeatedly drops out. Which disadvantage of virtual communication does this show?
o: It can never involve more than two participants
It always takes far longer than a face-to-face meeting
It leaves no possibility of recording the session
It depends on reliable technology and stable connectivity
Communication.w: Virtual communication depends on reliable technology and connectivity; technical failures can disrupt or degrade the exchange.

Communication.q: A project posts updates only on a physical noticeboard, and remote staff never see them. Which disadvantage of this method does this reveal?
o: It is far too fast for considered messages
It provides no permanent written record
It reaches only those physically present
It prevents any interpretation of tone
Communication.w: Physical, paper-based communication only reaches people at the location, excluding remote or dispersed stakeholders.

Communication.q: Which disadvantage is most closely linked to communicating solely through written reports?
o: They offer no opportunity for immediate feedback
They cannot be stored or referred back to
They depend on continuous internet access
They always reach the wrong recipients
Communication.w: Written reports are one-way and asynchronous, offering no immediate opportunity to clarify or give feedback, so misunderstandings can persist.

Communication.q: Within the context of a project, how is the term 'communication' best defined?
o: The method used to estimate the project's overall budget
The exchange of information between stakeholders to help achieve the objectives
The process used to sequence the project's scheduled activities
The technique used to identify and assess the project's risks
Communication.w: Communication is the exchange of information so that the right stakeholders have the right information at the right time.

Communication.q: Which of the following would typically be found within a project's communication plan?
o: The identified risks together with their planned responses
The decomposition of the final product into its components
Stakeholders' information needs and the methods used to meet them
The hierarchy of work packages making up the scope
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who needs what information, when, how and by whom it will be provided.

Communication.q: A sponsor asks for a progress update by email every Friday. Which element of the communication plan does this define?
o: The frequency and channel of the communication
The sourcing approach for external suppliers
The acceptance criteria for the deliverable
The sequence of the activities in the schedule
Communication.w: Specifying weekly delivery by email defines the frequency and the channel that the communication plan records for that stakeholder.

Communication.q: A team member misreads a decision because tone and body language were absent. Which drawback of communication does this show?
o: Physical communication always reaches the wrong recipients
Virtual communication guarantees that every message is understood
Virtual communication can lose the non-verbal cues that face-to-face provides
Face-to-face communication prevents any written record being kept
Communication.w: Virtual communication without video removes the non-verbal cues available face-to-face, increasing the chance of misinterpretation.

Communication.q: You must share a confidential budget report with the sponsor alone. Which communication method is most appropriate?
o: A secure, private one-to-one discussion
A post on the open project wiki
An email to the whole project team
An announcement at the all-hands meeting
Communication.w: A secure, private one-to-one method preserves confidentiality and ensures the information reaches only the intended recipient.

Leadership.q: Which of the following best defines leadership in a project context?
o: Recording risks and issues in the relevant registers
Enforcing compliance with procurement procedures
Monitoring the budget and updating the schedule
Providing vision, motivation and direction to the team
Leadership.w: Leadership is about inspiring and guiding people towards achieving the project's objectives, rather than administering controls.

Leadership.q: How does leadership differ from management within a project environment?
o: Leadership focuses on scheduling, while management inspires the team
Leadership sets the vision and direction, while management ensures delivery
Leadership handles procurement, while management handles risk
Leadership and management are effectively identical in project delivery
Leadership.w: Leadership provides vision and inspires others, whereas management concentrates on planning, control and execution.

Leadership.q: Which behaviour is most closely associated with strong project leadership?
o: Providing a clear vision and empowering others to deliver
Focusing only on completing technical tasks personally
Delaying every decision until all data is fully confirmed
Micromanaging each individual task within the team
Leadership.w: Effective leaders set direction and empower others to deliver while keeping the team focused on the overall goals.

Leadership.q: A project manager regularly shares the vision, encourages initiative and supports team learning. Which leadership quality is being demonstrated?
o: Inspirational leadership that aligns the team
Purely reactive decision-making
Detailed cost and budget management
A command-and-control leadership style
Leadership.w: Inspirational leaders energise and align their teams around a shared sense of purpose.

Leadership.q: Why is effective leadership important to team performance within a project environment?
o: It removes the need for the team to hold any meetings
It motivates the team and supports collaboration towards shared goals
It guarantees that project risk will be completely eliminated
It ensures that all project contracts are signed on time
Leadership.w: Leadership sets direction and motivates and aligns individuals so that the team works collaboratively towards the project’s shared goals.

Leadership.q: How can a project team leader positively influence the performance of their team?
o: By withholding feedback in order to avoid any conflict
By micromanaging tasks and limiting the team's autonomy
By setting clear goals and recognising individual contributions
By delegating all responsibility to external suppliers
Leadership.w: Clear goals and genuine recognition improve motivation and alignment, which raises team performance.

Leadership.q: A leader creates an environment where team members feel trusted and encouraged to share ideas. What is this most likely to improve?
o: Team performance and innovation
The quality of the risk register
The accuracy of the project budget
The logistics of the project location
Leadership.w: Trust and inclusion encourage collaboration and allow teams to perform at their best.

Leadership.q: Which action by a team leader is most likely to boost performance during project execution?
o: Ignoring team conflicts to keep focus on delivery
Setting unrealistic deadlines to create a sense of urgency
Assigning every complex task to one individual
Coaching team members and providing development opportunities
Leadership.w: Coaching and development raise capability and motivation, which directly improves team performance.

Leadership.q: A team leader recognises a member's contribution during a sprint review. What effect is this most likely to have?
o: It boosts morale and encourages continued high performance
It delays the delivery of future sprints
It demotivates the remainder of the team
It reduces collaboration across the team
Leadership.w: Recognition reinforces positive behaviour and lifts morale, which can drive further high performance.

Leadership.q: Which leadership behaviour is most likely to improve team commitment and output?
o: Avoiding all feedback in order to prevent conflict
Withholding key information to retain control
Setting unrealistic targets to push performance
Encouraging collaboration, openness and shared decision-making
Leadership.w: Inclusive leadership builds trust and a sense of ownership, leading to stronger commitment and better results.

Leadership.q: A team member consistently struggles with their workload. How can the leader best influence performance positively?
o: Ignore the issue in order to protect team morale
Remove the member from the team immediately
Provide support, coaching or mentoring to the member
Publicly highlight the member's poor performance
Leadership.w: Effective leaders support struggling team members to build their capability and confidence rather than penalising them.

Leadership.q: How does active listening help a project leader to improve team performance?
o: It slows down necessary project decision-making
It builds trust and allows issues to be addressed early
It removes the need for any formal reporting
It promotes a culture of blame within the team
Leadership.w: Active listening creates a safe environment where concerns can be raised and resolved before they escalate.

Leadership.q: A project leader uses team feedback to improve work processes and decision-making. What effect is this likely to have?
o: It weakens the leader's authority over the team
It enhances team ownership and improves performance
It increases conflict between team members
It undermines the project's governance arrangements
Leadership.w: Involving the team in shaping decisions creates a sense of ownership that improves engagement and output.

Leadership.q: What is the result of a leader clearly aligning team tasks with the overall project objectives?
o: Increased scope creep across the project
Reduced accountability within the team
Less involvement from key stakeholders
Greater focus and improved team performance
Leadership.w: When people understand the purpose of their work, motivation and focus increase, improving results.

Leadership.q: A project leader encourages open dialogue, recognises effort and adapts their approach to the team's needs. What are they demonstrating?
o: Risk-based contingency planning
A purely authoritarian leadership style
Situational leadership that supports performance
Transactional management of the team
Leadership.w: Situational leaders adapt their behaviour to the maturity and context of the team, which supports its development and performance.

Leadership.q: Which of the following is a common challenge when building a project team?
o: Ensuring that every member has an identical working style
Relying on communication being clear from the first day
Balancing team members' roles, personalities and availability
Removing every difference in members' skills and experience
Leadership.w: Forming a cohesive team requires balancing individuals' roles, personalities, skills and availability.

Leadership.q: What is a key leadership challenge when managing a newly formed project team?
o: Resolving undefined roles and responsibilities
Delivering specialist technical training
Drafting the legal contracts for suppliers
Avoiding any emotional engagement with the team
Leadership.w: Early in a project, roles are often ambiguous, and the leader must clarify them to prevent confusion and inefficiency.

Leadership.q: Members drawn from several departments are struggling with unclear communication and low trust. Which challenge does this illustrate?
o: Difficulties with procurement planning
Cross-functional team dynamics
Work breakdown structure confusion
Disengagement of the project sponsor
Leadership.w: Cross-functional teams frequently face communication and cohesion challenges arising from differing priorities and norms.

Leadership.q: Which of the following is most likely to make it harder for a project manager to develop team cohesion?
o: Frequent changes in team membership
Consistent leadership behaviour over time
Early engagement in team development
Shared values and common goals
Leadership.w: Frequent membership changes disrupt trust and progress through the team's development stages, making cohesion harder to build.

Leadership.q: A high-performing team member frequently dominates discussions. Which team leadership challenge does this represent?
o: Improving weak procurement planning
Balancing assertiveness with inclusive collaboration
Correcting a failure in change control
Managing ineffective benefits realisation
Leadership.w: The leader must value strong contributors while encouraging balanced participation to maintain team harmony.

Leadership.q: What challenge might a project manager face when leading a team spread across multiple geographic locations?
o: Standardising tools that are already uniform everywhere
Reducing over-involvement from the team
Reconciling differing cultures and communication styles
Coping with excessive face-to-face interaction
Leadership.w: Differences in culture and communication style can cause misunderstanding and tension, requiring the leadership approach to be tailored.

Leadership.q: Members of a team with mixed experience are in conflict over task ownership. Which leadership challenge does this represent?
o: Slow approval cycles within governance
Inadequate quality assurance activity
Undefined roles and unclear expectations
Poor negotiation during procurement
Leadership.w: Conflict over ownership usually signals unclear roles, and it is the leader's task to clarify expectations and responsibilities.

Leadership.q: In what way does unclear authority within a project team present a leadership challenge?
o: It can cause delays and disputes over who makes decisions
It increases the speed of every decision that is made
It removes the need for a project sponsor
It boosts accountability throughout the whole team
Leadership.w: Unclear authority creates confusion and hesitation over decision-making, reducing efficiency and eroding trust.

Leadership.q: What challenge might a project manager face when trying to build motivation in a high-pressure delivery environment?
o: The team being consistently underloaded with work
Stress and burnout reducing morale and engagement
Receiving too much interest from stakeholders
Spending excessive time on detailed planning
Leadership.w: Sustained pressure can lead to burnout, which the project manager must manage to keep the team effective and motivated.

Leadership.q: How can frequently changing project priorities pose a leadership challenge when managing a team?
o: They automatically improve the team's confidence
They simplify communication with stakeholders
They can cause confusion and resistance if not communicated clearly
They remove the need for any scope reviews
Leadership.w: Shifting priorities can disrupt momentum and buy-in, so strong leadership and clear communication are needed to realign the team.

Leadership.q: A team member generates many ideas but often loses focus on follow-through. Which Belbin team role does this behaviour most closely reflect?
o: Completer Finisher
Plant
Implementer
Monitor Evaluator
Leadership.w: In Belbin's model the Plant is creative and idea-driven but may neglect the practical follow-up needed to complete work.

Leadership.q: In Tuckman's model of team development, which statement best describes what happens during the norming stage?
o: Members are newly brought together and remain cautious and reliant on the leader
Members work together seamlessly and need very little direction from the leader
Members begin to trust one another, settle into their roles and agree ways of working
Members openly challenge one another as roles and priorities are contested
Leadership.w: During norming, early conflict subsides, trust develops and the team agrees shared norms and ways of working.

Leadership.q: A project team has begun openly disagreeing as members assert their opinions and challenge each other's roles. Which Tuckman stage is this?
o: Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
Leadership.w: Storming is characterised by conflict as members assert their views and challenge roles and leadership.

Leadership.q: In Belbin's team role model, which role is most concerned with meeting deadlines and checking work thoroughly for errors?
o: Resource Investigator
Completer Finisher
Plant
Coordinator
Leadership.w: The Completer Finisher is conscientious and detail-focused, ensuring work is finished thoroughly and on time.

Leadership.q: A project team has reached the performing stage of Tuckman's model. Which leadership approach is most appropriate at this point?
o: Reassign the work frequently to keep the team stimulated
Revisit the ground rules and reset the team's agreed norms
Provide firm direction and closely define every role and task
Delegate and allow autonomy while monitoring for emerging issues
Leadership.w: A performing team is capable and self-managing, so the leader can delegate and facilitate rather than direct closely.

Leadership.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most associated with exploring opportunities outside the team and developing external contacts?
o: Resource Investigator
Coordinator
Implementer
Team Worker
Leadership.w: The Resource Investigator is an outgoing networker who explores opportunities and brings in ideas and contacts from outside the team.

Leadership.q: A newly formed project team is polite but hesitant and unsure of its direction. According to Tuckman's model, what should the leader mainly do?
o: Encourage members to work independently straight away
Avoid setting expectations to see how the team develops
Step back and let the team organise itself immediately
Provide clear direction and define the team's goals and roles
Leadership.w: In the forming stage the team looks to the leader for direction and structure to build its early confidence.

Leadership.q: A project manager finds the team has no Monitor Evaluator among its Belbin roles. Which risk is this most likely to create?
o: A shortage of new and creative ideas
Too great a reliance on outside stakeholders
Excessive attention to minor details
Weaker critical analysis and poorer decision-making
Leadership.w: The Monitor Evaluator supplies objective, analytical judgement; without one the team may reach poorly considered decisions.

Leadership.q: A previously settled team is joined by several new members who are unsure of their roles and look to the project manager for direction. To which Tuckman stage has the team most likely returned?
o: Adjourning
Forming
Norming
Storming
Leadership.w: In forming, members are polite, unsure of their roles and dependent on the leader, who should give clear direction. A big change in membership often takes a team back to this stage.

n.0: Adjourning happens when the task is complete and the team disbands.
n.2: Norming is when ways of working are agreed and the team is cohesive, which is not the case here.
n.3: Storming involves open conflict and challenge to roles; here members are uncertain and looking for direction.

Leadership.q: A team member regularly supports colleagues, smooths over disagreements and helps keep the group harmonious. Which Belbin role best fits?
o: Specialist
Shaper
Co-ordinator
Teamworker
Leadership.w: The Teamworker is co-operative and diplomatic, supporting others and easing friction so the team stays cohesive.

n.0: The Specialist brings in-depth knowledge of a particular subject.
n.1: The Shaper drives the team forward and challenges it, which can create friction.
n.2: The Co-ordinator clarifies goals, delegates and chairs, rather than mainly smoothing relationships.

Leadership.q: You take charge of a project team whose members have not worked together before. What should your leadership focus be in the early stages?
o: Concentrate solely on technical delivery
Clarify roles, responsibilities and shared expectations
Let the team manage itself from the very start
Offer performance-based incentives before any work begins
Leadership.w: An unfamiliar team needs clear direction and agreed expectations to form a cohesive structure and work effectively.

Leadership.q: Two strong personalities in a project team are repeatedly in conflict. Which Tuckman stage does this reflect, and how should the leader respond?
o: Storming; help resolve it through open, respectful discussion
Forming; avoid any confrontation between them
Norming; increase their workload to distract them
Performing; reassign both members elsewhere
Leadership.w: Conflict as roles are asserted is typical of storming; the leader should facilitate open resolution rather than suppress it.

Leadership.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most focused on turning ideas and plans into practical, workable actions?
o: Implementer
Resource Investigator
Plant
Monitor Evaluator
Leadership.w: The Implementer is disciplined and reliable, converting concepts and plans into organised, practical action.

Leadership.q: A new member joins a project team midway through, tension rises and productivity dips. What should the project leader do?
o: Return to team-building activity to rebuild cohesion
Keep the new member on separate tasks until things settle
Delegate more decisions so the team can sort it out alone
Escalate the tension to the sponsor as a project issue
Leadership.w: A change in membership can send a team back to forming or storming. The leader should recognise this and use team-building to rebuild cohesion and move the team on.

n.1: Keeping the new member apart delays integration and does nothing to resolve the tension.
n.2: Delegating suits a performing team; a team that has slipped back into storming needs the leader to coach it and manage the conflict.
n.3: Team tension is the project manager's responsibility to lead through; it is not an issue beyond tolerance for the sponsor.

Leadership.q: Which stage of Tuckman's model best describes a mature team that delivers effectively and needs little supervision?
o: Forming
Performing
Storming
Norming
Leadership.w: In the performing stage the team is capable, self-directing and works efficiently towards its shared goals.

Leadership.q: A team member habitually questions assumptions and weighs the options logically before decisions are made. Which Belbin role does this suggest?
o: Shaper
Monitor Evaluator
Coordinator
Implementer
Leadership.w: The Monitor Evaluator is a logical, impartial thinker who analyses options and offers balanced judgement.

Leadership.q: A project team has reached the adjourning stage of Tuckman's model. Which leadership action is most appropriate?
o: Introduce fresh team norms and ground rules
Increase the workload to sustain performance
Recognise the team's achievements and support the transition
Drive the team straight into a new forming phase
Leadership.w: Adjourning marks disbandment, so the leader should acknowledge contributions and help members transition smoothly.

Leadership.q: A project manager brings in an expert to supply in-depth knowledge the team currently lacks. Which Belbin role does this describe?
o: Specialist
Shaper
Team Worker
Coordinator
Leadership.w: The Specialist provides deep, focused expertise in a specific area that the rest of the team does not possess.

Leadership.q: Partway through a project the team resolves its own disagreements and no longer needs frequent check-ins. Which Tuckman stage is this?
o: Performing
Norming
Forming
Storming
Leadership.w: A performing team is mature and self-regulating, working effectively with minimal supervision from the leader.

Leadership.q: A team member regularly offers original, unorthodox ideas and creative solutions during workshops. Which Belbin role best describes them?
o: Completer Finisher
Team Worker
Plant
Shaper
Leadership.w: The Plant is the creative thinker who generates novel ideas and imaginative solutions to the team's problems.

Leadership.q: In a project, leadership is most closely concerned with which of the following?
o: Establishing direction and motivating people to achieve shared goals
Inspecting deliverables to confirm they meet their requirements
Aggregating the project's costs into reporting categories
Recording and controlling changes to the scope baseline
Leadership.w: Leadership is chiefly about establishing direction and motivating people towards shared goals, unlike technical control activities.

Leadership.q: What distinguishes genuine leadership from merely instructing a team to comply?
o: It concentrates on producing detailed progress reports
It motivates people to commit willingly towards shared goals
It focuses on allocating resources evenly across all tasks
It relies on enforcing rules so people obey through instruction
Leadership.w: Leadership motivates people to commit willingly to shared goals, rather than securing mere compliance through instruction.

Leadership.q: A project leader is described as providing 'direction'. What does this element of leadership involve?
o: Setting a clear vision and guiding the team towards shared objectives
Updating the configuration status of controlled items
Approving invoices submitted by the project's suppliers
Logging every risk that could affect the project outcome
Leadership.w: Providing direction is the leadership function of setting a vision and guiding the team towards shared objectives.

Leadership.q: A manager unites the team around a shared goal and motivates them to commit to it. Which capability are they chiefly demonstrating?
o: Assurance
Scheduling
Procurement
Leadership
Leadership.w: Uniting a team around a goal and motivating commitment is a demonstration of leadership.

Leadership.q: One manager plans and controls the work; another energises and directs the people. Which is chiefly exercising leadership?
o: Both equally, because leadership simply means administration
Neither, since the two activities are identical
The manager who energises and directs the people
The manager who plans and controls the work
Leadership.w: Leadership is about energising and directing people towards a vision, whereas planning and controlling the work is management.

Leadership.q: Beyond simply issuing orders, effective project leadership is best characterised by which behaviour?
o: Avoiding contact with the team to remain impartial
Issuing detailed instructions and requiring strict compliance
Focusing solely on the project's budget and schedule
Enabling and empowering people to contribute their best towards the goal
Leadership.w: Leadership enables and empowers people to contribute their best, going beyond merely issuing orders.

Leadership.q: Why can leading a team drawn from several different departments be challenging for a project manager?
o: Members automatically report only to the project manager
Members always share identical objectives and priorities
Members never require any form of communication
Members may have divided loyalties and competing priorities
Leadership.w: Cross-functional members often answer to home managers too, creating divided loyalties and competing priorities.

Leadership.q: A project team includes members who only work part-time on the project. Which leadership challenge does this most likely create?
o: They will never need any direction from the project manager
Their limited availability may conflict with their other duties
They will always prioritise the project above all other work
They automatically remove all risk from the project
Leadership.w: Part-time members split their time, so availability clashes with their other duties are a common challenge.

Leadership.q: Which factor most commonly makes it difficult to build trust within a newly assembled project team?
o: Members already know each other's strengths perfectly
Members have no individual roles to fulfil
Members have a long shared history of working together
Members are unfamiliar with one another's ways of working
Leadership.w: In a new team, members are unfamiliar with each other's styles, so trust takes time to establish.

Leadership.q: A project manager has no direct line-management authority over team members borrowed from other functions. Why is this a challenge?
o: The project no longer requires any leadership at all
The team can now be instructed without any negotiation
Influence must be relied upon because formal authority is limited
The members will automatically ignore their home managers
Leadership.w: With limited formal authority, the project manager must lead through influence rather than instruction.

Leadership.q: Two experienced specialists on a project team repeatedly clash over how the work should be done. What leadership challenge is this?
o: Removing the need for any communication between members
Guaranteeing that no member ever contributes an idea
Managing interpersonal conflict between strong team members
Ensuring every member holds an identical opinion
Leadership.w: Reconciling conflict between strong individuals is a genuine leadership challenge when developing a team.

Leadership.q: A newly formed team works entirely remotely and rarely meets in person. Which leadership challenge is most likely to arise?
o: Preventing the team from using any digital tools
Building rapport and trust without regular face-to-face contact
Ensuring members never communicate outside meetings
Guaranteeing that no member needs any direction
Leadership.w: Remote working makes building rapport and trust harder without the regular face-to-face contact that fosters it.

Leadership.q: Why might a project manager use models such as Belbin and Tuckman when developing a team?
o: To understand team roles and development stages and adapt their approach
To calculate the project's overall budget
To replace the need for a project schedule
To decide the project's procurement strategy
Leadership.w: Such models help the manager understand behavioural roles and development stages, so leadership can be adapted to support the team.

Leadership.q: Which aspect of a team does Belbin's model primarily help a project manager to understand?
o: The order in which risks should be addressed
The reporting lines shown in an organisational breakdown structure
The stages a team moves through as it matures
The balance of behavioural roles within the team
Leadership.w: Belbin's model describes behavioural team roles, helping the manager build a balanced and effective team.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to anticipate how their new team's behaviour will change as it matures. Which model is most relevant?
o: Tuckman's stages of team development
A responsibility assignment matrix
A PESTLE analysis
Belbin's team roles
Leadership.w: Tuckman's model describes forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, helping anticipate how a team develops over time.

Leadership.q: Using Belbin, a manager finds the team has no one focused on checking work for errors. Which action does the model suggest?
o: Escalate the whole project to the sponsor immediately
Move the team to Tuckman's adjourning stage
Add or develop a Completer Finisher role in the team
Abandon the use of any team development model
Leadership.w: Belbin's Completer Finisher focuses on accuracy and checking work, so filling that gap balances the team.

Leadership.q: Understanding that a team is at Tuckman's storming stage, how should a project manager use this insight?
o: By helping resolve conflict and clarifying roles and goals
By disbanding the team and starting again
By assuming the team is fully mature and self-managing
By stepping back entirely and giving no direction
Leadership.w: At the storming stage, conflict emerges, so the leader should facilitate resolution and clarify roles and objectives.

Leadership.q: A project manager applies Tuckman and Belbin, but a colleague expects them to remove all team problems. What is the correct view?
o: The models guide team development but do not guarantee a problem-free team
The models make leadership of the team unnecessary
The models ensure the team never reaches the storming stage
The models fix the project's budget and schedule automatically
Leadership.w: The models guide team development and role balance but do not guarantee a problem-free team; leadership is still required.

Leadership.q: How does setting clear and achievable objectives for team members influence their performance?
o: It removes any need for the leader to monitor progress
It transfers accountability for delivery entirely to the team
It guarantees that no risks will affect their work
It gives them focus and a shared sense of direction, improving performance
Leadership.w: Clear, achievable objectives focus effort and give direction, which lifts individual and team performance.

Leadership.q: A team leader gives regular, specific and constructive feedback to team members. What effect is this most likely to have?
o: It reduces the leader's own accountability for the outcome
It fixes the project's deployment baseline permanently
It helps members improve and sustains strong performance
It removes the need for any recognition or reward
Leadership.w: Regular constructive feedback helps team members learn and adjust, sustaining and improving their performance.

Leadership.q: How can appropriately delegating authority and trusting team members influence a project team's performance?
o: It always slows delivery because decisions take longer
It removes the leader's responsibility for the results
It can increase ownership and motivation, improving output
It prevents team members from developing new skills
Leadership.w: Appropriate delegation builds ownership and motivation, which tends to improve the team's output.

Leadership.q: A project leader actively removes obstacles and provides the resources their team needs. How does this influence performance?
o: It replaces the need for a project management plan
It transfers the project's risks onto the team members
It reduces the sponsor's interest in the project
It enables the team to work more effectively and maintain momentum
Leadership.w: Clearing obstacles and supplying resources lets the team work without interruption, supporting effective performance.

Leadership.q: How can a leader who communicates a clear and compelling vision of the goal influence team performance?
o: It removes the need to communicate progress to stakeholders
It reduces the clarity of individual responsibilities within the team
It can raise motivation and a sense of purpose, improving performance
It guarantees the project will finish ahead of its schedule
Leadership.w: A clear, compelling vision gives the team purpose and motivation, which tends to improve its performance.

Leadership.q: A team leader coaches members to build the skills their roles require. How does this most likely influence performance?
o: It strengthens capability and confidence, improving future output
It shifts accountability for the benefits to operations
It removes the need to plan the project schedule
It makes the team dependent on external suppliers
Leadership.w: Coaching develops skills and confidence, raising the team's capability and its future performance.

Leadership.q: How can a project leader who consistently models the standards and behaviours they expect influence their team?
o: It guarantees that no conflict will ever arise
It removes the need for any team ground rules
It transfers leadership responsibility to the team
It sets a clear example that encourages similar behaviour and effort
Leadership.w: Leading by example sets the standard others follow, encouraging the behaviour and effort that support performance.

Leadership.q: How can a leader who addresses conflict within the team promptly and fairly influence performance?
o: It restores focus and cooperation, protecting performance
It transfers responsibility for morale to the sponsor
It removes the need to hold any team meetings
It guarantees that the project will meet its budget
Leadership.w: Handling conflict promptly and fairly restores cooperation and focus, protecting the team's performance.

Leadership.q: How does adapting leadership style to the team's needs and maturity help influence its performance?
o: It removes the requirement to set any objectives
It provides the right level of support and direction to keep the team effective
It hands day-to-day control to the project sponsor
It ensures the team never needs feedback again
Leadership.w: Adapting style to the team's maturity gives the appropriate balance of support and direction, sustaining effective performance.

Leadership.q: In the context of a project, how is the term 'leadership' best defined?
o: The set of fixed procedures the team is required to follow
The act of allocating tasks to individuals and doing nothing further
The ability to inspire, guide and influence a team towards its goals
The formal chart that shows the project's reporting lines
Leadership.w: Leadership is the ability to establish vision and direction, and to inspire and influence people to achieve the project's goals.

Leadership.q: How can a project leader most effectively influence the performance of their team?
o: By focusing only on individual tasks rather than the shared goals
By taking every decision alone without seeking any input from others
By limiting communication so that the team can work undisturbed
By setting clear objectives, offering support and giving constructive feedback
Leadership.w: Leaders raise performance by clarifying objectives, supporting the team and using constructive feedback to develop individuals.

Leadership.q: Conflict and disagreement emerge as a newly formed team begins working together. Which Tuckman stage does this describe?
o: Storming
Forming
Performing
Norming
Leadership.w: In Tuckman's model, storming is the stage where interpersonal conflict and challenges to direction typically arise.

Leadership.q: You assign members to behavioural roles such as Coordinator, Plant and Completer Finisher. Which model are you applying?
o: Belbin's team roles
PESTLE analysis
Tuckman's stages of team development
Maslow's hierarchy of needs
Leadership.w: Belbin's model identifies behavioural team roles, such as Coordinator and Plant, that contribute to a balanced, effective team.

Leadership.q: Two team members are in dispute and trust must be rebuilt before work can resume. Which leadership capability is most needed?
o: Conflict management
Scope definition
Quality assurance
Resource levelling
Leadership.w: Conflict management enables a leader to address disagreements constructively and rebuild the trust needed for the team to perform.
